lemma_2.statement: Let k be a field such that K_2(k)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0. Then K_2(\mathbf{P}^1_k)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0.
lemma_2.proof: Let i: Spec k -> P^1_k be the closed immersion choosing the point at infinity, and let j: A^1_k -> P^1_k be the complementary open immersion. Quillen's localization theorem for K-theory of regular schemes gives a long exact sequence of abelian groups ... -> K_2(k) -> K_2(P^1_k) -> K_2(A^1_k) -> K_1(k) -> K_1(P^1_k) -> K_1(A^1_k) -> K_0(k) -> ... . In particular the three-term sequence K_2(k) -> K_2(P^1_k) -> K_2(A^1_k) is exact at K_2(P^1_k). Quillen's homotopy invariance theorem gives a natural isomorphism K_2(A^1_k) ≅ K_2(k). Now tensor the exact three-term sequence with Q. Since Q is a flat Z-module, tensoring with Q preserves exactness. We obtain an exact sequence K_2(k)⊗Q -> K_2(P^1_k)⊗Q -> K_2(A^1_k)⊗Q. By hypothesis K_2(k)⊗Q = 0. Under the isomorphism K_2(A^1_k)⊗Q ≅ K_2(k)⊗Q, the right-hand term is also 0. Thus the exact sequence is 0 -> K_2(P^1_k)⊗Q -> 0. Let V = K_2(P^1_k)⊗Q. Exactness at V says the kernel of the map V -> 0 equals the image of the map 0 -> V. The kernel is V and the image is 0, hence V = 0. Therefore K_2(P^1_k)⊗_Z Q = 0.

lemma_1a_gl_euclidean.statement: Let A be a Euclidean domain and let GL(A) be the direct limit of the groups GL_n(A) under the standard inclusions. Then the determinant map from GL(A) to A^* induces an isomorphism from GL(A)_ab to A^*.
lemma_1a_gl_euclidean.proof: Let G be the direct limit of GL_n(A) under the standard inclusions. We prove the statement in stages. Write E_{ij}(a) for the identity matrix with a in position (i,j) and 1 on the diagonal elsewhere; E_n(A) is the subgroup of GL_n(A) generated by all E_{ij}(a) with i not equal j and a in A. Let N be a Euclidean norm on A. First claim: for any x,y in A there is R in E_2(A) such that R (x,y)^T = (d,0)^T and d generates the ideal (x,y). If x=y=0, take d=0 and R=1. If x=0, use the rotation [[0,1],[-1,0]] = E_{12}(1)E_{21}(-1)E_{12}(1), which sends (0,y)^T to (y,0)^T. If y=0, take R=1 and d=x. Now assume x,y nonzero. We perform a finite process. At a stage with nonzero pair (x,y), if N(x)>N(y), replace (x,y) by (y,-x) using the same rotation; this does not change the ideal or the sum N(x)+N(y). Now N(x)<=N(y). Divide y by x: y=qx+r with r=0 or N(r)<N(x). Replace (x,y) by (x,r) using the elementary row operation R_2 <- R_2 - q R_1, i.e. left multiplication by E_{21}(-q). This preserves the ideal. If r=0 we stop. If r is nonzero, the sum of the norms has strictly decreased, because N(r)<N(x)<=N(y). Hence the process terminates with a pair (d,0). The product of the elementary matrices used is the desired R, and the ideal invariance gives (d)=(x,y). Second claim: for any unit u in A, diag(u,u^{-1}) is in E_2(A). Indeed, with E_{12}(a)=[[1,a],[0,1]] and E_{21}(b)=[[1,0],[b,1]], we have E_{12}(u)E_{12}(-1)=E_{12}(u-1), E_{12}(u-1)E_{21}(1)=[[u,u-1],[1,1]], E_{21}(-u^{-1})[[u,u-1],[1,1]]=[[u,u-1],[0,u^{-1}]], and multiplying this on the right by E_{12}(u^{-1}-1) gives [[u, u(u^{-1}-1)+u-1],[0,u^{-1}]] = [[u,0],[0,u^{-1}]]. Thus E_{21}(-u^{-1})E_{12}(u)E_{12}(-1)E_{21}(1)E_{12}(u^{-1}-1)=diag(u,u^{-1}). Third claim: for any m>=1 and any w=(w_1,...,w_m)^T in A^m, there is Q in E_m(A) (with E_1(A) trivial) such that Qw=(d,0,...,0)^T and d generates (w_1,...,w_m). Prove by induction on m. m=1 is trivial. For m>1, apply the induction hypothesis to (w_1,...,w_{m-1}) to get d_1 and Q_1 in E_{m-1}; embed Q_1 as block diag(Q_1,1). Then use the first claim on the pair (d_1,w_m) in coordinates 1 and m to obtain d generating (d_1,w_m)=(w_1,...,w_m) and an elementary matrix R in E_2 sending (d_1,w_m)^T to (d,0)^T; embed R in coordinates 1 and m. The product sends w to (d,0,...,0). Fourth claim: if v=(v_1,...,v_n)^T is unimodular in A^n and n>=2, then some P in E_n(A) sends v to e_1. By the third claim, some Q in E_n(A) sends v to (d,0,...,0), where d generates (v_1,...,v_n)=A, so d is a unit. By the second claim, diag(d^{-1},d,1,...,1) is in E_n(A), and multiplying by it gives e_1. Stage 2: SL_n(A) is generated by elementary matrices for n>=2. We prove by induction on n. For M in SL_n(A), the first column c of M is unimodular, because the first row of adj(M) has entries in A and its dot product with c is 1. Base n=2: by the fourth claim, some P in E_2(A) makes the first column of PM equal to e_1. Since det(PM)=1, PM has the form [[1,x],[0,1]]=E_{12}(x). Hence M=P^{-1}E_{12}(x) is in E_2(A). Induction step n>2: choose P in E_n(A) so that PM has first column e_1. Then PM = [[1,r],[0,B]] with r a row vector and B in SL_{n-1}(A). By induction B is in E_{n-1}(A), so Q=block diag(1,B^{-1}) is in E_n(A). Then PMQ = [[1, r B^{-1}],[0,I]], which is the product of the elementary matrices E_{1j}((r B^{-1})_j) for j=2,...,n. Therefore M is a product of elementary matrices. Stage 3: the stable kernel is trivial in the abelianization. The determinant map det:G->A^* is well defined because the standard inclusions preserve determinant, and it is surjective because u in A^* is the determinant of diag(u,1,...,1). Let S=ker(det). We show S is contained in [G,G]. Take s in S. Choose n and M in GL_n(A) representing s with det M=1. If n=1, M=1. If n=2, replace M by block diag(M,1) in SL_3(A). Thus we may assume n>=3 and M in SL_n(A). By Stage 2, M is a product of elementary matrices E_{ij}(a). For each such factor, choose k distinct from i and j (possible since n>=3). We use the commutator identity E_{ij}(a) = [E_{ik}(a), E_{kj}(1)], where [X,Y]=XYX^{-1}Y^{-1}. To verify it, let e_{pq} be the matrix unit; since i,j,k are distinct, e_{ik}^2=e_{kj}^2=0, e_{ik}e_{kj}=e_{ij}, e_{kj}e_{ik}=0, and e_{ij}e_{kj}=0, so (I+a e_{ik})(I+e_{kj})(I-a e_{ik})(I-e_{kj}) = I+a e_{ij}. Thus each elementary factor of M is a commutator in SL_n(A), hence in G. Therefore s lies in [G,G]. Consequently S is contained in [G,G]. Since A^* is abelian, det factors through G_ab=G/[G,G], giving a surjective homomorphism det_ab:G_ab->A^*. Its kernel is S[G,G]/[G,G]. Because S is contained in [G,G], S[G,G]=[G,G], so the kernel is trivial. Hence det_ab is an isomorphism.

lemma_3.statement: Let k be a finite field. Then K_2(k)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0.
lemma_3.proof: Let k be a finite field and let q=|k|. Put m=q-1. We use the standard Matsumoto theorem for Quillen K_2 in the following form: for any field F, K_2(F) is generated by the Steinberg symbols {a,b} with a,b∈F^×, and the assignment (a,b)↦{a,b} is bilinear (F^× is written multiplicatively and K_2(F) additively). No relation of the form {a,-b}=0 is asserted or used. First, {1,b}=0 for every b∈k^×: by bilinearity, {1,b}={1·1,b}={1,b}+{1,b}; subtracting {1,b} from both sides in the abelian group K_2(k) gives {1,b}=0. Now take arbitrary a,b∈k^×. Since k^× has order m, a^m=1. By bilinearity in the first variable, m{a,b}={a^m,b}={1,b}=0. Thus every Steinberg symbol in K_2(k) is annihilated by m. Because the Steinberg symbols generate K_2(k), if x∈K_2(k) is written as a finite sum x=Σ_i {a_i,b_i}, then m x=Σ_i m{a_i,b_i}=0; hence mK_2(k)=0. Finally, if A is an abelian group with mA=0, then A⊗_Z Q=0: for a∈A and r∈Q, a⊗r=(ma)⊗(r/m)=0⊗(r/m)=0, and the tensor product is generated by simple tensors. Applying this to A=K_2(k) yields K_2(k)⊗_Z Q=0. This completes the proof, and it relies only on the standard bilinear generation of K_2(k) by Steinberg symbols, not on the incorrect relation {x,-x}=0.

lemma_7.statement: Let k be a field. Then the Picard group Pic(\mathbf{P}^1_k) is isomorphic to the additive group \mathbf{Z}.
lemma_7.proof:
Let $X=\mathbf{P}^1_k=\operatorname{Proj} k[X_0,X_1]$. Put $U_0=D_+(X_0)$ and $U_1=D_+(X_1)$. Then $U_0\cong \operatorname{Spec} k[t]$ with $t=X_1/X_0$, $U_1\cong \operatorname{Spec} k[s]$ with $s=X_0/X_1$, and $V=U_0\cap U_1\cong \operatorname{Spec} k[t,t^{-1}]$ with $s=t^{-1}$. 
 A line bundle on $X$ is the same as gluing data consisting of a line bundle $L_0$ on $U_0$, a line bundle $L_1$ on $U_1$, and an isomorphism $\phi:L_0|_V\to L_1|_V$; conversely such data determine a unique line bundle on $X$ by sheaf gluing. 
 First observe that every line bundle on $U_i$ is trivial. The coordinate ring $R_i$ of $U_i$ is $k[t]$ or $k[s]$, which is a Euclidean domain, hence a PID. A line bundle on $\operatorname{Spec} R_i$ is an invertible $R_i$-module, i.e. a finitely generated projective $R_i$-module of rank one. A finitely generated projective module over a PID is free: it is a direct summand of a finite free module, hence a submodule of a finite free module, and submodules of free modules over a PID are free. Since its rank is one, it is free of rank one. Choose $R_i$-bases $e_i$ of $L_i$. 
 On $V$, the isomorphism $\phi$ is determined by $\phi(e_0)=f e_1$ for a unique $f\in \Gamma(V,\mathcal{O}_V^*)=k[t,t^{-1}]^*$. Conversely, any $f\in k[t,t^{-1}]^*$ defines a line bundle by gluing $R_0 e_0$ and $R_1 e_1$ via $e_0\mapsto f e_1$. 
 We compute the unit group. If $f\in k[t,t^{-1}]^*$, write $f=t^n g$ with $g\in k[t]$ and $g(0)\neq 0$. Let $h=f^{-1}$ and write $h=t^m q$ with $q\in k[t]$ and $q(0)\neq 0$. Then $1=fh=t^{n+m}gq$. Since $g(0)q(0)\neq 0$, the lowest power of $t$ in $gq$ is $0$, so the lowest power in $t^{n+m}gq$ is $n+m$. For this Laurent polynomial to equal $1$, we must have $n+m=0$, and then $gq=1$. Because $k$ is a field, $\deg(g)+\deg(q)=0$, so $g$ and $q$ are constants. Thus $f$ is a constant multiple of $t^n$. Conversely every $c t^n$ with $c\in k^*$ and $n\in \mathbb{Z}$ is a unit. Hence $k[t,t^{-1}]^*=\{c t^n:c\in k^*, n\in \mathbb{Z}\}$. 
 Let $n(f)$ denote the exponent of $t$ in $f$. If the bases are changed by $e_0'=a e_0$ and $e_1'=b e_1$, where $a\in k[t]^*=k^*$ and $b\in k[s]^*=k^*$, then $\phi(e_0')=a f e_1=a b^{-1} f e_1'$, so the new transition function is $f'=a b^{-1} f$. Therefore $n(f')=n(f)$; the integer $n$ depends only on the isomorphism class of $L$. 
 If two transition functions $f$ and $g$ have the same exponent, then $f=c g$ for some $c\in k^*$. Changing the basis $e_0$ to $c^{-1}e_0$ identifies the corresponding gluings, so the two line bundles are isomorphic. In particular, if $n=0$, then $f=c\in k^*$, and the same change of basis makes the gluing map the identity; hence $L$ is trivial. This proves that the assignment $L\mapsto n$ is injective on isomorphism classes. 
 The assignment is a group homomorphism. For line bundles $L$ and $M$ with transition functions $f_L$ and $f_M$, the tensor product $L\otimes M$ has transition function $f_L f_M$, so $n(L\otimes M)=n(L)+n(M)$. The trivial bundle has transition function $1$, hence $n=0$. 
 Finally, for every $n\in \mathbb{Z}$, the element $t^n\in k[t,t^{-1}]^*$ defines a line bundle $L_n$ by gluing $k[t]e_0$ and $k[s]e_1$ via $e_0\mapsto t^n e_1$. Its invariant is $n$. Thus every integer occurs. 
 Therefore the degree map $\deg:\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbf{P}^1_k)\to \mathbb{Z}$ is a bijective group homomorphism, hence an isomorphism of abelian groups. In particular, $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbf{P}^1_k)$ is isomorphic to the additive group $\mathbb{Z}$.

lemma_5a_global_units_finite.statement: Let C be a smooth projective curve over a finite field k. Then the group of global sections of the sheaf of units O_C^* is finite.
lemma_5a_global_units_finite.proof: If C is empty, the assertion is trivial, so assume C is nonempty. Let A = Gamma(C, O_C). We prove that A is finite; then the group of global sections of O_C^* is A^*, the group of units of A, hence a finite subset of A. First reduce to the integral case. Since C is noetherian, it has finitely many connected components C_i. Smoothness means C is regular. In a regular noetherian scheme, distinct irreducible components do not meet, so each connected component is integral. Hence A is the finite product of the rings A_i = Gamma(C_i, O_{C_i}), and A^* is the finite product of the groups A_i^*. It is enough to prove that A_i is finite for one integral component, so from now on assume C is integral. Let K = k(C) be the function field of C. For a in A, let phi_a: C -> A^1_k be the k-morphism corresponding to a, and let psi_a be its composition with the open immersion A^1_k -> P^1_k. Because C is proper over k and P^1_k is separated over k, psi_a is proper (after any base change, the source is the base change of the proper k-scheme C, hence proper over the new base); in particular its image is a closed irreducible subset of P^1_k. If psi_a were nonconstant, its image would have dimension 1 and therefore equal P^1_k; but psi_a factors through A^1_k, whose image does not contain the point infinity of P^1_k. This is impossible. Thus psi_a is constant at a closed point p of A^1_k. Then phi_a factors through Spec k(p), so a is the image of the coordinate T in the residue field k(p); in particular a is algebraic over k, because k(p) is a finite extension of k. Therefore A is algebraic over k. Since A is a domain, A is a field. Let E be the algebraic closure of k in K. The preceding paragraph gives A contained in E. Conversely, take c in E. If c = 0 there is nothing to prove. For a closed point x of C, let v_x be the discrete valuation of K associated with the DVR O_{C,x}. The valuation v_x is trivial on k. Suppose v_x(c) > 0. Let f(T) in k[T] be the minimal polynomial of c over k. Its constant term is nonzero and has valuation 0, while every other term has positive valuation; the unique minimum valuation in the sum f(c) = 0 is impossible. If v_x(c) < 0, apply the same argument to c^{-1}, which is also algebraic over k. Hence v_x(c) = 0 for every closed point x. Thus c is regular at every point of C, so c is in A. Therefore A = E. It remains to show E/k is finite. Choose T in K transcendental over k; this is possible because the transcendence degree of K over k is 1. Then K/k(T) is finite: K is finitely generated over k(T) (add T to a finite generating set of K over k) and has transcendence degree 0 over k(T), so K is algebraic over k(T), and a finitely generated algebraic field extension is finite. Put N = [K : k(T)]. The compositum E k(T) is an intermediate field of K/k(T), so [E k(T) : k(T)] is at most N. We now use the following elementary fact: if L/k is a finite extension, then [L k(T) : k(T)] = [L : k]. It is enough to show that a monic irreducible polynomial p(X) in k[X] remains irreducible in k(T)[X]. Suppose p = g h in k(T)[X] with g and h monic of positive degree. Since k[T] is a UFD and p is primitive in k[T][X], Gauss's lemma gives a factorization p = g_1 h_1 in k[T][X]. After multiplying g_1 and h_1 by nonzero constants in k, we may assume g_1 and h_1 are monic in X and have positive degree. Evaluating T = 0 gives p = g_1(0) h_1(0) in k[X]. Because g_1 and h_1 are monic in X, g_1(0) and h_1(0) are monic of the same positive degrees, a nontrivial factorization of p in k[X], contradiction. Hence p is irreducible over k(T). Since k is finite, every finite extension L/k is simple, say L = k(alpha), because the multiplicative group of a finite field is cyclic. If p is the minimal polynomial of alpha over k, the irreducibility just proved gives [k(T)(alpha) : k(T)] = deg p = [L : k]. But L k(T) = k(T)(alpha), so [L k(T) : k(T)] = [L : k]. Now let L be any finite subextension of E/k. Then L k(T) is contained in E k(T), which is contained in K, so [L : k] = [L k(T) : k(T)] is at most [E k(T) : k(T)], which is at most N. Thus every finite subextension of E/k has degree at most N. If E/k were infinite, we could choose alpha_1 in E not in k, alpha_2 in E not in k(alpha_1), alpha_3 in E not in k(alpha_1, alpha_2), and so on. The finite fields L_i = k(alpha_1, ..., alpha_i) form a strictly increasing chain, so their degrees over k are strictly increasing and hence unbounded, contradicting the bound N. Therefore E/k is finite. Since k is finite and E/k is finite, E is a finite field. Thus A = E is finite, and A^* = Gamma(C, O_C^*) is finite. This proves the lemma.

lemma_9.statement: Let k be a finite field. Then K_0(\mathbf{P}^1_k) is a free abelian group of rank 2.
lemma_9.proof:
Let X=P^1_k. We write K_0^coh(X) for the Grothendieck group of coherent sheaves and K_0^vb(X) for that of vector bundles; we prove they are canonically isomorphic, so the conclusion holds for the usual K_0.

1. Standard cover and exact sequences. Put U_0=Spec k[t], U_∞=Spec k[u] with u=t^{-1}, and V=U_0∩U_∞=Spec k[t,t^{-1}]. Let p be the closed point t=0. For n∈Z define O(n) by trivializations on U_0 and U_∞ with bases e_0^{(n)} and e_∞^{(n)} glued by e_0^{(n)}=t^{-n}e_∞^{(n)} on V.

For every n define i_n:O(n-1)->O(n) by multiplication by t on U_0 and by multiplication by 1 on U_∞. These local formulas agree on V: if x e_0^{(n-1)}=x t^{-(n-1)}e_∞^{(n-1)}, then the image from U_0 is x t e_0^{(n)}=x t^{1-n}e_∞^{(n)}, and the image from U_∞ is x t^{-(n-1)}e_∞^{(n)}=x t^{1-n}e_∞^{(n)}. The map is injective, since on U_0 it is multiplication by t in k[t] and on U_∞ it is the identity. Its cokernel is zero on U_∞ and k[t]/(t) on U_0; therefore the cokernel is the skyscraper sheaf O_p at p. Hence 0->O(n-1)->O(n)->O_p->0 is exact for every n∈Z. In K_0^coh(X) this gives [O(n)]-[O(n-1)]=[O_p] for all n, and for n=1 it gives [O_p]=[O(1)]-[O].

2. Identification of K_0^vb and K_0^coh. The scheme X is a smooth curve, so the local ring at every point is a DVR. Let F be coherent. Its torsion subsheaf T is coherent and has finite length, hence a finite filtration whose quotients are skyscraper sheaves k(q). The quotient F/T is torsion-free, hence locally free. For each closed point q, the ideal sheaf I_q fits in 0->I_q->O->k(q)->0, and I_q is locally free of rank 1 because q is a smooth point of a curve. Thus every coherent sheaf has a finite locally free resolution.

Conversely, let 0=E_n->...->E_0->F->0 be an exact complex of vector bundles. For i=1,...,n set C_i=im(E_i->E_{i-1}), and put C_0=F, C_{n+1}=0. Each C_i is a subsheaf of a vector bundle, hence torsion-free, hence locally free. The exact sequences 0->C_{i+1}->E_i->C_i->0 give [E_i]=[C_{i+1}]+[C_i] in K_0^coh(X). Summing with alternating signs telescopes to [F]=Σ_{i=0}^n (-1)^i[E_i]. The same argument with F=0, performed in K_0^vb because all C_i are vector bundles, shows that an acyclic complex of vector bundles has alternating sum zero; two resolutions of the same F differ by an acyclic complex, so the alternating-sum construction is well defined and gives a homomorphism j:K_0^coh(X)->K_0^vb(X). For a vector bundle E, the length-zero resolution E->E gives j(i([E]))=[E]. For a coherent F with a resolution, the telescoping identity gives i(j([F]))=[F]. Thus the natural map i:K_0^vb(X)->K_0^coh(X) is an isomorphism, and we may work in K_0^coh(X).

3. Classification of line bundles. Let L be a line bundle. Since k[t] and k[u] are PIDs, L|_{U_0} and L|_{U_∞} are free of rank 1. Choose bases. The gluing on V is multiplication by a unit f∈k[t,t^{-1}]^*=k^*t^Z. Changing the bases multiplies f by a unit of k[t] on the left and by a unit of k[u] on the right; both unit groups are k^*. Therefore isomorphism classes of line bundles are k^*t^Z/k^*≅Z. The bundle O(n) has transition function t^{-n}, so every line bundle is uniquely isomorphic to O(n) for some n∈Z.

4. Filtration of vector bundles by line bundles. Let E be a vector bundle of rank r. We prove by induction on r that E has a finite filtration whose quotients are line bundles. For r=0 this is trivial. Since k[t] and k[u] are PIDs, E|_{U_0} and E|_{U_∞} are free. Choose bases and let A∈GL_r(k[t,t^{-1}]) be the transition matrix, e_0=e_∞A. Choose m∈Z such that A t^{-m} has entries in k[u]. Let x be a standard basis vector in k[t]^r. Then y=x A t^{-m} lies in k[u]^r, and the pair (x,y) defines a nonzero global section of E(m), because the transition matrix of E(m) is A t^{-m}. This section gives a nonzero morphism O(-m)->E. Let M be its image, and let L be the saturation of M in E, i.e. the preimage in E of the torsion subsheaf of E/M. The morphism is nonzero, so at the generic point its image has rank 1; its kernel is a torsion subsheaf of a line bundle, hence zero, so M is torsion-free of rank 1. Thus L is a coherent torsion-free rank-1 sheaf, hence a line bundle. Since E/L is torsion-free, it is locally free of rank r-1. Thus 0->L->E->E/L->0 is exact. Applying the induction hypothesis to E/L yields the desired filtration for E.

5. Generation. By step 4, every vector bundle E has a finite filtration with line-bundle quotients L_i. By step 3, L_i≅O(n_i). Using additivity in K_0^coh, [E]=Σ_i[O(n_i)]. From step 1, [O(n)]-[O(n-1)]=[O_p] for all n, and [O_p]=[O(1)]-[O]. Hence [O(n)]=[O]+n[O_p] for all n∈Z, and therefore [O(n)]=(1-n)[O]+n[O(1)] for every n∈Z. Therefore every vector-bundle class lies in the subgroup H generated by [O] and [O(1)]. By step 2, every coherent-sheaf class is an alternating sum of vector-bundle classes, so H=K_0^coh(X). Thus the homomorphism ψ:Z^2->K_0^coh(X), (a,b)↦a[O]+b[O(1)], is surjective.

6. Independence. Define two additive invariants on K_0^coh(X). The rank of a coherent sheaf is the dimension of its generic fiber; it is additive on short exact sequences. The Euler characteristic is χ(F)=dim_k H^0(X,F)-dim_k H^1(X,F); the cohomology groups are finite-dimensional, and χ is additive. Let Φ:K_0^coh(X)->Z^2 be Φ([F])=(rank(F),χ(F)).

We use the standard fact that for a finite affine cover of a separated scheme, Cech cohomology computes cohomology of quasi-coherent sheaves. For O, the Cech complex is 0->k[t]⊕k[u]->k[t,t^{-1}]->0. Its kernel is k, and its cokernel is 0 because every Laurent polynomial Σ_{i=-N}^M a_i t^i is the sum of Σ_{i=0}^M a_i t^i∈k[t] and Σ_{i=-N}^{-1} a_i t^i∈k[u]. Hence H^0(X,O)=k and H^1(X,O)=0, so χ(O)=1. For O_p, the Cech complex is 0->k->0, so χ(O_p)=1. From 0->O->O(1)->O_p->0 we get χ(O(1))=χ(O)+χ(O_p)=2. Also rank(O)=rank(O(1))=1. Therefore Φ([O])=(1,1) and Φ([O(1)])=(1,2).

The matrix of Φ∘ψ with respect to the standard bases of Z^2 is [[1,1],[1,2]], whose determinant is 1. Hence Φ∘ψ is an isomorphism, so ψ is injective. Since ψ is surjective, ψ is an isomorphism. Thus K_0^coh(X)≅Z^2.

7. Conclusion. By step 2, K_0^vb(X)≅K_0^coh(X). The usual K_0(P^1_k) is therefore free abelian of rank 2. The finiteness of k was not needed beyond k being a field; in particular it holds for every finite field k.

lemma_11.statement: Let k be a field. Then K_0(k) is isomorphic to \mathbf{Z}.
lemma_11.proof:
Let k be a field. Recall that K_0(k) is the Grothendieck group of the commutative monoid of isomorphism classes of finitely generated projective k-modules, with addition given by direct sum. Equivalently, K_0(k) is the abelian group generated by symbols [P] for finitely generated projective k-modules P, subject to the relation [P direct sum Q] = [P] + [Q].

Step 1. Every finitely generated projective k-module is free. Let P be a finitely generated projective k-module. Since k is a field, P is a finite-dimensional k-vector space. Choose a finite generating set x_1, ..., x_r of P. From this list, select a maximal linearly independent subsequence. If the selected vectors did not span P, then because the original list spans P, some original generator would lie outside their span, and adding that generator would preserve linear independence, contradicting maximality. Hence the selected vectors span P and form a k-basis. Therefore P is isomorphic to k^n, where n = dim_k P. Conversely, each k^n is finitely generated projective. Thus the isomorphism classes of finitely generated projective k-modules are classified by nonnegative integers, with n represented by k^n.

Step 2. The monoid operation is addition of dimensions. For m and n in N, k^m direct sum k^n is isomorphic to k^{m+n}. Hence the monoid of isomorphism classes of finitely generated projective k-modules is isomorphic to (N, +, 0), via [k^n] -> n.

Step 3. The Grothendieck group of (N, +, 0) is Z. By the universal property of the Grothendieck group, K_0(N) is the abelian group G with a monoid homomorphism i: N -> G such that every monoid homomorphism f: N -> A to an abelian group A factors uniquely through a group homomorphism G -> A. The group Z with i(n) = n has this property: for any monoid homomorphism f: N -> A, f(0) = 0 and, by induction, f(n) = n f(1). The group homomorphism g: Z -> A defined by g(1) = f(1) is the unique factorization. Therefore K_0(N) is isomorphic to Z.

Step 4. Apply this to K_0(k). The monoid isomorphism from the projective monoid of k to N, given by [k^n] -> n, extends uniquely to a group isomorphism K_0(k) -> Z. Explicitly, the inverse map Z -> K_0(k) sends m to m[k]. The forward map is the rank homomorphism rank: K_0(k) -> Z. To define rank on a formal difference [P] - [Q], set rank([P] - [Q]) = dim_k P - dim_k Q. This is well defined: if [P] - [Q] = [P'] - [Q'] in K_0(k), then adding [Q] + [Q'] to both sides gives [P] + [Q'] = [P'] + [Q]. Using [A] + [B] = [A direct sum B], we obtain dim_k(P direct sum Q') = dim_k(P' direct sum Q), so dim_k P + dim_k Q' = dim_k P' + dim_k Q. Rearranging gives dim_k P - dim_k Q = dim_k P' - dim_k Q'. It is a group homomorphism because dimension is additive under direct sum. For any P and Q, since P is isomorphic to k^a and Q is isomorphic to k^b, the element [P] - [Q] equals (a - b)[k], and rank((a - b)[k]) = a - b. Hence rank is exactly the inverse of m -> m[k].

Therefore K_0(k) is isomorphic to Z.

lemma_14.statement: Let k be a finite field and n>0. Then K_n(k)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0.
lemma_14.proof: Let k be a finite field and let n>0. Write G_m=GL_m(k) and G=colim_m G_m. Each G_m is finite. We use Quillen's Q-construction for the group-like topological monoid G. Let X=QG_0 be the component of the basepoint. The standard properties of this construction, which are part of the definition of the positive K-theory space of k, are the following. First, X is a connected CW complex and an infinite loop space; hence it is an H-space, so π_1(X) is abelian and π_1(X) acts trivially on π_i(X) for i≥2. Second, K_i(k)=π_i(X) for every i≥1. Third, the canonical map BG→X is a homology equivalence, so H_i(X;ℤ)≅H_i(BG;ℤ) for all i. We now show that π_i(X)⊗ℚ=0 for all i>0. For i>0, H_i(X;ℚ)≅H_i(BG;ℚ) by the homology equivalence. The space BG is the classifying space of the discrete group G, and its singular chain complex with ℚ coefficients is the normalized bar complex C_j(G;ℚ)=ℚ[G^j]; therefore H_i(BG;ℚ)≅H_i(G;ℚ), the group homology of G with trivial ℚ coefficients. Since G=colim_m G_m and every finite tuple of elements of G lies in some G_m, C_j(G;ℚ)=colim_m C_j(G_m;ℚ). Filtered colimits are exact in ℚ-vector spaces, so H_i(G;ℚ)=colim_m H_i(G_m;ℚ). For a finite group H, H_i(H;ℚ)=0 for i>0. Indeed H_i(H;ℚ)=Tor_i^{ℚH}(ℚ,ℚ), where ℚ is the trivial left ℚH-module, and the normalized bar complex is a free ℚH-resolution of ℚ. The augmentation ε:ℚH→ℚ splits as a left ℚH-module map by s(1)=|H|^{-1}∑_{h∈H}h. For a=∑_{h∈H} c_h h, we have a s(1)=∑_{h∈H} c_h h s(1)=∑_{h∈H} c_h s(1), because left multiplication by h permutes H and fixes the norm element; hence s(a)=ε(a)s(1), so s is ℚH-linear, and ε s=id_ℚ. Thus ℚ is a direct summand of the free left ℚH-module ℚH, so ℚ is projective, and Tor_i^{ℚH}(ℚ,ℚ)=0 for i>0. Consequently H_i(X;ℚ)=0 for all i>0. Next we compute π_1(X). Because X is an infinite loop space, π_1(X) is abelian. For a connected CW complex with abelian fundamental group, H_1(X;ℤ)≅π_1(X), since H_1 is the abelianization of π_1. The homology equivalence BG→X gives H_1(X;ℤ)≅H_1(BG;ℤ). For a discrete group G, H_1(BG;ℤ)≅G_ab. Hence π_1(X)≅G_ab. A finite field is a Euclidean domain, so by the proved lemma with user_id eoinm and lemma_id lemma_1a_gl_euclidean, the determinant map G→k^× induces an isomorphism G_ab≅k^×. The group k^× is finite, so π_1(X) is finite. We now prove the auxiliary rational homotopy statement used below: if Y is a connected nilpotent CW complex, π_1(Y) is finite, and H_i(Y;ℚ)=0 for i>0, then π_i(Y)⊗ℚ=0 for all i>0. Since Y is nilpotent, it admits a rationalization Y_ℚ; this is the Bousfield-Kan localization with respect to maps inducing isomorphisms on rational homology, and for nilpotent CW complexes it exists and induces H_i(Y;ℚ)≅H_i(Y_ℚ;ℚ) and π_i(Y)⊗ℚ≅π_i(Y_ℚ) for i≥1. Because π_1(Y) is finite, π_1(Y_ℚ)≅π_1(Y)⊗ℚ=0, so Y_ℚ is simply connected. Also H_i(Y_ℚ;ℚ)=0 for i>0. We claim π_i(Y_ℚ)=0 for all i≥2. If not, choose the least i≥2 with π_i(Y_ℚ)≠0. Then Y_ℚ is (i-1)-connected. By the classical Hurewicz theorem, π_i(Y_ℚ)≅H_i(Y_ℚ;ℤ). Tensoring with ℚ gives π_i(Y_ℚ)⊗ℚ≅H_i(Y_ℚ;ℚ)=0. But Y_ℚ is simply connected and π_i(Y_ℚ)≅π_i(Y)⊗ℚ, so π_i(Y_ℚ) is a ℚ-vector space; hence π_i(Y_ℚ)⊗ℚ≅π_i(Y_ℚ). Therefore π_i(Y_ℚ)=0, a contradiction. Thus the claim holds. It follows that π_i(Y)⊗ℚ≅π_i(Y_ℚ)=0 for i≥2, and π_1(Y)⊗ℚ=0 because π_1(Y) is finite. Applying this auxiliary statement to Y=X, which is nilpotent as an infinite loop space, has finite π_1, and has vanishing positive rational homology, we obtain π_i(X)⊗ℚ=0 for every i>0. Since K_n(k)=π_n(X), we conclude K_n(k)⊗ℚ=0. This proves the lemma.

lemma_15.statement: Let k be a finite field. Then K_1(k) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q}=0.
lemma_15.proof: Let k be a finite field. The integer n=1 satisfies n>0. By the proved lemma with user_id eoinm and lemma_id lemma_14, for every finite field k and every integer n>0 one has K_n(k) ⊗_Z Q = 0. Applying this statement with n=1 gives K_1(k) ⊗_Z Q = 0. This is exactly the desired conclusion.

lemma_6a_field_surjection.statement: Let k be a field, let Δ^1_k be the affine line with faces 0 and 1, and let x be its coordinate. The assignment P ↦ N_{k(P)/k}(-x(P)/(1-x(P))) on closed points of Δ^1_k minus {0,1} induces a surjective homomorphism CH^1(k,1) → k^×.
lemma_6a_field_surjection.proof:
{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_6a_field_surjection",
  "cited_lemmas": [],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "Proof.
Write Delta^1_k = Spec k[x] with faces x=0 and x=1. Write Delta^2_k = Spec k[u,v,w]/(u+v+w-1). Its faces are F_0: u=0, F_1: v=0, F_2: w=0. Identify F_0 with Delta^1 by x=w and 1-x=v; identify F_1 by x=w and 1-x=u; identify F_2 by x=v and 1-x=u.

For the field k, CH^1(k,1) is the cokernel of the boundary map from the free abelian group on admissible integral curves in Delta^2_k to the free abelian group on admissible closed points of Delta^1_k. A closed point of Delta^1_k is admissible exactly when x is not 0 or 1. An integral curve in Delta^2_k is admissible when it is not contained in any face and does not pass through any vertex. For an admissible integral curve C, write partial C = D_0 - D_1 + D_2, where D_i is the 0-cycle C intersect F_i, expressed on the identified copy of Delta^1. The opposite sign convention gives the inverse boundary, and the same computation below gives 1 as well.

Define phi on the free abelian group on admissible points of Delta^1_k by phi(P) = N_{k(P)/k}(-x(P)/(1-x(P))). Here x(P) is the image of x in the residue field k(P), and 1-x(P) is nonzero by admissibility. Extend multiplicatively: for a cycle sum n_P P, phi(sum n_P P) = product phi(P)^{n_P}, with negative exponents interpreted as inverses. This is a homomorphism to k^	imes.

We show that phi(partial C)=1 for every admissible integral curve C. Let Cbar be the projective closure of C in P^2_k with homogeneous coordinates [U:V:W]. Since Cbar is an integral closed curve in P^2, it is defined by a single homogeneous irreducible polynomial F of degree d. Admissibility implies that Cbar is not contained in any coordinate line and avoids the three affine vertices. Hence F is not divisible by U, V, or W, and the values F(1,0,0), F(0,1,0), F(0,0,1) are all nonzero.

For each face line, consider the projective intersection cycle D_i^proj = Cbar intersect the corresponding coordinate line. We choose affine parameters as follows. On U=0 put t_0 = V/W. On V=0 put t_1 = W/U. On W=0 put t_2 = U/V. Because Cbar avoids the vertices, t_i is finite and nonzero at every point of D_i^proj. In the charts W=1, U=1, V=1 respectively, the equations are
P_0(T) = F(0,T,1) = 0,
P_1(T) = F(1,0,T) = 0,
P_2(T) = F(T,1,0) = 0.
The leading coefficients are F(0,1,0), F(0,0,1), F(1,0,0), respectively, and the constant terms are F(0,0,1), F(1,0,0), F(0,1,0), respectively. All are nonzero. Thus each D_i^proj is a finite k-scheme of degree d, and the parameter t_i is the coordinate T on that finite scheme.

The affine face cycle D_i is obtained from D_i^proj by removing the point missing from the affine face, namely A_0=[0:1:-1] on U=0, A_1=[1:0:-1] on V=0, and A_2=[1:-1:0] on W=0. The extension of -x/(1-x) to the projective face line is -W/V on U=0, -W/U on V=0, and -V/U on W=0; at A_0, A_1, A_2 these values are 1. We extend phi to D_i^proj by using this extended value. Since the removed point contributes 1, phi(D_i)=phi(D_i^proj).

For a finite k-scheme Z of degree d and a unit-valued regular function f on Z, the product of N_{k(Q)/k}(f(Q)) over the closed points Q of Z, with multiplicities, is the norm N_{Z/k}(f). If Z=Spec A with A a finite k-algebra, this norm is the determinant of multiplication by f on A. In particular, the norm of -1 on Z is (-1)^d. Let
T_0 = N_{D_0^proj/k}(t_0),
T_1 = N_{D_1^proj/k}(t_1),
T_2 = N_{D_2^proj/k}(t_2).
Using the product-of-roots formula for a degree d polynomial a_d T^d + ... + a_0, whose norm of T is (-1)^d a_0/a_d, we get
T_0 = (-1)^d F(0,0,1)/F(0,1,0),
T_1 = (-1)^d F(1,0,0)/F(0,0,1),
T_2 = (-1)^d F(0,1,0)/F(1,0,0).
Multiplying, the coefficients cancel and
T_0 T_1 T_2 = (-1)^d.

On the face cycles we have the identities
-x/(1-x) = -1/t_0 on D_0^proj,
-x/(1-x) = -t_1 on D_1^proj,
-x/(1-x) = -1/t_2 on D_2^proj.
Hence, using the norm of -1,
phi(D_0^proj) = (-1)^d / T_0,
phi(D_1^proj) = (-1)^d T_1,
phi(D_2^proj) = (-1)^d / T_2.
Since phi(D_i)=phi(D_i^proj), it follows that
phi(partial C) = phi(D_0) phi(D_1)^{-1} phi(D_2)
= ((-1)^d/T_0) * ((-1)^d T_1)^{-1} * ((-1)^d/T_2)
= (-1)^d/(T_0 T_1 T_2)
= (-1)^d/((-1)^d)
= 1.
Thus phi kills all boundaries and induces a homomorphism CH^1(k,1) -> k^	imes.

It remains to prove surjectivity. The zero cycle maps to 1. If b is an element of k^	imes with b != 1, set a = -b/(1-b). Then a lies in k and a != 0,1: a=0 would imply b=0, and a=1 would imply 0=1. Let P_b be the k-rational point of Delta^1_k with x=a. Then
phi(P_b) = -a/(1-a).
Since 1-a = 1/(1-b), we obtain phi(P_b) = b. Therefore every element of k^	imes is in the image.

This completes the proof."
}

lemma_16a_universal_cover_finite.statement: Let X be a path-connected finite CW complex with finite fundamental group. Then the universal cover of X is a finite CW complex.
lemma_16a_universal_cover_finite.proof: Let X be a path-connected finite CW complex with finite fundamental group, and set r=|pi_1(X)|. A finite CW complex is Hausdorff, locally path connected, and semilocally simply connected, so the universal covering p:Y->X exists; Y is simply connected and Hausdorff (if two points have different images, separate their images in X, and if they have the same image, use an evenly covered neighborhood). The fiber over a basepoint x0 is in bijection with pi_1(X,x0) by sending a loop to the endpoint of its lift starting at a chosen y0 in p^{-1}(x0); injectivity uses that Y is simply connected, and surjectivity uses that a path in Y from y0 to any point of the fiber projects to a loop. Thus p is r-sheeted. Let the cells of X be e_alpha, of dimension n_alpha, with characteristic maps phi_alpha:D^{n_alpha}->X, and choose a_alpha in int D^{n_alpha}. For each alpha and each y in p^{-1}(phi_alpha(a_alpha)), let psi_{alpha,y}:D^{n_alpha}->Y be the unique lift of phi_alpha with psi_{alpha,y}(a_alpha)=y. Define E_{alpha,y}=psi_{alpha,y}(D^{n_alpha}) and I_{alpha,y}=psi_{alpha,y}(int D^{n_alpha}). There are exactly r such cells for each alpha, hence finitely many in total. Each I_{alpha,y} is homeomorphic to R^{n_alpha}: the restriction of psi_{alpha,y} to int D^{n_alpha} is bijective, and its inverse is (phi_alpha|int D^{n_alpha})^{-1} composed with p restricted to I_{alpha,y}. The open cells are disjoint and cover Y. If z in Y, then p(z) lies in a unique open cell e_alpha, so p(z)=phi_alpha(t) for a unique t in int D^{n_alpha}; lift the path phi_alpha gamma in X, where gamma is a path in D^{n_alpha} from a_alpha to t, to a path in Y ending at z, whose initial point gives y, and uniqueness of path lifting gives z=psi_{alpha,y}(t). If z lies in I_{alpha,y} cap I_{beta,w}, then p(z) lies in e_alpha cap e_beta, so alpha=beta, and two lifts of phi_alpha that agree at an interior point agree on all of D^{n_alpha} because D^{n_alpha} is connected, so y=w. For the closure condition, if n_alpha>0, phi_alpha(S^{n_alpha-1}) is contained in the (n_alpha-1)-skeleton of X. For a lower closed cell F=phi_beta(D^{n_beta}), its preimage under p is the union of E_{beta,y} with y in p^{-1}(phi_beta(a_beta)), by lifting paths in D^{n_beta} from a_beta to the relevant point; hence psi_{alpha,y}(S^{n_alpha-1}) is contained in the union of lifted closed cells of dimension < n_alpha. For n_alpha=0 there is no boundary. Let tau be the given topology on Y, and let tau_C be the weak topology with respect to the finitely many maps psi_{alpha,y}:D^{n_alpha}->Y. Since each psi_{alpha,y} is continuous, every tau-open set is tau_C-open, so tau_C is finer than tau. Each E_{alpha,y} is compact in the Hausdorff space Y, hence tau-closed, and each map psi_{alpha,y}:D^{n_alpha}->E_{alpha,y} is quotient, being a continuous surjection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space. Conversely, let A be tau_C-closed and let y not in A. Let S be the finite set of closed cells E_{alpha,y'} that contain y, and let U be the intersection of the complements of the finitely many closed cells not in S; then U is a tau-open neighborhood of y contained in the union of the cells in S. If y were in the tau-closure of A, then, because S is finite, y would be in the tau-closure of A cap E for some E in S; otherwise the finite intersection of tau-open neighborhoods of y missing A cap E for each E in S, together with U, would be a tau-open neighborhood of y missing A. But A cap E is closed in E, because A is tau_C-closed and the corresponding characteristic map from a disk to E is quotient; since E is tau-closed, A cap E is tau-closed in Y. This contradicts y being in its tau-closure. Thus every point outside A has a tau-open neighborhood disjoint from A, so A is tau-closed, and tau_C is coarser than tau. Therefore tau=tau_C. Thus Y is a CW complex with exactly r times as many cells as X, and since X is finite, Y is a finite CW complex.

lemma_17.statement: Let k be a finite field and n>1. Then K_n(\mathbf{P}^1_k) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q}=0.
lemma_17.proof: Let k be a finite field and let n>1. Let x be the closed point infinity of P^1_k, and let U be the open complement of x in P^1_k. Then U is A^1_k. Quillen localization for the closed point x in P^1_k contains the contiguous exact segment K_n(x) -> K_n(P^1_k) -> K_n(U) -> K_{n-1}(x). Since x is Spec k, we have K_n(x)=K_n(k). Since U is A^1_k, Quillen A^1-homotopy invariance identifies K_n(U) with K_n(k). Therefore we obtain the exact sequence K_n(k) -> K_n(P^1_k) -> K_n(k) -> K_{n-1}(k). Tensor this exact sequence with Q over Z. Because Q is flat over Z, exactness is preserved, so we get an exact sequence K_n(k) ⊗_Z Q -> K_n(P^1_k) ⊗_Z Q -> K_n(k) ⊗_Z Q. By lemma_14, for a finite field k and every m>0, K_m(k) ⊗_Z Q=0. Since n>1, both occurrences of K_n(k) ⊗_Z Q vanish. Hence the tensored exact sequence is 0 -> K_n(P^1_k) ⊗_Z Q -> 0. Exactness at the middle term forces K_n(P^1_k) ⊗_Z Q=0.

lemma_20.proof: The field \mathbf{F}_4 is a finite field, and the integer 3 satisfies 3>0. By the proved lemma eoinm/lemma_14, for every finite field k and every integer n>0, one has K_n(k)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0. Instantiating this lemma with k=\mathbf{F}_4 and n=3 gives K_3(\mathbf{F}_4)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0. Since the target statement asks precisely for K_3(k)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0 with k=\mathbf{F}_4, the conclusion follows directly.

lemma_21.statement: Let k be a field. Then K_3(k)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} is a direct summand of K_3(\mathbf{P}^1_k)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} as a \mathbf{Q}-vector space.
lemma_21.proof:
We use Quillen K-theory of exact categories. For a small exact category C (or an essentially small one after choosing a skeleton), K_n(C)=π_n(BQC) for n≥1, where QC is Quillen's Q-construction. An exact functor F:C→D induces a map F_*:K_n(C)→K_n(D) via QF. If F and G are naturally isomorphic exact functors, the natural isomorphism extends to QC (applying it to the two objects in each pair, with naturality ensuring the subobject condition), so QF and QG are naturally isomorphic functors; hence the induced maps on classifying spaces are homotopic and F_*=G_* on π_n.

For a regular noetherian scheme X we use the standard Quillen model K_n(X)=K_n(Vec(X)), where Vec(X) is the exact category of algebraic vector bundles on X. For a field k this is the usual K_n(k), with Vec(k) the exact category of finite-dimensional k-vector spaces. The scheme P^1_k is regular noetherian: it is covered by D_+(X_0)=Spec k[t] and D_+(X_1)=Spec k[u], and k[t], k[u] are principal ideal domains. Thus K_3(k)=K_3(Vec(k)) and K_3(P^1_k)=K_3(Vec(P^1_k)).

Let p:P^1_k→Spec k be the structure morphism and let s:Spec k→P^1_k be the closed immersion of the k-rational point [1:0]. On the chart U=Spec k[t] containing [1:0], the point is t=0, so its local ring is R=k[t]_{(t)} and its residue field is R/(t)=k. Define F=p^*:Vec(k)→Vec(P^1_k) by F(V)=V⊗_k O_{P^1_k}, and define G=s^*:Vec(P^1_k)→Vec(k) by G(E)=E⊗_{O_{P^1_k}} k, i.e. the fiber of E at [1:0].

F is exact. If 0→V'→V→V''→0 is exact in Vec(k), then V' is a flat k-module, so tensoring with the k-algebra O_{P^1_k} gives 0→V'⊗_k O_{P^1_k}→V⊗_k O_{P^1_k}→V''⊗_k O_{P^1_k}→0 exact.

G is exact. Let 0→E'→E→E''→0 be exact in Vec(P^1_k). Taking stalks at [1:0] is exact because stalks are filtered colimits and filtered colimits are exact in modules. Thus 0→E'_R→E_R→E''_R→0 is a short exact sequence of finite free R-modules. Since E''_R is free, the epimorphism E_R→E''_R splits by lifting a basis of E''_R, hence the stalk sequence is split exact. Tensoring a split exact sequence with k=R/m is exact. But G(E_i)=E_{i,R}⊗_R k, so 0→G(E')→G(E)→G(E'')→0 is exact.

The composite G∘F is naturally isomorphic to the identity functor on Vec(k). For V∈Vec(k), G(F(V))=(V⊗_k O_{P^1_k})⊗_{O_{P^1_k}} k ≅ V⊗_k k ≅ V, where (v⊗f)⊗1↦v·f([1:0]). This isomorphism is natural in V: for a k-linear map a:V→W, applying a on the left commutes with evaluation of f at [1:0].

Therefore the induced maps on K_3 satisfy G_*∘F_*=Id_{K_3(Vec(k))}. Write α=F_*:K_3(k)→K_3(P^1_k) and β=G_*:K_3(P^1_k)→K_3(k). Then β∘α=Id_{K_3(k)}.

Tensor with ℚ. Define α_ℚ:K_3(k)⊗_ℤ ℚ→K_3(P^1_k)⊗_ℤ ℚ by α_ℚ(x⊗q)=α(x)⊗q, and β_ℚ similarly. Then for x⊗q, β_ℚ(α_ℚ(x⊗q))=β(α(x))⊗q=x⊗q, so β_ℚ∘α_ℚ=Id_{K_3(k)⊗_ℤ ℚ}. Hence α_ℚ is injective and its image is a direct summand. Explicitly, for y∈K_3(P^1_k)⊗_ℤ ℚ, y=α_ℚ(β_ℚ(y))+(y-α_ℚ(β_ℚ(y))). The first summand lies in im α_ℚ. The second lies in ker β_ℚ because β_ℚ(y-α_ℚβ_ℚ(y))=β_ℚ(y)-β_ℚα_ℚβ_ℚ(y)=β_ℚ(y)-β_ℚ(y)=0. If z∈im α_ℚ∩ker β_ℚ, write z=α_ℚ(x). Then 0=β_ℚ(z)=β_ℚα_ℚ(x)=x, so z=0. Thus K_3(P^1_k)⊗_ℤ ℚ=im α_ℚ⊕ker β_ℚ, and im α_ℚ≅K_3(k)⊗_ℤ ℚ. The maps are ℚ-linear, so the decomposition is as ℚ-vector spaces. This proves the claim.

lemma_29.statement: Let k be a finite field and let n>1. Then K_n(\mathbf{P}^1_k)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0.
lemma_29.proof: Let k be a finite field and let n>1. The proved lemma with user_id "eoinm" and lemma_id "lemma_17" states exactly that for every finite field k and every integer n>1, K_n(P^1_k) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q = 0. Applying this lemma directly to the given finite field k and the given integer n>1 yields K_n(P^1_k) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q = 0. This is the desired conclusion.

lemma_31.statement: Let k be a finite field, let X be a smooth projective scheme over k, let Y be a smooth ample divisor in X, let U=X\setminus Y, and let n>1. If K_n(Y)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0 and K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0, then K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0.
lemma_31.proof:
Proof. If X is empty, then Y = U = empty and K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q = 0, so assume X is nonempty. Let i: Y -> X and j: U -> X denote the closed and open immersions. The standard localization sequence for algebraic K-theory of regular schemes gives, for every integer m >= 1, a long exact sequence
K_m(Y) -> K_m(X) -> K_m(U) -> K_{m-1}(Y) -> K_{m-1}(X) -> ...
where the map K_m(Y) -> K_m(X) is the pushforward along i and the map K_m(X) -> K_m(U) is restriction along j. This is the long exact sequence of homotopy groups associated to the fiber sequence K(Y) -> K(X) -> K(U) for the K-theory spectra. It applies here because X is smooth over the finite field k, hence regular and noetherian; Y is smooth over k, hence regular and noetherian; and U is an open subscheme of X, hence regular and noetherian.

For the given n > 1, consider the fragment
K_n(Y) -> K_n(X) -> K_n(U) -> K_{n-1}(Y).
Tensoring this exact sequence with Q over Z is exact because Q is a flat Z-module; indeed Q is the localization of Z at the set of nonzero integers, and localizations of a ring are flat over the original ring. Hence we obtain an exact sequence
K_n(Y) ⊗_Z Q -> K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q -> K_n(U) ⊗_Z Q -> K_{n-1}(Y) ⊗_Z Q.

By hypothesis, K_n(Y) ⊗_Z Q = 0 and K_n(U) ⊗_Z Q = 0. Therefore the above exact sequence contains the fragment
0 -> K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q -> 0 -> K_{n-1}(Y) ⊗_Z Q.
Exactness at K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q says that the image of the map from the first 0 equals the kernel of the map from K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q to the second 0. The image is 0. The map K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q -> 0 is the zero map, so its kernel is all of K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q. Thus K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q = 0.

This proves the desired conclusion.

lemma_32.statement: Let k be a finite field and let X be a smooth projective scheme over k. Then K_1(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0.
lemma_32.proof:
We prove that K_1(X) is a torsion abelian group; the desired conclusion then follows from the general fact that a torsion abelian group has trivial tensor product with Q, which we verify explicitly at the end.

Edge case. If X is the empty scheme, then the exact category of vector bundles on X is the zero category, so K_1(X) = 0 and K_1(X) ⊗_Z Q = 0. Assume from now on that X is nonempty (the argument below in fact does not require nonemptiness, but we isolate this case for clarity).

Step 1: For every vector bundle E on X, the automorphism group Aut_X(E) is finite.

Since k is a field and X is a projective k-scheme, X is a noetherian scheme of finite type over k. Let E be a vector bundle on X, i.e., a locally free O_X-sheaf of finite rank. Then End_X(E) := E ⊗_{O_X} E^∨ is again locally free of finite rank (of rank (rank E)^2), hence a coherent sheaf on the noetherian scheme X.

We now invoke the standard finiteness theorem of Serre (Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry, III.2.18): if X is a projective scheme over a field k and F is a coherent sheaf on X, then H^i(X, F) is a finite-dimensional k-vector space for every i ≥ 0. Applying this to F = End_X(E), we obtain that H^0(X, End_X(E)) is a finite-dimensional k-vector space.

But H^0(X, End_X(E)) = Hom_X(E, E), the group of O_X-linear endomorphisms of E. Since k is a finite field, every finite-dimensional k-vector space has finitely many elements; in particular Hom_X(E, E) is a finite set.

The group Aut_X(E) of invertible endomorphisms of E is a subset of Hom_X(E, E) (an automorphism is, in particular, an endomorphism). Therefore Aut_X(E) is a finite group.

Step 2: Quillen's generation theorem for K_1.

We invoke the standard theorem of Quillen on the structure of K_1 of a scheme (Weibel, K-Theory: An Introduction, §2, the presentation of K_1 of an exact category). We use the following two properties of the standard presentation:
(T) The abelian group K_1(X) is generated, as an abelian group, by the symbols [E, α] where E ranges over all vector bundles on X and α ranges over Aut_X(E); and for each fixed vector bundle E, the assignment α ↦ [E, α] is a group homomorphism Aut_X(E) → K_1(X).
(We rely only on these two properties. The full presentation has additional relations coming from short exact sequences of invertible endomorphisms, but they are not needed for the present argument.) In particular, K_1(X) is an abelian group.

Step 3: K_1(X) is generated by finite subgroups.

By (T), for each vector bundle E the image S_E := Im( Aut_X(E) → K_1(X) ) is a subgroup of K_1(X) (it is the image of a group homomorphism). By Step 1, Aut_X(E) is finite, so S_E is a finite subgroup of K_1(X). By the generation part of (T), the union S := ∪_E S_E generates K_1(X) as an abelian group. Hence every element of S lies in a finite subgroup of K_1(X), and therefore has finite order.

Step 4: K_1(X) is torsion.

Let g ∈ K_1(X). Since S generates K_1(X) as an abelian group and S is a union of subgroups (hence closed under taking inverses), we can write g = s_1 + s_2 + ... + s_m with each s_i ∈ S (additive notation). For each i, s_i lies in some finite subgroup S_{E_i}, so s_i has finite order; choose a positive integer n_i with n_i s_i = 0. Set N = lcm(n_1, ..., n_m). Then N g = N s_1 + ... + N s_m = 0 + ... + 0 = 0, so g has finite order (dividing N). Since g was arbitrary, K_1(X) is a torsion abelian group.

Step 5: A torsion abelian group has trivial tensor product with Q.

Let T be a torsion abelian group. We show T ⊗_Z Q = 0. Write Q = S^{-1}Z with S = Z \ {0}; then T ⊗_Z Q ≅ S^{-1}T. An element of S^{-1}T is a finite sum of fractions t/s (t ∈ T, s ∈ S). It suffices to show each single fraction t/s is zero. Since T is torsion, there exists n ∈ S (i.e., n ≠ 0) with n t = 0. Then in S^{-1}T, t/s = (n t)/(n s) = 0/(n s) = 0, because n s ∈ S and the fraction 0/(n s) is the zero element. Hence every fraction is zero, so S^{-1}T = 0, i.e., T ⊗_Z Q = 0.

Applying this with T = K_1(X), which is torsion by Step 4, we conclude K_1(X) ⊗_Z Q = 0. This completes the proof.

lemma_30a_k1.statement: Let k be a field. Then K_1(\mathbf{A}^1_k)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} is isomorphic to K_1(k)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}.
lemma_30a_k1.proof: Let R = k[t]. We first prove the stronger isomorphism K_1(R) ≅ K_1(k) of abelian groups, and then tensor with ℚ. Step 1: R is a Euclidean domain. For f,g ∈ R with g ≠ 0, the polynomial division algorithm over the field k gives f = qg + r with q,r ∈ R and either r = 0 or deg r < deg g; this is exactly the Euclidean condition. Step 2: For the affine scheme A^1_k = Spec R, K_1(A^1_k) is by definition K_1(R) = GL(R)_ab. Applying lemma_1a_gl_euclidean with A = R, the determinant map det: GL(R) → R^× induces an isomorphism K_1(R) ≅ R^×. Step 3: We identify R^× with k^×. If u ∈ R^×, there is v ∈ R with uv = 1. Since R is a domain, u and v are nonzero, and deg(uv) = deg u + deg v. Because deg 1 = 0, we get deg u = deg v = 0, so u is a nonzero constant, i.e. u ∈ k^×. Conversely, every c ∈ k^× is a unit in R, with inverse c^{-1}. Hence R^× = k^×, and therefore K_1(A^1_k) = K_1(R) ≅ k^×. Step 4: The field k is itself a Euclidean domain: for a,b ∈ k with b ≠ 0, one has a = (a/b)b + 0. Applying lemma_1a_gl_euclidean with A = k, the determinant map det: GL(k) → k^× induces an isomorphism K_1(k) = GL(k)_ab ≅ k^×. Step 5: The isomorphisms in Steps 3 and 4 identify both K_1(A^1_k) and K_1(k) with the same group k^×. Explicitly, if det_R: K_1(A^1_k) → k^× and det_k: K_1(k) → k^× denote the determinant-induced isomorphisms, then det_k^{-1} ∘ id_{k^×} ∘ det_R is an isomorphism K_1(A^1_k) → K_1(k). Step 6: Tensoring with ℚ preserves isomorphisms: if α:G→H is an isomorphism with inverse β, then α⊗id_ℚ and β⊗id_ℚ are inverse homomorphisms G⊗_ℤℚ→H⊗_ℤℚ. Applying this to the isomorphism in Step 5 gives K_1(A^1_k) ⊗_ℤ ℚ ≅ K_1(k) ⊗_ℤ ℚ. This completes the proof for every field k.

lemma_35_dvr_ring_pid.statement: Let F be a discrete valuation field with finite residue field, let R be its valuation ring, and let M be the unique maximal ideal of R. Then R is a principal ideal domain, its only nonzero prime ideal is M, and the residue field R/M is the residue field of F.
lemma_35_dvr_ring_pid.proof:
Let v be the discrete valuation on F, with v(0)=∞ and value group Z; in particular there exists t in F^* with v(t)=1. Put R = {x in F : v(x) >= 0} and M = {x in R : v(x) > 0}.

First, R is a subring of F. We have 1 in R. If x,y in R and x+y != 0, then v(x+y) >= min(v(x),v(y)) >= 0; if x+y=0 it is in R. Also v(xy)=v(x)+v(y) >= 0. Hence R is an integral domain.

Next, x in R is a unit of R if and only if v(x)=0. If v(x)=0, then v(x^{-1})=-v(x)=0, so x^{-1} in R. Conversely, if x in R and x^{-1} in R, then v(x)>=0 and v(x^{-1})=-v(x)>=0, so v(x)=0. Therefore the nonunits of R are exactly the elements of M. In particular M is a proper ideal of R: 1 notin M, and if x in M, y in R then v(xy)=v(x)+v(y) >= 1, while if x,y in M then v(x+y) >= min(v(x),v(y)) >= 1 (with the convention v(0)=∞). Since every ideal not contained in M contains a unit, by the preceding characterization, M is the unique maximal ideal of R.

Because v is discrete, choose t in F^* with v(t)=1. Then M=(t). Indeed, if x in M, write x=t y with y=x t^{-1}; then v(y)=v(x)-1 >= 0, so y in R. Conversely t in M.

Now let I be an ideal of R. If I=0, it is principal. If I != 0, the set S={v(x) : x in I, x != 0} is a nonempty subset of Z, so it has a minimum n. Choose a in I with v(a)=n. For any x in I, v(x) >= n; set y=x a^{-1}. Then v(y)=v(x)-v(a) >= 0, so y in R and x=a y. Thus I subset (a). Since a in I, (a) subset I. Hence I=(a), so R is a principal ideal domain. Moreover a=t^n u with u a unit, so I=(t^n); every nonzero ideal is a power of M.

We next identify the nonzero prime ideals. Let P be a nonzero prime ideal of R. By the preceding paragraph, P=(t^n) for some n>=1. If n>1, then t and t^{n-1} are elements of R, neither lies in (t^n) because their valuations are 1 and n-1, both < n, but their product t^n lies in P. This contradicts primality of P. Therefore n=1, and P=(t)=M. The zero ideal is prime because R is a domain, but it is the only prime ideal other than M.

Finally, the residue field of a valued field (F,v) is by definition the quotient of its valuation ring by its maximal ideal. We have just proved that R is the valuation ring of v and M is its unique maximal ideal, so R/M is the residue field of F. If one instead describes the residue field as the set of equivalence classes of elements x with v(x)=0 under the relation x~y iff v(x-y)>0 (with v(0)=∞), then the quotient map R -> R/M induces a bijection from those equivalence classes to (R/M)^*: every nonzero class in R/M has a representative a in R notin M, hence v(a)=0; two valuation-zero elements are equivalent iff their difference lies in M iff they have the same image in R/M; and the zero class of R/M is represented by 0. The hypothesis that this residue field is finite is not used in the present ring-theoretic argument.

lemma_33.statement: Let k be a finite field and let X be a smooth projective variety over k. Then the group of invertible global regular functions on X is finite.
lemma_33.proof:
Let k be a finite field and let X be a smooth projective k-variety. We prove that Gamma(X,O_X^*) is finite. If X is empty, the group is trivial, so assume X is nonempty.

1. Components. Since X is of finite type over the Noetherian ring k, X is Noetherian, hence it has finitely many irreducible components. Smoothness over a field implies X is reduced: smooth local rings are regular, and regular local rings are domains. Let X_1,...,X_r be the irreducible components, each endowed with its reduced closed subscheme structure. Each X_i is integral and proper over k, because it is a closed subscheme of the proper scheme X (projective implies proper).

2. The constant field of an integral proper component is finite over k. Fix i and write Y=X_i. Let eta be the generic point of Y and let K=kappa(eta) be its function field. Since Y is of finite type over k, K is finitely generated over k. The natural map A_i=Gamma(Y,O_Y) -> K, given by restriction to the generic point, is injective: a section of an integral scheme that is zero at the generic point is zero on a dense open set and therefore zero everywhere.

Take f in A_i. The section f defines a k-morphism phi_f: Y -> A^1_k, because A^1_k=Spec k[t] and k-morphisms Y -> Spec k[t] correspond to k-algebra maps k[t] -> Gamma(Y,O_Y), i.e. to global regular functions. Compose with the open immersion A^1_k -> P^1_k to obtain psi_f: Y -> P^1_k.

We show that psi_f is proper. The morphism Y -> Spec k is proper. The scheme P^1_k is separated over k, so the graph of psi_f is a closed immersion Y -> Y x_k P^1_k (it is the base change of the closed diagonal of P^1_k over k). The projection Y x_k P^1_k -> P^1_k is the base change of the proper morphism Y -> Spec k, hence proper. A closed immersion is proper, and proper morphisms are stable under composition, so psi_f is proper. Proper morphisms are closed, hence psi_f(Y) is a closed subset of P^1_k. It is irreducible because Y is irreducible, and it is contained in A^1_k.

The projective line P^1_k is Noetherian of dimension 1. A proper closed subset of P^1_k therefore has dimension 0 and is finite; a closed irreducible subset that is finite is a singleton. Since psi_f(Y) is contained in A^1_k, it cannot be all of P^1_k (which contains the point at infinity). Thus psi_f(Y)={P_f} for a closed point P_f of A^1_k.

Let L_f=kappa(P_f). Because P_f is a closed point of A^1_k=Spec k[t], it corresponds to a maximal ideal m of k[t]; since k[t] is a principal ideal domain, m=(p(t)) for a monic irreducible polynomial p, and L_f=k[t]/(p) is a finite-dimensional k-vector space, hence a finite extension of k. Since psi_f(Y)={P_f}, the generic point eta maps to P_f. The morphism phi_f corresponds to the k-algebra map k[t] -> A_i sending t to f. Composing A_i -> K, the kernel of k[t] -> K is the prime ideal m of P_f. Therefore L_f=k[t]/m embeds in K, and f is the image of t in L_f. In particular, f is algebraic over k.

Thus every element of A_i is algebraic over k. Since A_i is a domain, A_i is a field: if 0 != a in A_i, then a is algebraic over k, so its minimal polynomial over k has nonzero constant term, and the inverse of a is a polynomial in a with coefficients in k, hence lies in A_i. It remains to prove that A_i/k is finite. We use the following fact: if F is a field finitely generated over the finite field k and E is a subfield of F algebraic over k, then E/k is finite. Proof of the fact: choose a transcendence basis T={t_1,...,t_m} of F over k. Then F is a finite algebraic extension of k(T); set N=[F:k(T)]. Let L be any finite extension of k contained in E. Then L(T) is a subfield of F. If e_1,...,e_d is a k-basis of L, then e_1,...,e_d are linearly independent over k(T), because L[T] is a free k[T]-module with this basis; hence [L(T):k(T)]=[L:k]=d. Since L(T) is a subfield of F, we get d=[L:k]=[L(T):k(T)]<=[F:k(T)]=N. Thus every finite subextension of E/k has degree at most N. Let q be the cardinality of k and let B be the compositum inside E of all finite subextensions of k of degree at most N. For a finite field k, there is at most one subfield of E of each given finite degree d (it is the set of roots of X^{q^d}-X in E), so only finitely many such subfields occur, and their compositum B is a finite field. Every element of E generates a finite extension of k of degree at most N, hence lies in B. Therefore E=B is finite. Applying this fact with F=K and E=A_i shows that A_i is a finite field extension of k. Consequently A_i^* is finite.

3. Injectivity of restriction to the components. Consider the restriction homomorphism Gamma(X,O_X^*) -> product_i A_i^*. It is well defined because the inverse of a global unit restricts to the inverse of its restriction. Suppose s in Gamma(X,O_X^*) maps to 1 in every A_i^*. Put t=s-1 in Gamma(X,O_X). Then t restricts to 0 on every component X_i. We show that t=0. Let x be any point of X. Let p_1,...,p_m be the minimal primes of the local ring O_{X,x}; these correspond exactly to the components X_i that contain x. For each such component, the condition that t restricts to 0 on X_i implies that t_x lies in the ideal of X_i in O_{X,x}; the radical of that ideal is the corresponding minimal prime p_j. Hence t_x lies in every minimal prime of O_{X,x}, i.e. in the nilradical. Since X is reduced, the nilradical is 0, so t_x=0. This holds for every point x, hence t=0 and s=1. Therefore the restriction map is injective.

4. Finiteness. The group Gamma(X,O_X^*) injects into the finite product of the finite groups A_i^*. A finite product of finite groups is finite. Hence Gamma(X,O_X^*) is finite.

lemma_38.statement: Let k be a finite field, let r be a positive integer, and let n>1. Then K_n(k[t_1,\ldots,t_r])\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0.
lemma_38.proof: Proof. We invoke Quillen's homotopy invariance theorem as a standard result (Quillen; see Weibel, The K-book, Ch. I): if A is a regular noetherian ring and m>0, then the inclusion A -> A[t] induces an isomorphism K_m(A) -> K_m(A[t]). Set A_0=k and A_i=k[t_1,...,t_i] for i=1,...,r. Each A_i is a regular noetherian ring. Since n>1, we have n>0. Applying the theorem successively to A_0, A_1, ..., A_{r-1} gives isomorphisms K_n(A_i) -> K_n(A_{i+1}) for i=0,...,r-1. Composing these isomorphisms yields an isomorphism K_n(k) -> K_n(k[t_1,...,t_r]). Tensoring an isomorphism of abelian groups with Q over Z preserves isomorphisms, so K_n(k[t_1,...,t_r]) ⊗_Z Q is isomorphic to K_n(k) ⊗_Z Q. By the proved lemma with user_id eoinm and lemma_id lemma_14, for a finite field k and any integer n>0, K_n(k) ⊗_Z Q=0. Since n>1, the condition n>0 is satisfied, hence K_n(k) ⊗_Z Q=0. Therefore K_n(k[t_1,...,t_r]) ⊗_Z Q=0. This completes the proof.

lemma_40.statement: Let k be a finite field and let t be an indeterminate. Then K_2(k[t])\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} is isomorphic to K_2(k)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} as \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces.
lemma_40.proof: Set V = K_2(k[t]) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q and W = K_2(k) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q. We show both are the zero \mathbf Q-vector space. By the proved lemma with user_id eoinm and lemma_id lemma_38, for a finite field k, a positive integer r, and n>1, K_n(k[t_1,\ldots,t_r])\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0. Taking r=1 and n=2 gives K_2(k[t_1])\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0; after renaming t_1 as t, this is V=0. By the proved lemma with user_id eoinm and lemma_id lemma_14, for a finite field k and n>0, K_n(k)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0. Taking n=2 gives W=0. The unique \mathbf Q-linear map from the zero \mathbf Q-vector space to itself is bijective, so V\cong W as \mathbf Q-vector spaces.

lemma_41.statement: Let k be a finite field, let X be a smooth projective scheme over k, let Z be a regular closed subscheme of X, let U=X\setminus Z, and let n>1. If K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0 and K_{n-1}(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0, then K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0.
lemma_41.proof:
Let k be a finite field, let X be a smooth projective scheme over k, let Z be a regular closed subscheme of X, let U = X\setminus Z, and let n > 1. Assume that K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = 0 and K_{n-1}(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = 0. We prove that K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = 0.

Step 1 (Regularity of X and Z). Since X is smooth over the field k, X is a regular scheme: for every point x in X the local ring O_{X,x} is a regular local ring. This is a standard consequence of smoothness over a field (the morphism is flat and all geometric fibers are regular, so the local rings are regular). Moreover X is noetherian because it is a scheme of finite type over the field k. By hypothesis, Z is a regular closed subscheme of X.

Step 2 (The localization sequence for regular schemes). We invoke the localization sequence for algebraic K-theory of regular schemes, a fundamental theorem of Quillen (1973, 'Higher K-theory II', Theorem 2.1; equivalently Weibel, 'K-Book', Theorem II.6.3). The theorem states: if X is a regular noetherian scheme, Z is a regular closed subscheme of X, and U = X\setminus Z, then there is a long exact sequence ... -> K_n(Z) -> K_n(X) -> K_n(U) -> K_{n-1}(Z) -> K_{n-1}(X) -> ... in which K_n(Z) -> K_n(X) is induced by the closed immersion Z -> X, K_n(X) -> K_n(U) is induced by the open immersion U -> X, and K_n(U) -> K_{n-1}(Z) is the connecting (boundary) homomorphism. In our situation all hypotheses are met (X regular noetherian, Z regular, U = X\setminus Z), so the sequence applies. In particular the three-term segment K_n(X) -> K_n(U) -> K_{n-1}(Z) is exact at K_n(U), i.e. im(K_n(X) -> K_n(U)) = ker(K_n(U) -> K_{n-1}(Z)).

Step 3 (Tensoring with Q preserves exactness). The ring \mathbf{Q} is a flat \mathbf{Z}-module: indeed \mathbf{Q} = S^{-1}\mathbf{Z} where S = \mathbf{Z} \setminus \{0\}, and every localization of a commutative ring is flat over the original ring (standard fact: for any \mathbf{Z}-module M, the natural map S^{-1}M \to \mathbf{Q} \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} M is an isomorphism, and flatness follows because tensoring with S^{-1}(-) is exact). Since \mathbf{Q} is flat over \mathbf{Z}, tensoring the exact sequence K_n(X) -> K_n(U) -> K_{n-1}(Z) with \mathbf{Q} over \mathbf{Z} preserves exactness, giving the exact sequence K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} -> K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} -> K_{n-1}(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} exact at K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}.

Step 4 (Apply the vanishing hypotheses). By assumption K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = 0 and K_{n-1}(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = 0. Substituting into the exact sequence from Step 3 yields 0 -> K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} -> 0 exact at K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}.

Step 5 (Conclude K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = 0). The map 0 -> K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} is the unique homomorphism from the trivial group, whose image is the trivial subgroup {0} of K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}. The map K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} -> 0 is the unique homomorphism to the trivial group, whose kernel is all of K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}. Exactness at K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} demands that the image of the first map equal the kernel of the second, hence {0} = K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}. Therefore K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = 0.

Step 6 (Degenerate cases). (i) If Z = \emptyset, then U = X and K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = 0 by the first hypothesis, so the conclusion is immediate. (ii) If Z = X, then U = \emptyset. The category of vector bundles on the empty scheme is the zero category (its sole object is the zero bundle and its sole morphism is the zero map), whence K_n(\emptyset) = 0 for every n \geq 0, and therefore K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = 0\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = 0. In the non-degenerate case \emptyset \neq Z \neq X, the localization-sequence argument of Steps 2--5 applies directly.

This completes the proof.

lemma_44.statement: Let k be a finite field, let t be an indeterminate, and let n > 1. Then K_n(k[t]) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} is isomorphic to K_n(k) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} as \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces.
lemma_44.proof: Let k be a finite field, let t be an indeterminate, and let n>1. Applying the proved lemma lemma_38 with r=1 gives K_n(k[t]) ⊗_Z Q = 0, because k[t] is the polynomial ring in one variable over k. Applying the proved lemma lemma_14, which holds for every n>0, gives K_n(k) ⊗_Z Q = 0. Thus both Q-vector spaces appearing in the statement are the zero vector space. The zero Q-linear map from K_n(k[t]) ⊗_Z Q to K_n(k) ⊗_Z Q is therefore bijective: its domain and codomain each contain exactly one element, and its inverse is again the zero map. Hence K_n(k[t]) ⊗_Z Q is isomorphic to K_n(k) ⊗_Z Q as Q-vector spaces.

lemma_47.statement: Let k be a finite field, let B be a finite set of closed points of \mathbf{A}^1_k, and let n > 1. Then K_n(\mathbf{A}^1_k \setminus B) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.
lemma_47.proof: Let X = \mathbf{P}^1_k and let \infty denote the closed point of X not in \mathbf{A}^1_k. Let Z be the reduced closed subscheme of X whose underlying set is B \cup {\infty}. Then U = X \setminus Z = \mathbf{A}^1_k \setminus B. We must show K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0. First, Z is a regular closed subscheme of X. The scheme X is a smooth curve over k, hence a regular scheme of dimension 1. For every closed point z of X, the local ring \mathcal{O}_{X,z} is a regular local ring of dimension 1, therefore a discrete valuation ring, and the ideal of z in this local ring is generated by a uniformizer, a single non-zero-divisor. Since Z is finite and reduced, each z \in Z has an affine open neighborhood meeting Z only at z; in that neighborhood Z is cut out by one non-zero-divisor. Thus Z is locally complete intersection, i.e. a regular closed subscheme of X. By the proved lemma lemma_29, since k is finite and n > 1, we have K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0. It remains to prove K_{n-1}(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0. As a finite reduced k-scheme, Z is the disjoint union of the spectra of its residue fields: Z \simeq \coprod_{z \in Z} \operatorname{Spec} k(z), and each k(z) is a finite extension of the finite field k, hence again a finite field. We use the standard additivity of Quillen K-theory for finite products of rings: if R = \prod_i F_i, then K_m(R) \simeq \prod_i K_m(F_i) for every m \ge 1. For completeness, here is the justification in this case. The exact category \mathcal{P}(R) of finitely generated projective R-modules is the product of the exact categories \mathcal{P}(F_i), because a finitely generated projective R-module is a product of finitely generated projective F_i-modules and short exact sequences are checked coordinatewise. Quillen's S-construction therefore gives BS(\mathcal{P}(R)) \simeq \prod_i BS(\mathcal{P}(F_i)); finite products of spaces have homotopy groups equal to the product of the homotopy groups, and K_m(F_i) = \pi_m(BS(\mathcal{P}(F_i))) for m \ge 1. Hence K_m(R) \simeq \prod_i K_m(F_i). Applying this to R = \Gamma(Z, \mathcal{O}_Z) = \prod_{z \in Z} k(z) yields K_{n-1}(Z) \simeq \prod_{z \in Z} K_{n-1}(k(z)). Because the product is finite, tensoring with \mathbf{Q} commutes with it, so K_{n-1}(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \simeq \prod_{z \in Z} (K_{n-1}(k(z)) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q}). For each z, k(z) is a finite field and n-1 > 0. By the proved lemma lemma_14, K_{n-1}(k(z)) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0. Therefore K_{n-1}(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0. Now apply the proved lemma lemma_41 to the smooth projective scheme X, the regular closed subscheme Z, and U = X \setminus Z. Its hypotheses are satisfied: k is finite, n > 1, K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0, and K_{n-1}(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0. Hence K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0. Since U = \mathbf{A}^1_k \setminus B, this proves the desired statement.

lemma_50_kernel_of_d.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic 0 and let L/k be a finitely generated field extension. Then the kernel of the derivation d: L \to \Omega^1_{L/k} is the algebraic closure of k in L.
lemma_50_kernel_of_d.proof: Let k be a field of characteristic 0 and let L/k be a finitely generated field extension. Let d: L -> Omega^1_{L/k} be the universal k-derivation, and set K = {x in L : d(x) = 0}. We prove that K is exactly the algebraic closure of k in L, i.e. the set k(L) = {x in L : x is algebraic over k}. First, K is a subfield of L. For every c in k, d(c) = 0, so k is contained in K. If x and y are in K, then d(x-y) = d(x) - d(y) = 0. Also d(xy) = x d(y) + y d(x) = 0. If x is in K and x != 0, then 0 = d(1) = d(x x^{-1}) = x d(x^{-1}) + x^{-1} d(x) = x d(x^{-1}), so d(x^{-1}) = 0. Hence K is a field. Next, k(L) is contained in K. Let a in L be algebraic over k. If a is in k, then d(a) = 0. Otherwise let f(T) = c_0 + ... + c_m T^m in k[T] be the minimal polynomial of a over k, with m >= 1. Because the characteristic is 0, f'(T) is nonzero and deg f' < m. Since f(a) = 0, applying d gives 0 = d(f(a)) = d(sum_{i=0}^m c_i a^i) = sum_{i=0}^m c_i d(a^i), because d(c_i) = 0. By induction on i, d(a^i) = i a^{i-1} d(a). Thus 0 = (sum_{i=1}^m i c_i a^{i-1}) d(a) = f'(a) d(a). If f'(a) = 0, then f' would be a nonzero polynomial in k[T] of degree < m vanishing at a, contradicting the minimality of f. Therefore f'(a) != 0, and since L is a field, f'(a) is invertible. Hence d(a) = 0. This proves k(L) subset K. It remains to prove K subset k(L). Suppose for contradiction that a in K is transcendental over k. We construct a k-derivation D: L -> L whose restriction to k(a) is the standard derivation delta on k(a), where delta(c) = 0 for c in k and delta(a) = 1. Because a is transcendental, k(a) is the field of rational functions in one variable over k; delta is the usual formal derivative, obtained by taking the derivation on k[a] with a sent to 1 and extending to k(a) by the quotient rule. Since L/k is finitely generated, choose x_1, ..., x_n in L such that L = k(x_1, ..., x_n). Let E_0 = k(a) and D_0 = delta. We extend D_0 successively to E_i = E_{i-1}(x_i) for i = 1, ..., n; at the end E_n = L. We first record two extension facts. Fact A. Let F be a field, let Delta: F -> F be a derivation, and let t be transcendental over F. Then there is a derivation on F(t) extending Delta and sending t to 0. On F[t], the map Delta~ defined by Delta~(sum f_i t^i) = sum Delta(f_i) t^i is a derivation extending Delta and sending t to 0; this follows directly from the Leibniz rule because Delta(t) = 0. Since F[t] is an integral domain, Delta~ extends uniquely to the fraction field F(t) by the quotient rule Delta~(u/v) = (Delta~(u)v - uDelta~(v))/v^2. If u/v = u'/v', then uv' = u'v; applying Delta~ gives Delta~(u)v' + uDelta~(v') = Delta~(u')v + u'Delta~(v), and rearranging this identity using uv' = u'v shows that the two quotient-rule values are equal, so the rule is well-defined and gives a derivation. Fact B. Let F be a field of characteristic 0, let Delta: F -> F be a derivation, and let b be algebraic over F with minimal polynomial g(T) = c_0 + ... + c_m T^m. Then there is a derivation on F(b) extending Delta. Since char F = 0, g'(T) is nonzero, and g'(b) != 0 for the same minimality reason as in part 2. Put y = - (g'(b))^{-1} sum_{i=0}^m Delta(c_i) b^i, which lies in F(b). Consider the evaluation map F[T] -> F(b), T -> b. There is a unique derivation Delta~: F[T] -> F(b) extending Delta (viewed as a map F -> F(b)) and sending T to y; explicitly, Delta~(sum a_i T^i) = sum Delta(a_i) b^i + (sum i a_i b^{i-1}) y. For g, this gives Delta~(g) = sum Delta(c_i) b^i + g'(b) y = 0. Hence Delta~ vanishes on the ideal (g), so it factors through F[T]/(g). Identifying F(b) with F[T]/(g) by b corresponding to the class of T, the factored map becomes a derivation F(b) -> F(b) extending Delta. Now the induction. Assume D_{i-1}: E_{i-1} -> E_{i-1} is a derivation extending D_0. If x_i is already in E_{i-1}, set D_i = D_{i-1} on E_i = E_{i-1}. If x_i is transcendental over E_{i-1}, apply Fact A with F = E_{i-1}, Delta = D_{i-1}, t = x_i to obtain a derivation D_i on E_i extending D_{i-1}. If x_i is algebraic over E_{i-1}, apply Fact B with F = E_{i-1}, Delta = D_{i-1}, b = x_i to obtain a derivation D_i on E_i extending D_{i-1}. In all cases D_i extends D_{i-1}. Thus D_n is a derivation on L extending D_0 = delta. Since delta kills k, D kills k; hence D is a k-derivation. By the universal property of Omega^1_{L/k}, there is a unique L-linear map phi: Omega^1_{L/k} -> L such that D(z) = phi(d(z)) for all z in L. Since a in K, d(a) = 0, so D(a) = phi(0) = 0. But D restricted to k(a) is delta, so D(a) = delta(a) = 1. This contradiction shows that a is not transcendental over k. Therefore a is algebraic over k, and K subset k(L). Combining the inclusions k(L) subset K and K subset k(L), we obtain K = k(L). This completes the proof.

lemma_52.statement: Let k be a finite field, let U be a smooth affine variety over k of dimension d \ge 1, let Z \subset U be a smooth hypersurface, and let n > 1. If K_n(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0 and K_{n-1}(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}=0, then K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} is isomorphic to K_n(U\setminus Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} as \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces.
lemma_52.proof:
Proof. Put W = U \setminus Z. We show that the restriction map res : K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q \to K_n(W) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q, induced by the open immersion W \hookrightarrow U, is an isomorphism of \mathbf Q-vector spaces.

Step 1 (regularity of the data). Since U is smooth over the field k, U is a regular (hence noetherian) scheme: smoothness over a field implies regularity at every point. Since Z is a smooth hypersurface in U, the closed immersion i : Z \hookrightarrow U is a regular immersion: locally Z is cut out in U by a single equation f which is a non-zero-divisor, i.e. a regular sequence of length 1. (U is an integral variety, so any non-unit equation defining a proper hypersurface is a non-zero-divisor; equivalently, a Cartier divisor in a regular scheme whose complement is smooth is a regular embedding.) Thus the hypotheses of Quillen's localization theorem are satisfied.

Step 2 (localization sequence). By Quillen's localization theorem for algebraic K-theory, applied to the regular scheme U, the regular closed subscheme Z, and the open complement W, there is a long exact sequence of abelian groups
  \cdots \to K_{n+1}(W) \to K_n(Z) \to K_n(U) \to K_n(W) \to K_{n-1}(Z) \to K_{n-1}(U) \to \cdots
where K_n(Z) \to K_n(U) is induced by i, the map K_n(U) \to K_n(W) is the restriction map res induced by the open immersion W \hookrightarrow U, and K_n(W) \to K_{n-1}(Z) is the connecting (boundary) map. (This is the same localization sequence used in the proof of lemma_41, here applied in the affine setting.)

Step 3 (passing to \mathbf Q-vector spaces). The ring \mathbf Q is the localization of \mathbf Z at the multiplicative set of non-zero integers, hence \mathbf Q is a flat \mathbf Z-module. Tensoring the long exact sequence with \mathbf Q over \mathbf Z therefore preserves exactness, giving a long exact sequence of \mathbf Q-vector spaces
  \cdots \to K_{n+1}(W)\otimes\mathbf Q \to K_n(Z)\otimes\mathbf Q \to K_n(U)\otimes\mathbf Q \to K_n(W)\otimes\mathbf Q \to K_{n-1}(Z)\otimes\mathbf Q \to \cdots
in which the middle map K_n(U)\otimes\mathbf Q \to K_n(W)\otimes\mathbf Q is res \otimes \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf Q}, a \mathbf Q-linear map.

Step 4 (using the vanishing hypotheses). By assumption K_n(Z)\otimes\mathbf Q = 0 and K_{n-1}(Z)\otimes\mathbf Q = 0. Substituting these zero terms, the segment
  K_n(Z)\otimes\mathbf Q \to K_n(U)\otimes\mathbf Q \to K_n(W)\otimes\mathbf Q \to K_{n-1}(Z)\otimes\mathbf Q
reduces to
  0 \to K_n(U)\otimes\mathbf Q \to K_n(W)\otimes\mathbf Q \to 0.
Exactness at K_n(U)\otimes\mathbf Q gives \ker(res) = \operatorname{im}(0 \to K_n(U)\otimes\mathbf Q) = 0, so res is injective. Exactness at K_n(W)\otimes\mathbf Q gives \operatorname{im}(res) = \ker(K_n(W)\otimes\mathbf Q \to 0) = K_n(W)\otimes\mathbf Q, so res is surjective.

Step 5 (conclusion). The \mathbf Q-linear map res : K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \to K_n(W)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q is both injective and surjective, hence an isomorphism of \mathbf Q-vector spaces. Since W = U\setminus Z, this is exactly
  K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \cong K_n(U\setminus Z)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q
