(6) The sequence in (4) therefore reads 0 \to K_n(W_i)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \xrightarrow{g_i} K_n(W_{i+1})\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \to 0 and is exact at the two middle terms. Exactness at K_n(W_i)\otimes\mathbf Q gives \ker g_i = \mathrm{im}(K_n(Z_i)\otimes\mathbf Q \to K_n(W_i)\otimes\mathbf Q)=0, so g_i is injective. Exactness at K_n(W_{i+1})\otimes\mathbf Q gives \mathrm{im}\,g_i = \ker(K_n(W_{i+1})\otimes\mathbf Q \to K_{n-1}(Z_i)\otimes\mathbf Q)=K_n(W_{i+1})\otimes\mathbf Q (the last equality because the target is 0), so g_i is surjective. Hence g_i is an isomorphism of Q-vector spaces. This proves the claim.

Step 3 (composition). Compose the isomorphisms from the claim:
K_n(C)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q = K_n(W_0)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \xrightarrow{g_0} K_n(W_1)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \xrightarrow{g_1} \cdots \xrightarrow{g_{m-1}} K_n(W_m)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q = K_n(C\setminus S)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q.
Each g_i is the restriction map attached to the open immersion W_{i+1}\hookrightarrow W_i. By functoriality of Quillen K-theory with respect to composition of open immersions, the composite g_{m-1}\circ\cdots\circ g_1\circ g_0 : K_n(W_0)\to K_n(W_m) equals the restriction map attached to the composite open immersion C\setminus S = W_m \hookrightarrow W_0 = C; tensoring with the flat Z-module \mathbf Q commutes with taking this composite, so the displayed composite of the g_i is exactly j^*\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf Q} for j:C\setminus S\hookrightarrow C. A composition of isomorphisms is an isomorphism, so j^*\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf Q}: K_n(C)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \to K_n(C\setminus S)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q is an isomorphism of Q-vector spaces. Together with Step 1 this completes the proof.

lemma_87.statement: Let k be a finite field and let X be a smooth projective variety over k of dimension at least 1. Then there exists a finite separable extension k'/k such that X_{k'} has a nonempty smooth hyperplane section for some projective embedding over k'.
lemma_87.proof:
Let d = dim X >= 1. Let K be an algebraic closure of k. Since k is a finite field, every finite extension of k is separable; it suffices to find a finite extension k'/k.

1. Choose a very ample line bundle L on X. This exists because X is projective. Put V = H^0(X,L), a finite dimensional k-vector space. The complete linear system of L gives a closed immersion i: X -> P(V^*)_k. For any field extension F/k, base change gives a very ample line bundle L_F on X_F and a closed immersion i_F: X_F -> P(V_F^*)_F, where V_F = H^0(X_F,L_F) = V tensor_k F (cohomology and base change for projective morphisms).

2. Over K, set X_K = X times_k K. We prove that there is a nonzero section s of L_K whose zero scheme Y = V(s) is nonempty and smooth over K.

Let J^1(L_K) be the first jet bundle of L_K. Its fiber at a point x is the space of first jets of sections of L_K at x; since X_K is smooth of dimension d, this fiber has dimension d+1. For a section s and a point x, j^1_x(s)=0 iff s(x)=0 and the differential of s at x is zero.

The evaluation map ev_1: V_K tensor O_{X_K} -> J^1(L_K), sending a constant section of the trivial bundle to its first jet, is fiberwise surjective. Indeed, L_K is very ample, so i_K is a closed immersion. At a point x choose a section s_0 with s_0(x) not equal to 0. In the local trivialization by s_0, the remaining sections give local functions f_1,...,f_N whose values and differentials at x are the local coordinates of i_K near x. The value part gives the whole fiber L_K,x, and because i_K is an immersion the differentials df_1,...,df_N span the cotangent space (L_K,x) tensor Omega^1_{X_K/K,x}. Hence every first jet at x is obtained. Thus ev_1 is a surjection of vector bundles. Let E be its kernel; E is a vector bundle of rank r = dim V_K - (d+1).

Consider the subset Z = { (x, [s]) in X_K times P(V_K) : j^1_x(s)=0 } of X_K times P(V_K). The condition is homogeneous in s and is given by linear equations in the coordinates of s, so Z is closed. Its fiber over x is the projective space of lines in E_x, so Z is a projective bundle over X_K (empty if r=0) of relative dimension r-1 = dim V_K - d - 2. Therefore dim Z = d + dim V_K - d - 2 = dim V_K - 2 (with the convention that Z is empty when r=0). Let pi: Z -> P(V_K) be the second projection. Since Z is closed in the product of two projective K-varieties, pi is proper, and B = pi(Z) is a closed subset of P(V_K). By construction, B is exactly the set of sections [s] for which the zero scheme V(s) has a point at which the first jet vanishes, i.e. a singular point.

The ambient projective space P(V_K) has dimension dim V_K - 1. Hence dim B is at most dim Z = dim V_K - 2, so B is a proper closed subset. Choose [s] in the nonempty open complement U = P(V_K) minus B.

For this s, no point of X_K has j^1_x(s)=0. We show Y=V(s) is nonempty and smooth. If Y were empty, s would be nowhere vanishing and would trivialize L_K. But L_K is very ample, hence ample, and the trivial line bundle is not very ample on a positive-dimensional projective scheme: its complete linear system is given by global regular functions, which are constant on each connected component, so the associated morphism is constant on positive-dimensional components and cannot be a closed immersion. Thus Y is nonempty. Now take any y in Y. In a local trivialization of L_K near y, s corresponds to a regular function f with f(y)=0. The condition j^1_y(s) not equal to 0 means df_y not equal to 0. Since O_{X_K,y} is a regular local ring of dimension d, an element of the maximal ideal whose differential is nonzero is part of a regular system of parameters. Consequently O_{X_K,y}/(f) is a regular local ring of dimension d-1. By the hypersurface criterion (the Jacobian criterion), Y is smooth over K at y. Since y was arbitrary, Y is a nonempty smooth K-scheme of dimension d-1.

3. Descent to a finite extension. Write s as a K-linear combination of a k-basis of V: s = a_1 e_1 + ... + a_m e_m with a_i in K. Let k' be the finite subextension of K generated by the a_i. Since k is a finite field, k'/k is finite and separable. Then s lies in V_{k'} = H^0(X_{k'}, L_{k'}). Let H be the hyperplane in P(V_{k'}^*) corresponding to s, and let Y' = X_{k'} intersect H. By construction, the base change of Y' to K is exactly Y.

Smoothness descends under faithfully flat base change: K/k' is a field extension, hence faithfully flat, and (Y')_K = Y is smooth over K; therefore Y' is smooth over k'. If Y' were empty, its base change to K would be empty, contradicting that Y is nonempty. Hence Y' is nonempty.

The morphism i_{k'}: X_{k'} -> P(V_{k'}^*)_{k'} is a projective embedding, and Y' is the hyperplane section cut out by H. This gives the required finite separable extension k'/k and required smooth nonempty hyperplane section.

lemma_89.statement: Let k be a finite field, let k'/k be a finite separable extension, let X be a regular noetherian scheme over k, and let n > 0. Then the homomorphism K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \to K_n(X_{k'}) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} induced by the base change X \mapsto X_{k'} is injective.
lemma_89.proof: Let d = [k':k] and let f: X_{k'} → X be the projection. We prove that f^* is injective. Step 1. f is finite locally free of rank d and X_{k'} is regular noetherian. Since k' is a finite free k-module of rank d, Spec k' → Spec k is finite locally free of rank d; base change by X gives a finite locally free morphism f of rank d. Because k'/k is finite separable, Spec k' → Spec k is finite étale, hence f is finite étale. The scheme X_{k'} is noetherian because f is finite and X is noetherian. To see regularity, take an affine open U = Spec A of X and a point y of f^{-1}(U) = Spec B with B = A ⊗_k k', and let p ⊂ A and q ⊂ B be the corresponding primes. Let m_p and m_q be the maximal ideals of A_p and B_q. Then B_q is finite étale over A_p. Since B_q is finite over A_p, dim B_q = dim A_p. The quotient B_q / m_p B_q is a finite étale algebra over the field A_p / m_p, hence a product of finite separable field extensions; because B_q is local, this quotient is local, so it is a field and its maximal ideal is zero. Therefore m_q = m_p B_q. The ring A_p is regular, so m_p is generated by dim A_p elements. Their images generate m_p B_q = m_q, so m_q is generated by dim A_p = dim B_q elements. Thus B_q is a regular local ring. Since y was arbitrary, X_{k'} is regular. Step 2. The pushforward f_* O_{X_{k'}} is isomorphic to O_X^{⊕ d}. Choose a k-basis e_1, ..., e_d of k'. For every affine open U = Spec A ⊂ X, the restriction of f_* O_{X_{k'}} to U is A ⊗_k k', and the map A^{⊕ d} → A ⊗_k k', (a_i) ↦ Σ a_i ⊗ e_i, is an isomorphism of A-modules. These isomorphisms are compatible on overlaps because they use the same basis, so they glue to a global sheaf isomorphism f_* O_{X_{k'}} ≅ O_X^{⊕ d}. Consequently, in K_0(X), [f_* O_{X_{k'}}] = [O_X^{⊕ d}] = d [O_X]. Step 3. Apply the proved lemma with user_id eoinm and lemma_id lemma_58 to the finite locally free morphism f: X_{k'} → X of rank d. The hypotheses are satisfied: X and X_{k'} are regular noetherian, d ≥ 1, n > 0, and the class condition from Step 2 holds. Hence the composite f_* ∘ f^*: K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q → K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q is multiplication by d. Step 4. Let x ∈ K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q with f^*(x) = 0. Then d x = (f_* ∘ f^*)(x) = f_*(0) = 0. Since K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q is a Q-vector space and d is a positive integer, multiplication by d is injective; thus x = 0. Therefore f^* is injective.

lemma_90.statement: Let k be a finite field, let k'/k be a finite separable extension, let X be a regular noetherian scheme over k, and let n > 0. If K_n(X_{k'}) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0, then K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.
lemma_90.proof:
Let k be a finite field, let k'/k be a finite separable extension, let X be a regular noetherian scheme over k, and let n > 0. Assume K_n(X_{k'}) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0. We must show K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.

Step 1 (the base change map). Let \varphi: K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \to K_n(X_{k'}) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} denote the homomorphism of \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces induced by the base change morphism X_{k'} = X \times_k k' \to X (i.e., \varphi is the map on K-theory with rational coefficients induced by the structural morphism X \to \mathrm{Spec}\,k followed by the inclusion \mathrm{Spec}\,k \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Spec}\,k', equivalently the pullback along X_{k'} \to X). Since tensoring with \mathbf{Q} is exact, both K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} and K_n(X_{k'}) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} are \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces and \varphi is \mathbf{Q}-linear.

Step 2 (injectivity, via lemma_89). The hypotheses of the proved lemma (user_id "eoinm", lemma_id "lemma_89") are: k a finite field, k'/k a finite separable extension, X a regular noetherian scheme over k, and n > 0. These are precisely the hypotheses of the present statement, so lemma_89 applies and yields that \varphi is injective, i.e., \ker \varphi = \{0\}.

Step 3 (conclusion). Let v \in K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} be arbitrary. Its image \varphi(v) lies in the codomain K_n(X_{k'}) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q}, which is the zero vector space by hypothesis. Hence \varphi(v) = 0. Since \varphi is injective by Step 2, v \in \ker \varphi = \{0\}, so v = 0. As v was arbitrary, every element of K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} is zero, i.e., K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.

This completes the proof.

lemma_91.statement: Let k be a finite field and let F/k be a finitely generated field extension of transcendence degree 1. Let k_0 be the algebraic closure of k in F. Then there exists a smooth projective geometrically integral curve C over k_0 whose function field is F.
lemma_91.proof:
We prove the assertion in four steps.

Step 1. k_0 is a finite field. Let S={x_1,...,x_m} be a finite set of generators of F over k. Choose u\in F transcendental over k; such an element exists because trdeg_k F=1. Since k_0/k is algebraic, u is transcendental over k_0: if u were algebraic over k_0, it would be algebraic over k. Hence trdeg_{k_0} F=1 and F is algebraic over k_0(u).

First, F is finite over k(u). Indeed F=k(S) is generated over k(u) by the finite set S, and F is algebraic over k(u) because F is algebraic over k_0(u) and k_0(u) is algebraic over k(u). A field extension that is algebraic and finitely generated as a field extension is finite (Zariski's lemma), so [F:k(u)] is finite.

Second, F is finite over k_0(u). We have F=k_0(S), because k_0\subset F and S\subset F imply k_0(S)\subset F, while F=k(S)\subset k_0(S). This is algebraic and finitely generated over k_0(u), hence finite.

Now k(u)\subset k_0(u)\subset F. By the tower law for field degrees, [k_0(u):k(u)] is finite. If {e_i} is a k-basis of k_0 (possibly infinite), then the e_i are k(u)-linearly independent: a relation \sum_i e_i f_i(u)=0 with f_i(u)\in k(u) can be cleared of denominators to a relation \sum_i e_i g_i(u)=0 with g_i(u)\in k[u], and comparing coefficients forces every g_i(u)=0. Therefore [k_0(u):k(u)]\ge [k_0:k]. Since the left-hand side is finite, [k_0:k] is finite. As k is finite, k_0 is a finite field.

Step 2. Choose a separating variable. The field k_0 is finite, hence perfect. Since k_0/k is finite and F/k is finitely generated, F/k_0 is finitely generated. By construction k_0 is algebraically closed in F: if x\in F is algebraic over k_0, then x is algebraic over k, so x\in k_0. Since k_0 is perfect, every finitely generated extension of k_0 is separably generated (standard field-theoretic fact); as F/k_0 is finitely generated and k_0 is algebraically closed in F, F/k_0 is a regular extension. Hence there exists a separating transcendence basis; because trdeg_{k_0} F=1, it consists of one element t\in F, transcendental over k_0, such that F/k_0(t) is finite separable.

Step 3. An affine smooth model. Let R=k_0[t]. This is a principal ideal domain, hence a Dedekind domain. Let A be the integral closure of R in F. Because F/k_0(t) is finite separable, the standard integral closure theorem for Dedekind domains says that A is a finite R-module and is a Dedekind domain. Its fraction field is F.

Since A is finite over R, it is a finitely generated k_0-algebra: if a_1,...,a_s is a set of R-module generators of A, then A=k_0[t,a_1,...,a_s]. As a one-dimensional Noetherian integrally closed domain, A is regular. A regular scheme of finite type over a perfect field is smooth, so X=Spec A is a smooth affine curve over k_0 with function field F.

Moreover X is geometrically integral. We use the standard criterion: if B is a k_0-domain of finite type with fraction field L, then B is geometrically integral over k_0 whenever L/k_0 is regular. For completeness, if L/k_0 is regular then L\otimes_{k_0} k_0' is a domain for every field extension k_0'/k_0; since B\subset L and k_0' is flat over k_0, the map B\otimes_{k_0} k_0'\to L\otimes_{k_0} k_0' is injective, so B\otimes_{k_0} k_0' is a domain. Here B=A and L=F, and F/k_0 is regular as shown in Step 2.

Step 4. Projective smooth completion. Embed X as a closed subscheme of affine space \mathbf{A}^N_{k_0} using the finite generators of A. Let Y be the projective closure of X in \mathbf{P}^N_{k_0}. Then Y is an integral projective curve over k_0, X is a nonempty dense open subscheme of Y, and the function field of Y is F.

Let C be the normalization of Y in its function field F. For a projective integral curve, the normalization is finite and projective. Hence C is an integral projective curve over k_0 with function field F. Since C is normal and one-dimensional, it is regular; over the perfect field k_0 this implies C is smooth. Finally, C is a k_0-domain of finite type whose fraction field is F, and F/k_0 is regular; by the same criterion as in Step 3, C is geometrically integral.

Thus C is a smooth projective geometrically integral curve over k_0 whose function field is F.

lemma_94_milnor_K2_finite_field.statement: Let k be a finite field, and let K_2^M(k) be the abelian group generated by symbols {a,b} with a,b in k^*, subject to the relations {a,bc} = {a,b} + {a,c}, {ab,c} = {a,c} + {b,c}, and {a,1-a} = 0 for a in k^*, a \neq 1. Then K_2^M(k) = 0.
lemma_94_milnor_K2_finite_field.proof:
Let G=K_2^M(k) be the abelian group in the statement, written additively. Put q=|k| and n=q-1.

Step 1. Symbols with a 1 are zero. For any a,c in k^*, the relation {a,bc}={a,b}+{a,c} with b=1 gives {a,c}={a,1}+{a,c}; adding the inverse of {a,c} yields {a,1}=0. Similarly, the relation {ab,c}={a,c}+{b,c} with a=1 gives {b,c}={1,c}+{b,c}; hence {1,c}=0.

Step 2. The case q=2. Then k^*={1}, so the only generator is {1,1}. By Step 1, {1,1}=0, and G=0.

Step 3. The case q>2. Let H=k^*. We first show H is cyclic. Let e be the exponent of H, the least common multiple of the orders of all its elements. Every element of H satisfies x^e=1, so the polynomial T^e-1 over k has all n elements of H as roots; a nonzero polynomial of degree e over a field has at most e roots, hence n<=e. Also e divides n, because every element order divides n and the lcm of divisors of n divides n. Thus e=n. For each prime p dividing e, by definition of e there is some element of H whose order is divisible by p^{v_p(e)}; raising that element to the power obtained by removing the p-part gives an element h_p of order p^{v_p(e)}. The h_p commute and have pairwise coprime orders. Their product h has order e. Since each h_p has order dividing e, h^e=1, so the order m of h divides e. Let E_p=e/p^{v_p(e)}. If h^m=1, then h^{mE_p}=1. For q different from p, the order of h_q divides E_p, so h_q^{mE_p}=1; hence h_p^{mE_p}=1. Because E_p is coprime to p^{v_p(e)}, p^{v_p(e)} divides m. This holds for every p, so e divides m. Thus m=e. Therefore h has order n and generates H. Choose such a generator g.

Let x={g,g}. We claim that for all positive integers i,j, {g^i,g^j}=ij x. First, by induction on i using {ab,c}={a,c}+{b,c}, {g^i,g}=i x: the case i=1 is x, and {g^{i+1},g}={g^i g,g}={g^i,g}+{g,g}. Second, for fixed a and by induction on j using {a,bc}={a,b}+{a,c}, {a,g^j}=j{a,g}: the case j=1 is {a,g}, and {a,g^{j+1}}={a,g^j g}={a,g^j}+{a,g}. Taking a=g^i gives {g^i,g^j}=j{g^i,g}=j(i x)=ij x.

Since g^n=1, Step 1 gives {g^n,g}={1,g}=0. The formula with i=n,j=1 gives n x=0.

For each i=1,...,n-1, g^i is not 1. The element 1-g^i is nonzero, and it is not 1 because 1-g^i=1 would imply g^i=0. Hence 1-g^i lies in H and can be written uniquely as g^{k_i} with k_i in {1,...,n-1}. The Steinberg relation with a=g^i gives {g^i,1-g^i}=0, i.e. {g^i,g^{k_i}}=0. By the power formula, i k_i x=0 for every i=1,...,n-1.

The map i->k_i is a permutation of {1,...,n-1}. Indeed, the map t->1-t from H minus {1} to H minus {1} is bijective, with inverse itself; as t runs through the n-1 elements g^i (i=1,...,n-1), 1-t runs through the n-1 elements g^{k_i} in the same way.

Let D be the gcd of the integers n, k_1, 2k_2, ..., (n-1)k_{n-1}. The relations n x=0 and i k_i x=0 show that D x=0. We prove D=1. Suppose a prime ell divides D. Then ell divides n. For every i in {1,...,n-1} with ell not dividing i, we have ell | i k_i, hence ell | k_i. The number of such i is n - n/ell. Since i->k_i is a permutation, the corresponding k_i are distinct multiples of ell in {1,...,n-1}. The number of positive multiples of ell not exceeding n-1 is n/ell - 1. Therefore n - n/ell <= n/ell - 1, which is equivalent to ell(n+1) <= 2n. This is impossible for ell>=2, since ell(n+1) >= 2n+2. Thus no prime divides D, so D=1.

By Bezout's identity, there are integers u, v_1,...,v_{n-1} such that u n + v_1 k_1 + v_2 (2k_2)+...+v_{n-1}((n-1)k_{n-1})=1. Multiplying x by this identity and using n x=0 and i k_i x=0 for each i gives x=0.

Finally, take arbitrary a,b in H. Write a=g^i and b=g^j with i,j in {0,...,n-1}. If i=0 or j=0, then a=1 or b=1, and Step 1 gives {a,b}=0. If 1<=i,j<=n-1, the power formula gives {a,b}=ij x=0. Thus every generator of G is zero, so G=0. This completes the proof.

lemma_88_only_if.statement: Let k be a finite field and let Z be a smooth affine scheme of dimension at most 2 over k. If K_1(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0, then \mathcal{O}_Z^* is torsion.
lemma_88_only_if.proof: Let R = Gamma(Z, O_Z). Since Z is affine, we use the standard identification K_1(Z) = K_1(R) = GL_infty(R)/E_infty(R), where GL_infty(R) is the direct limit of GL_m(R) under A -> diag(A,1) and E_infty(R) is generated by elementary matrices. The determinant gives a homomorphism det: K_1(R) -> R^*, defined by det([A]) = det(A) for A in GL_m(R). It is well-defined because elementary matrices have determinant 1 and adding an identity block does not change the determinant. It is a homomorphism because det(AB) = det(A)det(B). The map i: R^* -> K_1(R), i(u) = [(u)] (the class of the 1x1 invertible matrix u), is a homomorphism and det(i(u)) = u. Hence det is surjective, so R^* is a quotient of K_1(R). Let A = K_1(R), B = R^*, and q = det. The hypothesis is A tensor_Z Q = 0. For any element b tensor r of B tensor_Z Q, choose a in A with q(a) = b. Then b tensor r = q(a) tensor r = (q tensor id_Q)(a tensor r) = 0, since a tensor r lies in A tensor_Z Q = 0. Therefore B tensor_Z Q = 0. We now show that B tensor_Z Q = 0 implies B is torsion. Let S be the set of nonzero integers; Q is the localization of Z at S, so B tensor_Z Q is canonically isomorphic to the localization of B at S, denoted B_S. Under this isomorphism, b tensor 1 corresponds to b/1. In a localization, b/1 = 0 if and only if there exists s in S with s b = 0: if b/1 = 0/1, then some t in S satisfies t b = 0; conversely, if s b = 0, then b/1 = 0/s. Since B_S = 0, b/1 = 0 for every b in B, so every b is annihilated by some nonzero integer. Thus B is torsion. Applying this to B = R^* = O_Z^* proves that O_Z^* is torsion. The assumptions that k is finite and that dim Z <= 2 are not needed for this direction; the argument works for any affine scheme.

lemma_97_milnor_K2_tame_symbol.statement: Let k be a finite field, let F=k((t)) with t-adic valuation v, and let K_2^M(F) be the abelian group generated by symbols {a,b} (a,b in F^*) subject to {ab,c}={a,c}+{b,c}, {a,bc}={a,b}+{a,c}, and {a,1-a}=0. For a,b in F^* write a=t^{v(a)}u_a and b=t^{v(b)}u_b with u_a,u_b in k[[t]]^*, and set ts({a,b})=(-1)^{v(a)v(b)} (u_a mod t)^{v(b)} (u_b mod t)^{-v(a)} in k^*, where (-1)^m is 1 if m is even and -1 if m is odd. Then ts is a surjective group homomorphism K_2^M(F) -> k^*.
lemma_97_milnor_K2_tame_symbol.proof: Let F^* be the multiplicative group of F. For z in F^* write z=t^{m_z}u_z with m_z=v(z) and u_z in k[[t]]^*, and set z_0 = u_z mod t in k^*. Define f: F^* x F^* -> k^* by f(x,y)=(-1)^{m_x m_y} x_0^{m_y} y_0^{-m_x}; powers with negative exponents are interpreted in the abelian group k^*. We first check the two bilinearity relations. For x,y,z in F^*, m_{xy}=m_x+m_y and (xy)_0=x_0 y_0 because the t-adic valuation is additive and reduction modulo t is a ring homomorphism k[[t]]^* -> k^*. Hence f(xy,z)=(-1)^{(m_x+m_y)m_z} (x_0 y_0)^{m_z} z_0^{-(m_x+m_y)} = (-1)^{m_x m_z}(-1)^{m_y m_z} x_0^{m_z} y_0^{m_z} z_0^{-m_x} z_0^{-m_y} = f(x,z) f(y,z). Similarly f(x,yz)=(-1)^{m_x(m_y+m_z)} x_0^{m_y+m_z} (y_0 z_0)^{-m_x} = (-1)^{m_x m_y}(-1)^{m_x m_z} x_0^{m_y} x_0^{m_z} y_0^{-m_x} z_0^{-m_x} = f(x,y) f(x,z). Now check the relation {a,1-a}=0. Let a in F^*, a != 1, and put y=1-a. If m_a>0, then y is a unit with y_0=1, so f(a,y)=(-1)^{m_a 0} a_0^0 1^{-m_a}=1. If m_a<0, write m=-m_a>0 and a=t^{-m}u with u_0=c in k^*. Then y=1-a=t^{-m}(t^m-u). The element t^m-u is a unit: its residue is -c, which is nonzero. Thus m_y=-m and y_0=-c. Therefore f(a,y)=(-1)^{(-m)(-m)} c^{-m} (-c)^m = (-1)^{m^2} (-1)^m = (-1)^{m^2+m}=1, since m^2+m=m(m+1) is even. If m_a=0, write a=u with u_0=c. If c=1, then u-1 has positive valuation, hence y=1-a has positive valuation, and f(a,y)=(-1)^0 c^{m_y} y_0^0=1. If c != 1, then y_0=1-c != 0, so m_y=0, and f(a,y)=(-1)^0 c^0 y_0^0=1. Thus f vanishes on all defining relations of K_2^M(F). Since K_2^M(F) is the quotient of the free abelian group on F^* x F^* by the subgroup generated by (xy,z)-(x,z)-(y,z), (x,yz)-(x,y)-(x,z), and (a,1-a), the checks above induce a unique group homomorphism ts: K_2^M(F) -> k^* with ts({x,y})=f(x,y). For surjectivity, let c in k^*. Take x=c (viewed as a constant element of F^*) and y=t. Then m_x=0, x_0=c, m_y=1, y_0=1, so ts({c,t})=f(c,t)=(-1)^0 c^1 1^0=c. Hence the image of ts contains every element of k^*, so ts is surjective. This completes the proof.

lemma_95.statement: Let k be a finite field, let X be a smooth projective variety over k, let D \subset X be a smooth very ample divisor, let U = X \setminus D, let n > 1, and suppose K_n(D)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q = 0 and K_{n-1}(D)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q = 0. Then the restriction homomorphism K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \to K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q is an isomorphism of \mathbf Q-vector spaces.
lemma_95.proof:
I have confirmed lemma_54. Now I have all the ingredients for a clean proof. Let me verify the hypotheses carefully:

- $X$ smooth projective over $k$ (a field) $\Rightarrow$ $X$ is regular noetherian (smooth over a field implies regular; projective over a noetherian ring implies noetherian).
- $D$ a smooth divisor in $X$ $\Rightarrow$ $D$ is a regular closed subscheme of $X$ (smooth over a field implies regular; a divisor is a closed subscheme).
- $U = X \setminus D$ is the open complement.
- $n > 1$ is given.

So lemma_54 applies with $(U, Z, V) = (X, D, U)$, giving the exact sequence
$$K_n(D)\otimes\mathbf{Q} 	o K_n(X)\otimes\mathbf{Q} 	o K_n(U)\otimes\mathbf{Q} 	o K_{n-1}(D)\otimes\mathbf{Q}.$$
The vanishing hypotheses kill the outer terms, making the middle map bijective; since it is $\mathbf{Q}$-linear, it is an isomorphism of $\mathbf{Q}$-vector spaces.

  "lemma_id": "lemma_95",
  "cited_lemmas": [

  ],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "We prove that the restriction homomorphism res: K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} is an isomorphism of \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces.

Step 1 (X is regular noetherian). Since k is a field, k is noetherian. The variety X is projective over k, hence of finite type over k, and therefore X is a noetherian scheme. Moreover, X is smooth over the field k; a scheme smooth over a field is regular (each local ring is a regular local ring, since smoothness implies the local rings are regular and flat over k, and k has regular local rings, i.e., fields). Thus X is a regular noetherian scheme.

Step 2 (D is a regular closed subscheme of X). By hypothesis D \subset X is a smooth divisor. A divisor in a scheme is a closed subscheme, so D is a closed subscheme of X. Since D is smooth over the field k, D is a regular scheme (same reasoning as in Step 1: smooth over a field implies regular). Hence D is a regular closed subscheme of X.

Step 3 (Apply the localization exact sequence). We invoke lemma_54 (user_id eoinm, lemma_id lemma_54), which states: let U be a regular noetherian scheme, let Z be a regular closed subscheme of U, let V = U \setminus Z, and let n > 1; then the sequence
K_n(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(V)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \to K_{n-1}(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}
induced by the inclusion and restriction maps is exact.

We apply lemma_54 with the following identifications: the regular noetherian scheme of lemma_54 is our X (Step 1); the regular closed subscheme Z of lemma_54 is our D (Step 2); the open complement V of lemma_54 is X \setminus D, which is exactly our U; and the integer n of lemma_54 is our n, which satisfies n > 1 by hypothesis. All hypotheses of lemma_54 are therefore met. The conclusion is that the sequence
K_n(D)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \xrightarrow{i^*} K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \xrightarrow{res} K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \xrightarrow{\partial} K_{n-1}(D)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}
is exact, where i^* is induced by the closed immersion i: D \hookrightarrow X, res is the restriction map induced by the open immersion U \hookrightarrow X, and \partial is the boundary map.

Step 4 (Injectivity of res). By hypothesis K_n(D)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = 0. Exactness of the sequence at K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} says that ker(res) = im(i^*). Since the domain of i^* is the zero \mathbf{Q}-vector space, im(i^*) = {0}. Therefore ker(res) = {0}, so res is injective.

Step 5 (Surjectivity of res). By hypothesis K_{n-1}(D)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} = 0. Exactness of the sequence at K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} says that im(res) = ker(\partial). Since the codomain of \partial is the zero \mathbf{Q}-vector space, ker(\partial) = K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} (the whole space). Therefore im(res) = K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}, so res is surjective.

Step 6 (res is \mathbf{Q}-linear). The restriction map res_0: K_n(X) \to K_n(U) on integral K-groups is a homomorphism of abelian groups (it is induced by the open immersion U \hookrightarrow X). Since such simple tensors span K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}, res is \mathbf{Q}-linear.

Step 7 (Conclusion). From Steps 4 and 5, res is a bijective homomorphism of abelian groups; from Step 6, res is \mathbf{Q}-linear. A bijective \mathbf{Q}-linear map between \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces is an isomorphism of \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces (its inverse is automatically \mathbf{Q}-linear: for the inverse res^{-1}, we have res^{-1}(v\cdot\lambda) = res^{-1}(res(res^{-1}(v)\cdot\lambda)) = res^{-1}(res(res^{-1}(v)))\cdot\lambda = res^{-1}(v)\cdot\lambda, using \mathbf{Q}-linearity of res). Hence res: K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} is an isomorphism of \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces, as required. (The 'very ample' hypothesis on D is not needed for this argument; it is part of the standing setup in which this lemma is used.)"
}

lemma_96.statement: Let k be a finite field, let d be a positive integer, and let t_1,\ldots,t_d be indeterminates. Then K_2(k[t_1,\ldots,t_d,t_d^{-1}])\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q = 0.
lemma_96.proof: Let R = k[t_1,...,t_d] and let A = R[t_d^{-1}] = k[t_1,...,t_d,t_d^{-1}]. Put U = Spec R, Z = V(t_d) = Spec R/(t_d), and V = U minus Z = Spec A. For affine schemes, K_n(Spec S) is K_n(S), so we may identify K_2(U) with K_2(R), K_2(V) with K_2(A), and K_1(Z) with K_1(k[t_1,...,t_{d-1}]), with the convention that for d=1 the coordinate ring of Z is k. The closed subscheme Z is regular because R is a polynomial ring over a field and t_d is a nonzerodivisor. Apply the localization exact sequence in lemma_54 with n=2 to the pair (U,Z). It gives an exact sequence K_2(Z) tensor_Z Q -> K_2(U) tensor_Z Q -> K_2(V) tensor_Z Q -> K_1(Z) tensor_Z Q. First, K_2(U) tensor_Z Q = 0 by lemma_38, since U is affine d-space over the finite field k and 2>1. Second, K_1(Z) tensor_Z Q = 0. For a commutative ring S, the standard determinant isomorphism gives K_1(S) = S^*. Hence K_1(Z) = (k[t_1,...,t_{d-1}])^*. If d=1, this is k^*. If d>=2, every unit of k[t_1,...,t_{d-1}] is constant: if f g = 1 and deg denotes total degree, then 0 = deg(1) = deg(fg) = deg(f)+deg(g), so deg(f)=deg(g)=0, and thus f is a nonzero constant. Therefore (k[t_1,...,t_{d-1}])^* = k^*. In both cases K_1(Z) is isomorphic to k^* = K_1(k), and by lemma_15, K_1(k) tensor_Z Q = 0. Thus K_1(Z) tensor_Z Q = 0. Returning to the exact sequence, the middle term K_2(U) tensor_Z Q is zero and the right term K_1(Z) tensor_Z Q is zero. Exactness at K_2(V) tensor_Z Q says that the kernel of the map K_2(V) tensor_Z Q -> K_1(Z) tensor_Z Q equals the image of K_2(U) tensor_Z Q -> K_2(V) tensor_Z Q. The image is zero because the domain is zero. The map to the zero group has kernel all of K_2(V) tensor_Z Q. Hence K_2(V) tensor_Z Q = 0. Since V = Spec A, this is exactly K_2(k[t_1,...,t_d,t_d^{-1}]) tensor_Z Q = 0.

lemma_72_rational_field.statement: Let k be a finite field, let t be an indeterminate over k, and let n > 1. Then K_n(k(t)) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q = 0.
lemma_72_rational_field.proof:
Now I have all the information I need. My proof will use a clean route via $\mathbb{P}^1_k$ and lemma_83, avoiding the need for the filtered colimit theorem (which isn't among the available lemmas).

**Plan:**
1. Let $C = \mathbb{P}^1_k$; its function field is $k(t)$.
2. Apply the localization sequence (lemma_54) to $U = C$, $Z = \{\infty\} = \mathrm{Spec}(k)$, $V = \mathbb{A}^1_k$.
3. The end terms $K_n(k)\otimes\mathbf{Q}$ and $K_{n-1}(k)\otimes\mathbf{Q}$ vanish by lemma_14, giving $K_n(\mathbb{P}^1_k)\otimes\mathbf{Q} \cong K_n(\mathbb{A}^1_k)\otimes\mathbf{Q}$.
4. $K_n(\mathbb{A}^1_k)\otimes\mathbf{Q} = K_n(k[t])\otimes\mathbf{Q} = 0$ by lemma_38 ($r=1$).
5. By lemma_83, $K_n(k(t))\otimes\mathbf{Q} \cong K_n(\mathbb{P}^1_k)\otimes\mathbf{Q} = 0$.

  "cited_lemmas": [

    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_14"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_38"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_83"}
  ],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "Let k be a finite field, let t be an indeterminate over k, and let n > 1. We prove K_n(k(t)) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.

Step 1 (setup). Let C = \mathbf{P}^1_k = \mathrm{Proj}(k[x_0,x_1]). We record the standard facts about C that we will use, with brief justifications:
  (a) C is a smooth projective curve over k. Smoothness: \mathbf{P}^1_k is the projective line, a smooth k-scheme (its homogeneous coordinate ring k[x_0,x_1] is regular, and \mathbf{P}^1_k is covered by the two standard affine charts \mathrm{Spec}(k) and \mathrm{Spec}(k[u]) with u = x_1/x_0, both regular). Projectivity: by definition, C = \mathrm{Proj}(k[x_0,x_1]) is projective over \mathrm{Spec}(k).
  (b) C is geometrically integral. Base change to the algebraic closure \bar{k} gives C_{\bar{k}} = \mathbf{P}^1_{\bar{k}} = \mathrm{Proj}(\bar{k}[x_0,x_1]). Since \bar{k}[x_0,x_1] is a polynomial ring over a field, it is an integral domain, and the Proj of a domain is an integral scheme. Hence C_{\bar{k}} is integral, so C is geometrically integral over k.
  (c) The function field of C is k(t). The open chart U_0 = D_+(x_0) \subset C is \mathrm{Spec}(k[x_1/x_0]) = \mathrm{Spec}(k[t]) with t = x_1/x_0. Since U_0 is a nonempty open subset of the integral scheme C, the function field k(C) equals the fraction field of \mathcal{O}(U_0) = k[t], namely k(t).

Step 2 (localization sequence). Let Z = {\infty} = V_+(x_0) \subset C be the closed point at infinity, i.e. Z = \mathrm{Spec}(k) via the quotient k[x_0,x_1]/(x_0) \cong k (with x_1 mapping to 1). Let V = C \setminus Z = D_+(x_0) = \mathrm{Spec}(k[t]) = \mathbf{A}^1_k.
We verify the hypotheses of the localization sequence (lemma_54):
  - U = C = \mathbf{P}^1_k is a regular noetherian scheme: C is a smooth projective curve over the field k, hence regular (the local ring at every point is a regular local ring, since C is nonsingular) and noetherian (a projective scheme over a noetherian ring is noetherian).
  - Z = \mathrm{Spec}(k) is a regular closed subscheme of U: Z is closed in C (it is the zero locus of the global section x_0 of \mathcal{O}_C(1)), and it is regular because its unique local ring is the field k, which is a regular local ring (equivalently, a field has Krull dimension 0 and the embedding dimension is 0).
  - V = U \setminus Z = \mathbf{A}^1_k.
  - n > 1 by hypothesis.
By lemma_54, the sequence
  K_n(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \longrightarrow K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \longrightarrow K_n(V) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \longrightarrow K_{n-1}(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q}
induced by the inclusion Z \hookrightarrow U and the restriction U \to V is exact. Substituting Z = \mathrm{Spec}(k), U = \mathbf{P}^1_k, V = \mathbf{A}^1_k, this reads
  K_n(k) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \longrightarrow K_n(\mathbf{P}^1_k) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \longrightarrow K_n(\mathbf{A}^1_k) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \longrightarrow K_{n-1}(k) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q}.   (\*)

Step 3 (vanishing of the end terms). By lemma_14, for every m > 0 we have K_m(k) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0. Since n > 1, we have n > 0, so K_n(k) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0. Also n - 1 \geq 1 > 0, so K_{n-1}(k) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.

Step 4 (isomorphism K_n(\mathbf{P}^1_k) \otimes \mathbf{Q} \cong K_n(\mathbf{A}^1_k) \otimes \mathbf{Q}). From the exact sequence (\*) and the vanishing in Step 3, the sequence
  0 \longrightarrow K_n(\mathbf{P}^1_k) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \longrightarrow K_n(\mathbf{A}^1_k) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \longrightarrow 0
is exact. Therefore the restriction map K_n(\mathbf{P}^1_k) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \to K_n(\mathbf{A}^1_k) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} is an isomorphism of \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces.

Step 5 (vanishing of K_n(\mathbf{A}^1_k) \otimes \mathbf{Q}). We have \mathbf{A}^1_k = \mathrm{Spec}(k[t]), so K_n(\mathbf{A}^1_k) = K_n(k[t]). By lemma_38 with r = 1 (the single indeterminate t_1 = t) and n > 1, we get
  K_n(k[t]) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.
Hence K_n(\mathbf{A}^1_k) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0, and by the isomorphism of Step 4,
  K_n(\mathbf{P}^1_k) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.   (\dagger)

Step 6 (passing from the curve to its function field). We apply lemma_83 with C = \mathbf{P}^1_k (a smooth projective geometrically integral curve over the finite field k, as established in Step 1(a) and 1(b)), F = k(C) = k(t) (its function field, as established in Step 1(c)), and n > 1. Lemma_83 states that the natural map
  K_n(C) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \longrightarrow K_n(F) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q}
is an isomorphism of \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces. Therefore
  K_n(k(t)) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \cong K_n(\mathbf{P}^1_k) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q}.
By (\dagger), the right-hand side is 0. Hence
  K_n(k(t)) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.

This completes the proof."
}

lemma_99_dvr_k_t_base.statement: Let k be a finite field, let f be a monic irreducible polynomial in k[t], let R = k[t]_{(f)}, and let n > 1. Then K_n(R) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q = 0.
lemma_99_dvr_k_t_base.proof: Let A = k[t]. The ring A is a PID because it is a Euclidean domain with Euclidean function given by polynomial degree. Since f is monic irreducible, (f) is a nonzero prime ideal of A. Let S be the multiplicative set of all elements of A not lying in (f), so R = S^{-1}A = A_{(f)}. First, R is a DVR. The localization R is a local ring with maximal ideal fR. It is a PID: if J is an ideal of R and I = J ∩ A, then J = S^{-1}I; indeed every element of J has the form a/s with a = sx ∈ I, and S^{-1}I ⊂ J is immediate. Since A is a PID, I = (g) for some g ∈ A, hence J = (g)R. Thus R is a local PID. It is not a field because fR is a nonzero proper ideal. In a local PID, let m = fR. Every nonzero element x of R is either a unit or lies in m. If x is not a unit, then x ∈ m, so x = f y. Because R is a PID, x has a finite factorization into irreducibles; in a local ring every irreducible lies in m, and if q ∈ m then q = f u for some u ∈ R, so irreducibility of q forces u to be a unit. Hence every irreducible is an associate of f, and x = u f^r for a unit u and a unique integer r ≥ 0. The uniqueness of r gives additivity on products, and the fact that the sum of a unit and an element of m is a unit gives the ultrametric inequality, so v(x) = r for x ≠ 0 and v(0) = ∞ is a discrete valuation whose valuation ring is R. Therefore R is a discrete valuation ring. Next, the fraction field of R is k(t). The natural map A → R identifies R with a subring of Frac(A) = k(t), so Frac(R) ⊂ k(t) and A ⊂ Frac(R). Take any element a/b of k(t) with a,b ∈ A and b ≠ 0. In the PID A, factor b with respect to the irreducible f: b = u f^m c, where u ∈ k^*, m ≥ 0, and c ∈ A is not divisible by f (equivalently c ∉ (f)); if f does not divide b, take m = 0 and c = b/u. Then u is a unit in R, c ∈ S so c is invertible in R, and f is nonzero in R so f is invertible in Frac(R). Hence b is invertible in Frac(R), and a/b ∈ Frac(R). Therefore Frac(R) = k(t). The residue field of R is finite. The maximal ideal is fR, and R/fR ≅ A/(f). To see this, in A/(f) every element of S is nonzero, hence a unit, so localizing A/(f) at S does not change it. Since f is monic irreducible over the finite field k, A/(f) = k[t]/(f) is a finite field extension of k, and therefore a finite field. Finally, R is essentially of finite type over k: A = k[t] is a finitely generated k-algebra, and R is a localization of A. Apply lemma_66 to the DVR R, which is essentially of finite type over the finite field k, has fraction field F = k(t) and finite residue field κ = k[t]/(f). Since n > 1, the natural homomorphism K_n(R) ⊗_Z Q → K_n(k(t)) ⊗_Z Q is an isomorphism of Q-vector spaces. By lemma_73, K_n(k(t)) ⊗_Z Q = 0. An isomorphism onto the zero vector space implies the source is zero. Thus K_n(R) ⊗_Z Q = 0.

lemma_101.statement: Let k be a field, let U be a smooth affine variety of dimension d \ge 1 over k. Then there exists a finite surjective k-morphism U \to \mathbf{A}^d_k.
lemma_101.proof: Let A = Gamma(U,O_U). Since U is affine of finite type over k, A is a finitely generated k-algebra. Smoothness over k implies A is regular, hence reduced. Put dim A = d. We use the Noether normalization lemma in the following standard form: if R is a finitely generated k-domain of Krull dimension e, then there exist y_1,...,y_e in R which are algebraically independent over k and such that R is a finite module over k[y_1,...,y_e]. For e=0 this is Zariski's lemma, and for e>0 it is the usual Noether normalization argument, valid for every field k. If U is not assumed integral, write U as the finite disjoint union of its irreducible components U = U_1 ∐ ... ∐ U_r. This is possible because U is regular and reduced, so its irreducible components are disjoint; each U_i is a smooth affine integral variety. Let e_i = dim U_i. Since dim U = d, at least one e_i equals d. Let A_i = Gamma(U_i,O_{U_i}); then A ≅ A_1 × ... × A_r. For each i with e_i = d, apply Noether normalization to A_i. We obtain f_{i,1},...,f_{i,d} in A_i algebraically independent over k and A_i finite over B_i = k[f_{i,1},...,f_{i,d}]. The corresponding k-morphism φ_i: U_i -> A^d_k is finite. It is surjective: B_i -> A_i is an integral extension, so by lying over every prime of B_i has a prime of A_i above it; equivalently, the image is closed and contains the generic point because B_i -> A_i is injective. For each i with e_i < d, apply Noether normalization to A_i to obtain g_{i,1},...,g_{i,e_i} in A_i algebraically independent over k and A_i finite over C_i = k[g_{i,1},...,g_{i,e_i}]. This gives a finite surjective k-morphism ψ_i: U_i -> A^{e_i}_k. Compose ψ_i with the standard finite k-morphism ι_i: A^{e_i}_k -> A^d_k, (t_1,...,t_{e_i}) ↦ (t_1,...,t_{e_i},0,...,0). On rings, ι_i^#: k[x_1,...,x_d] -> k[t_1,...,t_{e_i}] sends x_j to t_j for j ≤ e_i and x_j to 0 for j > e_i; the target is finite over the source because it is the quotient k[x_1,...,x_d]/(x_{e_i+1},...,x_d). Thus ι_i is finite, and φ_i = ι_i ∘ ψ_i is finite. If e_i = 0, the same description gives a finite map to the origin. Now define φ: U -> A^d_k by φ|_{U_i} = φ_i. In affine terms this is the k-algebra homomorphism k[x_1,...,x_d] -> A = ∏ A_i whose i-th component is the map described above. Since each A_i is a finite k[x_1,...,x_d]-module, their finite product A is a finite k[x_1,...,x_d]-module. Hence φ is finite. It is surjective because for an index i with e_i = d, φ_i is surjective, and the image of φ is the union of the images of the φ_i. Therefore φ is a finite surjective k-morphism U -> A^d_k. If one uses the convention that a variety is integral, the component decomposition is unnecessary and the argument is just the single application of Noether normalization to A.

lemma_103_split_pushforward.statement: Let f: X' \to X be a finite locally free morphism of rank r \ge 1 between regular noetherian schemes, let E be a vector bundle on X, and suppose the sheaf f_*\mathcal{O}_{X'} is isomorphic to \mathcal{O}_X^{\oplus r}. Then f_* f^* E is isomorphic to E^{\oplus r} as a vector bundle on X.
lemma_103_split_pushforward.proof:
Let f: X' -> X be a finite locally free morphism of rank r >= 1 between regular noetherian schemes, let E be a vector bundle on X (i.e. a locally free O_X-module of finite rank), and let phi: f_*O_{X'} -> O_X^{oplus r} be an isomorphism of O_X-modules (the splitting hypothesis). We prove f_* f^* E is isomorphic to E^{oplus r} as a vector bundle on X. (Regularity of X and X' is not used anywhere below; it is an extra hypothesis of the statement. The argument is functorial in E.)

STEP 1 (affine computation; the projection formula with F = O_{X'}). Let U = Spec(A) be an affine open subscheme of X. Because f is finite, f^{-1}(U) is affine; write f^{-1}(U) = Spec(B) with B a finite A-algebra. Because f is finite locally free of rank r, the A-module B = (f_*O_{X'})(U) is projective of constant rank r (equivalently, f_*O_{X'}|_U is locally free of rank r). Note we do NOT assert B is free on this arbitrary affine U: local freeness of f gives only that B is projective of constant rank r over A. Let Q be the finite projective A-module corresponding to the vector bundle E|_U, so E|_U = ~Q (Q is projective of finite rank over A because E is locally free of finite rank).

We identify the relevant modules on U:
(i)  (f^* E)|_{f^{-1}(U)} corresponds to the B-module B tensor_A Q, by the definition of pullback of quasi-coherent sheaves along Spec(B) -> Spec(A).
(ii) (f_* f^* E)|_U corresponds to the A-module (f^* E)(f^{-1}(U)) = B tensor_A Q, where the A-module structure on B tensor_A Q is induced by the ring map A -> B (for a morphism with affine source and target, the pushforward of a quasi-coherent sheaf on U = Spec(A) is the quasi-coherent sheaf associated to the same module viewed as an A-module).
(iii) (f_* O_{X'})|_U corresponds to the A-module B.
(iv) (f_* O_{X'} tensor_{O_X} E)|_U corresponds to the A-module B tensor_A Q, since the tensor product of quasi-coherent sheaves on the affine U corresponds to the tensor product of the associated A-modules.

From (ii) and (iv), both (f_* f^* E)|_U and (f_* O_{X'} tensor_{O_X} E)|_U correspond to the A-module B tensor_A Q. Define alpha_U: (f_* f^* E)|_U -> (f_* O_{X'} tensor_{O_X} E)|_U to be the identity map on the A-module B tensor_A Q. This is an isomorphism of O_U-modules. (Concretely, alpha_U is the projection-formula isomorphism f_*(O_{X'} tensor f^* E) -> f_* O_{X'} tensor E in the special case F = O_{X'}: under the canonical identification O_{X'} tensor_{O_{X'}} f^* E = f^* E, the map is b tensor (b' tensor q) -> (b b') tensor q on B tensor_B (B tensor_A Q) -> B tensor_A Q, which is the identity after the standard identification B tensor_B (B tensor_A Q) = B tensor_A Q.)

The maps alpha_U are natural in E and compatible with restriction to smaller affine opens: if W = Spec(C) is an affine open with W subset U cap V for two affine opens U = Spec(A), V = Spec(A'), then alpha_U|_W and alpha_V|_W are both the identity map on the corresponding C-module (the module over W is C tensor_A Q_U = C tensor_{A'} Q_V), hence they agree. Since the affine opens form an open cover of X and the isomorphisms agree on overlaps, they glue to a global natural isomorphism of O_X-modules
    f_* f^* E  ~=  f_* O_{X'} tensor_{O_X} E.        (1)

STEP 2 (apply the splitting). Tensor the splitting isomorphism phi: f_* O_{X'} -> O_X^{oplus r} with E to obtain an isomorphism phi tensor id_E: f_* O_{X'} tensor_{O_X} E -> O_X^{oplus r} tensor_{O_X} E (tensoring an isomorphism with any O_X-module preserves it). Compose (1) with phi tensor id_E and with the canonical isomorphism O_X^{oplus r} tensor_{O_X} E -> E^{oplus r}, which on sections over any open is (a_1,...,a_r) tensor e -> (a_1 e, ..., a_r e) and whose inverse is (e_1,...,e_r) -> sum_{i=1}^r (0,...,1,0,...,0)_i tensor e_i. The composite is an isomorphism of O_X-modules
    f_* f^* E  ~=  f_* O_{X'} tensor_{O_X} E  ~=  O_X^{oplus r} tensor_{O_X} E  ~=  E^{oplus r}.        (2)

STEP 3 (both sides are vector bundles). We show the two O_X-modules in (2) are locally free of finite rank, so (2) is an isomorphism of vector bundles.
- f_* O_{X'} is locally free of rank r on X: this is part of the definition of 'f finite locally free of rank r' (f_* O_{X'} is locally free of rank r); it also follows directly from the splitting phi since O_X^{oplus r} is locally free of rank r.
- E is locally free of finite rank s on X, by hypothesis (E is a vector bundle).
- f_* O_{X'} tensor_{O_X} E is locally free of finite rank on X: the opens W = Spec(C) over which f_* O_{X'}|_W ~= C^{oplus r} and E|_W ~= C^{oplus s} form an open cover of X (both sheaves are locally free, so each is trivial on some open cover, and the intersection of two such covers is again a cover). On each such W we have (f_* O_{X'} tensor E)|_W ~= C^{oplus r} tensor_C C^{oplus s} ~= C^{oplus rs}, so the tensor product is locally free of rank rs. (This argument uses only that a tensor product of two finite free C-modules is finite free; no choice of a basis of B over an arbitrary affine is required.)
- By (1), f_* f^* E ~= f_* O_{X'} tensor E, so f_* f^* E is locally free of rank rs, hence a vector bundle.
- E^{oplus r} is a vector bundle of rank rs (finite direct sum of the vector bundle E).

Therefore (2) is an isomorphism of vector bundles on X: f_* f^* E ~= E^{oplus r}. QED

lemma_105.statement: Let k be a finite field and let X be a smooth projective variety over k. Then K_1(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.
lemma_105.proof: Let k be a finite field and let X be a smooth projective variety over k. Step 1: By the standard definition used for higher K-theory of varieties, a smooth projective variety over k is, in particular, a smooth projective scheme over k. Step 2: The proved lemma with user_id eoinm and lemma_id lemma_32 states that if k is a finite field and X is a smooth projective scheme over k, then K_1(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0. Step 3: Applying this lemma directly to the given smooth projective variety X over the finite field k yields K_1(X) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0. This is exactly the desired conclusion.

lemma_108.statement: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field K, let F: V → V be a K-linear endomorphism, and suppose ker(F − id_V) = {0}. Then F − id_V is an isomorphism of V.
lemma_108.proof:
No lookup is needed: the target lemma is a purely linear-algebraic statement about a finite-dimensional vector space over an arbitrary field, and none of the provided lemmas (all of which concern K-theory over finite fields) are relevant. The proof is self-contained.

**Proof plan:**
1. T := F − id_V is K-linear (difference of K-linear maps).
2. ker(T) = {0} ⇒ T injective.
3. Finite-dimensionality: an injective endomorphism of a finite-dimensional space is surjective (image of a basis is a basis).
4. A bijective K-linear self-map has a K-linear inverse, hence is an isomorphism.

{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_108",
  "cited_lemmas": [],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "Let T := F - id_V : V -> V. We show T is an isomorphism of K-vector spaces.\n\nStep 1 (T is K-linear). For v, w in V and a, b in K, using that F and id_V are K-linear:\nT(av + bw) = F(av + bw) - (av + bw) = aF(v) + bF(w) - av - bw = a(F(v) - v) + b(F(w) - w) = aT(v) + bT(w).\nThus T is K-linear.\n\nStep 2 (T is injective). By hypothesis ker(T) = {0}. If T(v) = T(w) for v, w in V, then T(v - w) = T(v) - T(w) = 0 by linearity, so v - w in ker(T) = {0}, hence v = w. Therefore T is injective.\n\nStep 3 (T is surjective, using finite-dimensionality). Let n = dim_K V < infinity and let (v_1, ..., v_n) be a K-basis of V. We claim (T(v_1), ..., T(v_n)) is again a basis of V. First, linear independence: if a_1 T(v_1) + ... + a_n T(v_n) = 0 with a_i in K, then by linearity of T, T(a_1 v_1 + ... + a_n v_n) = 0, so a_1 v_1 + ... + a_n v_n in ker(T) = {0}. Since (v_1, ..., v_n) is a basis, a_1 = ... = a_n = 0. Thus (T(v_1), ..., T(v_n)) is linearly independent. Second, a linearly independent set of n = dim_K V vectors in V is a basis: indeed, extend it to a basis of V; that basis has exactly n elements (every basis of an n-dimensional space has n elements), and the independent set already has n, so the extension adds nothing. Hence (T(v_1), ..., T(v_n)) spans V. Now for any v in V, write v = c_1 T(v_1) + ... + c_n T(v_n) with c_i in K; then v = T(c_1 v_1 + ... + c_n v_n) in im(T). So im(T) = V and T is surjective.\n\nStep 4 (T is an isomorphism). T is a bijective K-linear map V -> V. Let S : V -> V be its set-theoretic inverse, so T(S(v)) = v and S(T(v)) = v for all v. We verify S is K-linear. (i) For a in K, v in V: T(aS(v)) = aT(S(v)) = av = aT(S(v))... precisely, T(aS(v)) = aT(S(v)) by linearity of T, and T(S(v)) = v, so T(aS(v)) = av. Also T(S(av)) = av by the inverse property. Hence T(aS(v)) = T(S(av)), and injectivity of T (Step 2) gives aS(v) = S(av). (ii) For v, w in V: T(S(v) + S(w)) = T(S(v)) + T(S(w)) = v + w = T(S(v + w)), and injectivity of T gives S(v) + S(w) = S(v + w). Thus S is K-linear and is a two-sided inverse of T. Therefore T = F - id_V is an isomorphism of K-vector spaces.\n\nRemark (role of the hypotheses). Finite-dimensionality is essential: for infinite-dimensional V, an injective endomorphism need not be surjective (e.g., the shift x -> x^2 on K[x] is injective but its image consists of polynomials with even content, so it is not onto). The argument above uses exactly the assumption dim_K V < infinity in Step 3 and the assumption ker(T) = {0} in Steps 2 and 4, and no further properties of F beyond K-linearity."
}

lemma_113_dvr_localization_iso.statement: Let $R$ be a discrete valuation ring with finite residue field $\kappa$ and fraction field $L$, and let $n > 1$. Then the inclusion $R \hookrightarrow L$ induces an isomorphism $K_n(R) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \cong K_n(L) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q}$.
lemma_113_dvr_localization_iso.proof:
Let R be a discrete valuation ring (DVR) with finite residue field \kappa and fraction field L, and let n > 1. We prove that the inclusion R \hookrightarrow L induces an isomorphism K_n(R) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \cong K_n(L) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q}.

Step 1 (the three schemes). Set U = Spec R, let Z = Spec \kappa be the closed point of U (the closed subscheme defined by the maximal ideal \mathfrak{m} of R), and let V = U \setminus Z be the generic point. A DVR has exactly two prime ideals, (0) and \mathfrak{m}: the point (0) is the generic point with residue field L, and the point \mathfrak{m} is the closed point with residue field R/\mathfrak{m} = \kappa. Hence U \setminus Z = {(0)} = Spec L, so V = Spec L.

Step 2 (hypotheses of the localization sequence). We verify that U is a regular noetherian scheme and that Z is a regular closed subscheme of U, so that lemma_54 applies.
(i) Noetherian: a DVR is by definition a noetherian local domain, so R is noetherian and U = Spec R is a noetherian scheme.
(ii) Regular: R is a local noetherian domain of Krull dimension 1 with principal maximal ideal \mathfrak{m} = (\pi) for a uniformizer \pi \neq 0. A local noetherian ring (R, \mathfrak{m}) is regular if and only if \dim R = \dim_{\kappa}(\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2). In a DVR one has \mathfrak{m}^2 = (\pi^2), so every element of \mathfrak{m}^2 has \pi-adic valuation at least 2, whereas v(\pi) = 1; thus \pi \notin \mathfrak{m}^2 and the class of \pi is a nonzero element of \mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2. Since \mathfrak{m} = (\pi) is generated by one element, \mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2 is a \kappa-vector space of dimension exactly 1. Therefore \dim_{\kappa}(\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2) = 1 = \dim R, so R is a regular local ring and U = Spec R is a regular scheme.
(iii) Z a regular closed subscheme: Z = Spec \kappa is a closed subscheme of U (defined by \mathfrak{m}), and \kappa is a field, hence a regular ring, so Z is regular.
(iv) n > 1 by hypothesis.

Step 3 (localization exact sequence). By lemma_54 applied to the regular noetherian scheme U, the regular closed subscheme Z, and V = U \setminus Z, with n > 1, the sequence
K_n(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \to K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \to K_n(V) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \to K_{n-1}(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q}
is exact, where the first arrow is induced by the closed immersion Z \hookrightarrow U and the second by the open immersion V \hookrightarrow U. Substituting Z = Spec \kappa, U = Spec R, V = Spec L gives the exact sequence
K_n(\kappa) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \xrightarrow{a} K_n(R) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \xrightarrow{b} K_n(L) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \xrightarrow{c} K_{n-1}(\kappa) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q}.
The map b is induced by the open immersion Spec L \hookrightarrow Spec R, i.e. by the ring inclusion R \hookrightarrow L; this is exactly the map whose isomorphism we must establish.

Step 4 (the end terms vanish). The residue field \kappa is finite. Since n > 1, we have n \ge 2, hence n > 0, and by lemma_14, K_n(\kappa) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0. Also n - 1 \ge 1, hence n - 1 > 0, and by lemma_14 again, K_{n-1}(\kappa) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.

Step 5 (conclude). With both end terms equal to 0, the exact sequence of Step 3 reads
0 \xrightarrow{a} K_n(R) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \xrightarrow{b} K_n(L) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \xrightarrow{c} 0.
Exactness at K_n(R) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} gives \ker(b) = \mathrm{im}(a) = 0 (a is the unique homomorphism out of the zero group), so b is injective. Exactness at K_n(L) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} gives \mathrm{im}(b) = \ker(c) = K_n(L) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} (c is the unique homomorphism into the zero group), so b is surjective. Hence b is an isomorphism of \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces.

Therefore the inclusion R \hookrightarrow L induces an isomorphism K_n(R) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \cong K_n(L) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q}, as required.

lemma_111.statement: Let k be a field, let d be a positive integer, let U be a smooth affine variety of dimension d over k, and let f: U -> A^d_k be a finite surjective k-morphism. Then f is finite locally free.
lemma_111.proof: Step 1. Write U = Spec B and A^d_k = Spec A with A = k[t_1,...,t_d]. The k-morphism f corresponds to a k-algebra homomorphism phi: A -> B. Since f is finite, B is a finite A-module. Since f is surjective and A is a domain, the image of Spec B -> Spec A is all of Spec A; the image is V(ker phi), so ker phi = 0. Thus A is an integral subring of B, because finite implies integral. Since U is smooth over k, B is a regular ring; hence B_q is a regular local ring for every q in Spec B. Since dim U = d, dim B = d. Step 2. A finite morphism is finite locally free if and only if it is flat. Indeed, if f is finite and flat, then f_*O_U is a finite flat O_{A^d_k}-module; over each local ring A_p a finite flat module is free, so f_*O_U is locally free. Conversely finite locally free implies flat. Flatness of f is local on the source: f is flat iff for every q in Spec B, B_q is flat over A_p with p = q cap A. We first note that B_q is finite over A_p. Since B is finite over A, B_p = B tensor_A A_p is finite over A_p. The prime q of B lying over p gives a prime of B_p, and (B_p)_q = B_q while (A_p)_q = A_p; localizing a finite module keeps it finite, so B_q is finite over A_p. Therefore B_q is flat over A_p if and only if B_q is free over A_p. It suffices to prove that B_q is a free A_p-module for every q in Spec B. Step 3. We use three standard commutative algebra facts. S1. The polynomial ring A = k[t_1,...,t_d] is regular: for every prime p of A, A_p is a regular local ring. This is the classical regularity of polynomial rings over a field; it follows from the Jacobian criterion because A is a smooth k-algebra, or equivalently by induction on d showing that the embedding dimension of A_p equals ht(p). S2. Every regular local ring is Cohen-Macaulay. Proof sketch: let (R,m) be regular local of dimension r. If r=0, R is a field. For r>0, choose x_1,...,x_r generating m. Standard subfacts are that a regular local ring is a domain and that if x is part of a minimal generating set of m, then R/xR is a regular local ring of dimension r-1. Inducting on r, x_1,...,x_r is a regular sequence: x_1 is a non-zero-divisor, and the images of x_2,...,x_r form a regular sequence in R/x_1R by induction. Hence depth R = r = dim R, and every system of parameters is a regular sequence. S3. Miracle flatness in Koszul form. Let (R,m) be a regular local ring of dimension r, let (S,n) be a Noetherian local ring finite over R such that rad(mS)=n, dim S=r, and S is Cohen-Macaulay. Then S is free over R. Proof: choose x_1,...,x_r generating m. Since R is regular local, x_1,...,x_r is an R-regular sequence, so the Koszul complex K_R(x) is a free R-resolution of k=R/m. Tensoring with S gives Tor_i^R(k,S) = H_i(K_S(x)). The ideal (x_1,...,x_r)S has radical n and S has dimension r, so x_1,...,x_r is a system of parameters of S. Because S is Cohen-Macaulay, every system of parameters is an S-regular sequence. Hence K_S(x) is exact in positive degrees, so Tor_i^R(k,S)=0 for all i>0. In particular Tor_1^R(k,S)=0. By the local criterion of flatness for finite modules, S is flat over R. A finite flat module over a local ring is free, so S is free. Step 4. Fix q in Spec B and put p = q cap A. Let R = A_p and S = B_q, with maximal ideals m = pA_p and n = qB_q. By S1, R is a regular local ring. By smoothness of U, S is a regular local ring, and by S2 it is Cohen-Macaulay. By Step 2, S is finite over R. We have rad(mS)=n: mS is contained in n, and if a prime of S contains mS, its contraction in R contains m, hence equals m; since S is integral over R, any prime over m is maximal, so it is n. We also have dim S = dim R. Incomparability for the integral extension R -> S gives dim S <= dim R: any chain of primes in S ending at n contracts to a strict chain of primes in R ending at m. For the reverse inequality, take a maximal chain m_0 < m_1 < ... < m_r = m of primes of R. Put q_r = n. For i = r-1,...,0, the extension R_{m_{i+1}} -> S_{q_{i+1}} is integral, and lying over gives a prime of S_{q_{i+1}} contracting to m_i R_{m_{i+1}}; its inverse image q_i in S satisfies q_i < q_{i+1} and q_i cap R = m_i. Thus dim S >= r = dim R. Therefore dim S = dim R. Applying S3 to R -> S shows that S = B_q is a free A_p-module. Step 5. Since B_q is free over A_p for every q in Spec B, f is flat at every point of U. As f is finite, f is finite locally free. More explicitly, for each p in Spec A the A_p-module B_p is finite, and all its localizations at maximal ideals (the B_q with q over p) are free over A_p, hence flat over A_p. Flatness is local on the spectrum of the module, so B_p is flat over A_p; a finite flat module over the local ring A_p is free. Thus f_*O_U is locally free on A^d_k. Step 6. The rank is positive and constant. For p in Spec A, the rank of f_*O_U at p is dim_{kappa(p)}(B_p tensor_{A_p} kappa(p)) = dim_{kappa(p)}(B tensor_A kappa(p)). The latter is the coordinate ring of the scheme-theoretic fiber f^{-1}(p). Since f is surjective, this fiber is nonempty, so the vector space is nonzero; it is finite-dimensional because B is finite over A. Hence the rank is at least 1. The base A^d_k is connected because A is a domain, and the rank of a locally free sheaf is locally constant, so the rank is a positive constant.

lemma_116_subfield_dvr.statement: Let k be a finite field, let t be an indeterminate, let F be a subfield of k((t)) containing k, and suppose F \neq k. Let O_F = F \cap k[[t]]. Then O_F is a discrete valuation ring with fraction field F and residue field k.
lemma_116_subfield_dvr.proof:
Let v denote the t-adic valuation on k((t)): v(0)=+infinity, and for x in k((t))^*, v(x)=n in Z iff x = t^n u with u in k[[t]]^* (equivalently, n is the degree of the lowest nonzero term of x). We use the standard identities v(xy)=v(x)+v(y), v(x+y)>=min(v(x),v(y)) (with equality if v(x)!=v(y)), v(x^{-1})=-v(x), together with k[[t]]={x in k((t)): v(x)>=0}, k[[t]]^*={x in k((t))^*: v(x)=0}, and the reduction (constant-term) map rho: k[[t]] -> k[[t]]/t k[[t]] ~ k with ker(rho)=t k[[t]]={x in k[[t]]: v(x)>=1}.

(1) O_F is the valuation ring of F for v. Since F is a subfield of k((t)), v restricts to a valuation on F. Moreover O_F = F cap k[[t]] = F cap {x in k((t)): v(x)>=0} = {x in F: v(x)>=0}. Hence O_F is a valuation domain: for x in F^*, either v(x)>=0 so x in O_F, or v(x)<0 so v(x^{-1})=-v(x)>0>=0 and x^{-1} in O_F. Its unit group is O_F^*={x in F^*: v(x)=0} (x in O_F is a unit iff x^{-1} in O_F iff v(x^{-1})>=0 iff -v(x)>=0 iff v(x)<=0, and v(x)>=0 by membership, so v(x)=0). The non-units form the ideal m={x in O_F: v(x)>0}: it is closed under addition because v(x+y)>=min(v(x),v(y))>0 when v(x),v(y)>0, and under multiplication by O_F because v(r x)=v(r)+v(x)>=0+v(x)>0. Thus O_F is a local domain with unique maximal ideal m.

(2) The value group is dZ for some d>=1. The set v(F^*) is a subgroup of Z, so v(F^*)=eZ for a unique e>=0. We show e>=1. Since F != k, choose x in F \ k. Case A: v(x)!=0. Then v(x) in v(F^*) is nonzero, so e>=1. Case B: v(x)=0. Then x in k[[t]]^*; let a=rho(x) in k^* be its constant term (a!=0). Since x notin k, x-a != 0; and x-a in F (as a in k subset F) with v(x-a)>=1 (its constant term is 0). Then (x-a)^{-1} in F^* satisfies v((x-a)^{-1})=-v(x-a)<=-1<0, so v(F^*) contains a negative element and e>=1. In both cases e>=1, so v(F^*)=dZ with d>=1. (In particular the uniformizer need not be t; we only use that the value group is a nonzero discrete subgroup of Z.)

(3) O_F is a DVR. First, m={x in O_F: v(x)>0}={x in O_F: v(x)>=d}, because for x in F^*, v(x) in dZ and d>=1, so v(x)>0 iff v(x)>=d. Pick pi in F^* with v(pi)=d (exists since v(F^*)=dZ); then pi in m. For y in m, v(y/pi)=v(y)-v(pi)>=d-d=0, so y/pi in O_F and y=pi(y/pi) in pi O_F; hence m subset pi O_F, and the reverse inclusion holds since pi in m. So m=pi O_F is principal and nonzero (v(pi)=d>0), in particular O_F is not a field. Next, every ideal of O_F is principal. Let I != 0 be an ideal and set S={v(x): x in I \ {0}} subset {0,d,2d,...}; S is nonempty and, being a subset of the well-ordered set N_0, has a minimum m=dn (n>=0). Choose x_0 in I \ {0} with v(x_0)=m. Then (x_0) subset I (I an ideal). Conversely, for y in I: if y=0 then y in (x_0); if y != 0 then v(y) in S so v(y)>=m=v(x_0), giving v(y/x_0)=v(y)-v(x_0)>=0, i.e. y/x_0 in O_F, so y=x_0(y/x_0) in (x_0). Thus I=(x_0). So O_F is a PID, hence Noetherian. A Noetherian local domain with a principal nonzero maximal ideal is a discrete valuation ring; therefore O_F is a DVR.

(4) The fraction field of O_F is F. Since O_F subset F and F is a field, Frac(O_F) subset F. Conversely, for x in F^*: if v(x)>=0 then x in O_F subset Frac(O_F); if v(x)<0 then v(x^{-1})=-v(x)>0>=0 so x^{-1} in O_F and x=(x^{-1})^{-1} in Frac(O_F). Hence F subset Frac(O_F), and Frac(O_F)=F.

(5) The residue field of O_F is k. Restrict rho to O_F: rho|_{O_F}: O_F -> k. It is surjective, because for a in k the element a (viewed in k subset F) has v(a)=0>=0, so a in O_F and rho|_{O_F}(a)=a. Its kernel is m: for x in O_F, x in ker(rho|_{O_F}) iff rho(x)=0 iff x in t k[[t]] iff v(x)>=1 (with v(0)=+infinity); for x != 0 we have v(x) in dZ_{>=0} with d>=1, so v(x)>=1 iff v(x)>=d iff v(x)>0, and x=0 satisfies all the displayed conditions. Thus ker(rho|_{O_F})={x in O_F: v(x)>0}=m. By the first isomorphism theorem, O_F/m ~ k; since m is the maximal ideal, the residue field of O_F is k.

Combining (3), (4), (5): O_F is a discrete valuation ring with fraction field F and residue field k.

lemma_117_projective_kt_free.statement: Let k be a field and let t be an indeterminate over k. Then every finitely generated projective k[t]-module is free.
lemma_117_projective_kt_free.proof: Let R = k[t]. We prove the statement in four steps. Step 1. R is a principal ideal domain. First, R is an integral domain: if f and g are nonzero polynomials with leading coefficients a and b, then the leading coefficient of fg is ab, which is nonzero because k is a field. For a nonzero polynomial f, let deg(f) be the largest exponent of t with nonzero coefficient. Division lemma. If f and g are in R and g != 0, then there exist q and r in R such that f = qg + r and either r = 0 or deg(r) < deg(g). Proof of the division lemma by induction on deg(f). If f = 0, take q = 0 and r = 0. If deg(f) < deg(g), take q = 0 and r = f. Otherwise, let m = deg(f), n = deg(g), and let a and b be the leading coefficients of f and g. Since k is a field, b has an inverse b^(-1). Put c = a b^(-1) and q0 = c t^(m-n). The leading term of q0 g is c b t^m = a t^m, so f - q0 g is either 0 or has degree strictly smaller than m. If f - q0 g = 0, take q = q0 and r = 0. If not, apply the induction hypothesis to the polynomial f - q0 g, whose degree is smaller than deg(f), to obtain q1 and r with f - q0 g = q1 g + r and r = 0 or deg(r) < deg(g). Then f = (q0 + q1) g + r, as required. Thus R is a Euclidean domain with Euclidean function deg. Now let I be a nonzero ideal of R. Choose 0 != h in I with minimal degree; such an h exists because the nonnegative integers are well ordered. For any f in I: if f = 0, then f is in (h). If f != 0, divide f by h: f = qh + r with r = 0 or deg(r) < deg(h). Since f and qh are in I, r = f - qh is in I. By minimality of deg(h), r cannot be nonzero, so r = 0 and f = qh is in (h). Hence I = (h). The zero ideal is (0). Therefore R is a PID. Step 2. Submodules of finite free modules over a PID are free. Let R be a PID (hence an integral domain) and let F be a finite free R-module. We prove by induction on n, the rank of F, that every submodule L of F is free. For n = 0 there is nothing to prove. For n = 1, write F = R e. A submodule L is of the form {a e : a in I} for the ideal I = {a in R : a e in L}. Since R is a PID, I = (d) for some d in R. Then L = R(d e), which is free. Assume n > 1 and the result holds for rank n-1. Write F = F' ⊕ R e_n, where F' = R e_1 ⊕ ... ⊕ R e_(n-1), and let π:F -> R e_n be the projection. Identify R e_n with R. Let L be a submodule of F. Then L' = L ∩ F' is a submodule of F', so by the induction hypothesis L' is free; choose a basis u_1,...,u_s of L'. The set π(L) is an ideal of R, so π(L) = R d for some d in R. If d = 0, then π(L) = 0, so L is contained in F', hence L = L', which is free. If d != 0, choose l in L with π(l) = d. Write l = l' + d e_n with l' in F'. We claim L = L' + R l and the sum is direct. For the inclusion L ⊂ L' + R l, take x in L and write x = x' + a e_n with x' in F'. Since a in π(L) = R d, there is b in R with a = b d. Then x - b l = x' - b l' + (a - b d) e_n = x' - b l' is in F'. It is also in L, because x and b l are in L. Therefore x - b l lies in L ∩ F' = L'. Hence x = (x - b l) + b l is in L' + R l. For directness, suppose y is in L' ∩ R l. Then y = b l = b l' + b d e_n for some b in R. Since y is in F', its e_n-coordinate is 0, so b d = 0. The ring R is a domain and d != 0, so b = 0, and y = 0. Thus L = L' ⊕ R l. Since L' is free with basis u_1,...,u_s, the module L is free with basis u_1,...,u_s,l. This completes the induction. Step 3. Finitely generated torsion-free modules over a PID are free. Let R be a PID and let M be a finitely generated torsion-free R-module. Let K be the fraction field of R. The natural map M -> M⊗_R K is injective: M⊗_R K is canonically isomorphic to the localization of M at S = R with 0 removed, and m/1 is zero in this localization exactly when some s in S annihilates m, by the definition of equality in a localization; torsion-freeness then forces m = 0. The module M⊗_R K is a finite-dimensional K-vector space. Choose elements m_1,...,m_N of M that generate M. Their images in M⊗K span this vector space. Select a maximal K-linearly independent subset of these images; after relabeling, suppose it is the images of e_1,...,e_r, where each e_i is one of the m_j. Maximality inside the spanning set implies that the selected images span M⊗K, so e_1,...,e_r form a K-basis of M⊗K. If r = 0, then M⊗K = 0, so M = 0 by the injectivity just proved, and M is free. Thus assume r > 0 for the rest of this step. They are also R-linearly independent: if a_1 e_1 + ... + a_r e_r = 0 with a_i in R, the same equation holds in M⊗K, forcing all a_i = 0. Let Q = R e_1 + ... + R e_r. Then Q is a free R-module of rank r, and Q is contained in M. Each generator m_j can be written in the K-basis as m_j⊗1 = (a_(j1)/b_(j1)) e_1⊗1 + ... + (a_(jr)/b_(jr)) e_r⊗1 with a_(ji), b_(ji) in R and b_(ji) != 0. Let d be the product of all the b_(ji); if there are no denominators, take d = 1. Then d != 0, and for each j the element d m_j⊗1 equals the image of q_j = (d a_(j1)/b_(j1)) e_1 + ... + (d a_(jr)/b_(jr)) e_r, which lies in Q because each coefficient d a_(ji)/b_(ji) is in R. By injectivity of M -> M⊗K, d m_j = q_j, so d m_j is in Q. Since m_1,...,m_N generate M, we have d M ⊂ Q. Multiplication by d gives an R-linear map μ:M -> d M, μ(m) = d m. This map is surjective by definition of d M. It is injective because M is torsion-free and d != 0: if d m = 0, then m = 0. Thus M is isomorphic to d M. The module d M is a submodule of the finite free module Q, so by Step 2 it is free. Therefore M is free. Step 4. Apply to projective k[t]-modules. Let P be a finitely generated projective R-module, where R = k[t]. We first show P is torsion-free. By the lifting property defining projective modules, P is a direct summand of a free R-module. Indeed, let F be the free R-module with basis the underlying set of P, and let π:F -> P be the canonical surjection. Since P is projective, the identity map P -> P lifts to a map s:P -> F with π s = id_P. Then F = s(P) ⊕ ker(π) (every element f is s(π(f)) + (f - s(π(f))), and the intersection is zero by π s = id_P), and s(P) is isomorphic to P. Let r be a nonzero element of R. Multiplication by r on the free module F is injective: if x is written as a finite sum x = sum c_i f_i in a basis of F, then r x = 0 implies r c_i f_i = 0 for each i, hence r c_i = 0, and since R is a domain and r != 0, c_i = 0. Now if p in P satisfies r p = 0, then under the identification p with s(p) in F we have r s(p) = s(r p) = 0, so s(p) = 0, hence p = 0. Thus P is torsion-free. By Step 1, R = k[t] is a PID. By Step 3, every finitely generated torsion-free module over R is free. Therefore P is free. This proves that every finitely generated projective k[t]-module is free.

lemma_119.statement: Let k be a field, and let C be a smooth projective geometrically integral curve over k. Then there exists a finite surjective k-morphism C \to \mathbf{P}^1_k.
lemma_119.proof: Let C be as in the statement. Geometrically integral implies integral, and a curve has dimension 1. Choose a nonempty affine open subset U of C; such an open exists because C is projective over k. Then U is a smooth affine integral curve over k, hence a smooth affine variety of dimension 1. By lemma_101, there is a finite surjective k-morphism phi: U -> A^1_k. Since U is affine, phi is induced by a k-algebra homomorphism k[t] -> Gamma(U,O_U). Let a be the image of t. Because U is a nonempty open subset of the integral scheme C, Gamma(U,O_U) injects into K = K(C), and K is the fraction field of Gamma(U,O_U). The morphism phi is finite, so Gamma(U,O_U) is a finite k[t]-module; therefore K is a finite extension of k(t) = k(a). The morphism phi is surjective, so a is transcendental over k; indeed, if a were algebraic over k, the image of phi would be contained in the finite set of points of A^1_k whose coordinate is a conjugate of a, contradicting surjectivity. We now define psi: C -> P^1_k. Write P^1_k = Proj k[X,Y] with charts U_0 = D_+(X) = Spec k[t] and U_inf = D_+(Y) = Spec k[s], where t = Y/X and s = X/Y. For any point x of C, O_{C,x} is a DVR: at the generic point it is K, and at a closed point it is a regular local ring of dimension 1. Since a is nonzero, either a or a^{-1} belongs to O_{C,x}. If a belongs to O_{C,x}, choose an open neighborhood V of x on which a is regular and define psi on V by the chart U_0 with t = a. If a^{-1} belongs to O_{C,x}, choose an open neighborhood W of x on which a^{-1} is regular and define psi on W by the chart U_inf with s = a^{-1}. On overlaps the two definitions agree because (1,a) = (a^{-1},1) in P^1_k. Thus psi is a k-morphism. On U, a is regular, so psi restricts to phi followed by the open immersion A^1_k -> P^1_k. The morphism psi is proper: C is proper over k because it is projective, P^1_k is separated over k, and a k-morphism from a proper k-scheme to a separated k-scheme is proper. Hence psi(C) is closed in P^1_k. Since psi|_U = phi and phi is surjective, psi(C) contains A^1_k, which is dense in P^1_k. A closed subset of an irreducible space containing a dense subset is the whole space, so psi is surjective. It remains to show psi is finite. The generic fiber of psi is Spec K as a k(a)-scheme, and K/k(a) is finite, so psi is generically finite. We now show psi is quasi-finite. Let y be a closed point of P^1_k. The fiber C_y is a closed subscheme of C. If it had positive dimension, then, since C is irreducible of dimension 1, it would be all of C, forcing the image of psi to be the single point y, contradicting surjectivity. Thus every closed fiber has dimension 0. A 0-dimensional noetherian scheme of finite type over k(y) is Artinian, hence finite. The generic fiber is already finite. Therefore all fibers of psi are finite, so psi is quasi-finite. A proper quasi-finite morphism of finite type is finite (standard proper-quasi-finite criterion). Since psi is proper and quasi-finite, psi is finite. Thus psi is a finite surjective k-morphism C -> P^1_k.

lemma_116_good_divisor.statement: Let k be a finite field, let X be a smooth projective variety over k, and let d = \dim X \ge 1. Then there exist a finite separable extension k'/k and a smooth effective Cartier divisor D' \subset X_{k'} such that \mathcal{O}_{X_{k'}}(D') is very ample and \dim D' = d-1.
lemma_116_good_divisor.proof: Let kbar be an algebraic closure of k. Since X is projective over k, choose a very ample invertible sheaf L on X. Put V=H^0(X,L) and N=dim_k V-1. The complete linear system of L gives a closed immersion i:X -> P(V^*) with i^*O(1) ≅ L and with the natural map H^0(P(V^*),O(1)) -> H^0(X,L) an isomorphism; identify H^0(P(V^*),O(1)) with V. Let S=P(V), so S parameterizes nonzero sections of L up to scalar and dim S=N. There is a universal section u of pr_1^*L ⊗ pr_2^*O_S(1) on X×S, obtained by restricting the tautological section of O_{P(V^*)×S}(1,1) to X×S; for a point [s] of S, the restriction of u to X×{[s]} is the section of L represented by s. Because X is smooth over k, the projection X×S -> S is smooth. Let J^1_{/S}(pr_1^*L⊗pr_2^*O_S(1)) be the relative 1-jet bundle along X. The relative 1-jet of u is a section of this vector bundle, and let I be its zero locus. Then I is closed in X×S. For a point x of X_{kbar}, the fiber I_{kbar,x} is the projective subspace P(ker e_x) of S_{kbar}, where e_x:V_{kbar} -> J^1_x(L_{kbar}) is the evaluation map sending a global section to its 1-jet at x. Indeed, the relative 1-jet of u at (x,[s]) is the linear map from the line [s] in V_{kbar} to J^1_x(L_{kbar}), and it is zero exactly when that line is contained in ker e_x.
