The projection I -> S is proper because I is closed in X×S and X is proper over k. Let B be the set-theoretic image of I in S; then B is closed in S. We now show that B is a proper closed subset of S. Work over kbar. If I_{kbar} is empty, then B_{kbar} is empty, so B is empty and proper. Otherwise, let x be a closed point of X_{kbar}, and let r=dim_{kbar} T_x X_{kbar}; equivalently r is the dimension of the irreducible component of X_{kbar} containing x. First we prove that e_x is surjective. On P(V^*)_{kbar}, the evaluation map H^0(O(1)) -> J^1_y(O(1)) is surjective at every closed point y. To see this, choose an affine chart A^N containing y. Global sections of O(1) restrict to affine linear forms. The map from the (N+1)-dimensional vector space of affine linear forms to the (N+1)-dimensional vector space of pairs (value at y, derivative at y) is injective, because an affine linear form with zero value and zero derivative at y lies in the square of the maximal ideal of y and hence is zero. Therefore it is surjective. For the closed immersion i, the pullback map on 1-jets J^1_y(O(1)) -> J^1_x(i^*O(1)) is surjective: given a 1-jet (lambda, phi) at x, where phi is a linear form on T_x X_{kbar}, extend phi to a linear form psi on T_y P(V^*)_{kbar} using the injectivity of the differential of i, choose a global section of O(1) with 1-jet (lambda, psi) at y, and restrict it to X. Since i^*O(1)=L and H^0(P(V^*),O(1))=V, e_x is surjective. Thus dim J^1_x(L_{kbar})=r+1, because the fiber of J^1(L) at x fits into 0 -> L_x⊗Ω^1_{X_{kbar},x} -> J^1_x(L) -> L_x ->0 and dim Ω^1_{X_{kbar},x}=r. Hence dim ker e_x = (N+1)-(r+1)=N-r. For a closed point z=(x,[s]) of I_{kbar}, the fiber I_{kbar,x} has dimension N-r-1. By the local dimension inequality for the morphism I_{kbar} -> X_{kbar}, dim_z I_{kbar} ≤ dim_x X_{kbar} + dim_z I_{kbar,x} = r+(N-r-1)=N-1. Closed points are dense in I_{kbar}, so dim I_{kbar} ≤ N-1. Since I_{kbar} -> S_{kbar} is proper, dim B_{kbar} ≤ N-1, where B_{kbar} is the image of I_{kbar} in S_{kbar}. But dim S_{kbar}=N, so B_{kbar} is a proper closed subset of S_{kbar}. If B were all of S, then the generic point of S would lie in B. There would be a point of I over the generic point, and the corresponding fiber over the function field of S would be a nonempty finite type scheme; its base change to the function field of S_{kbar} would still be nonempty. Hence the generic point of S_{kbar} would lie in B_{kbar}. As B_{kbar} is closed and S_{kbar} is irreducible, this would force B_{kbar}=S_{kbar}, a contradiction. Therefore B is a proper closed subset of S, and W=S\B is a nonempty open subset of S. Since k is finite and S is of finite type over k, the nonempty open W contains a closed point z. Indeed, take an affine open subset Spec A of W and a maximal ideal of A; the residue field is finite over k. Let k' be the residue field of z. Then k'/k is finite, hence separable because finite fields are perfect. The point z is a k'-rational point of S, so it determines a line in V_{k'}, and we choose a nonzero section s of L_{k'} representing this line. Because z lies in W, the base change of [s] to kbar does not lie in B_{kbar}; if it did, the fiber of I over z would become nonempty after base change to kbar, and therefore would already be nonempty, forcing z to lie in B. Therefore the relative 1-jet of s_{kbar} is nonzero at every point of X_{kbar}. It follows first that s_{kbar} is not locally zero at any point of X_{kbar}; otherwise its 1-jet would be zero. Since X_{kbar} is regular, its local rings are domains, so s_{kbar} is a nonzerodivisor on O_{X_{kbar}}. Its zero scheme D_{kbar} is an effective Cartier divisor and contains no irreducible component of X_{kbar}. It follows second that D_{kbar} is smooth over kbar. Indeed, let y be a point of D_{kbar}. Choose a local trivialization in which s_{kbar}=f. Then f belongs to the maximal ideal of y, and the nonvanishing of the 1-jet means f mod m_y^2 is nonzero. In the regular local ring O_{X_{kbar},y}, such an f is part of a regular system of parameters, so O_{D_{kbar},y}=O_{X_{kbar},y}/(f) is regular. Thus D_{kbar} is regular at all its points; being of finite type over the perfect field kbar, it is smooth over kbar. Let D' be the zero scheme of s in X_{k'}. Then D'×_{k'}kbar = D_{kbar}. Smoothness descends under faithfully flat base change, so D' is smooth over k'. The property that s is a nonzerodivisor on O_{X_{k'}} also descends: if s were locally zero at a point of X_{k'}, its base change would be locally zero at a point of X_{kbar}, which is impossible. Since X_{k'} is regular, its local rings are domains, so s is a nonzerodivisor, and D' is an effective Cartier divisor in X_{k'}. The section s defines an isomorphism O_{X_{k'}}(D') ≅ L_{k'}. Because L is very ample on X and very ampleness is stable under base change, L_{k'} is very ample on X_{k'}; hence O_{X_{k'}}(D') is very ample. Finally we compute dim D'. Base change by the finite extension k'/k preserves dimension, so dim X_{k'}=d. Since D' is an effective Cartier divisor, it contains no irreducible component of X_{k'}, and in particular no d-dimensional component; therefore dim D'≤d-1. Choose an irreducible component Y of X_{k'} of dimension d. Such a component exists, and because X_{k'} is smooth, Y is integral. The restriction s_Y of s to Y is a nonzero section of the very ample line bundle L_{k'}|_Y. Its zero scheme D'_Y is nonempty: if it were empty, s_Y would be nowhere zero and would trivialize L_{k'}|_Y, making the trivial line bundle on Y very ample, which is impossible for a projective integral variety of positive dimension because after base change to kbar the trivial line bundle on each positive-dimensional component has only scalar global sections and cannot separate distinct points. Thus D'_Y is a nonempty effective Cartier divisor on the integral d-dimensional scheme Y. By Krull's principal ideal theorem, dim D'_Y=d-1. Hence dim D'≥d-1, and combining with the upper bound gives dim D'=d-1. This completes the proof.

lemma_123_point_action_zero.statement: Let k be a finite field, let C be a smooth projective curve over k, let p be a closed point of C, and let n > 1. Then the endomorphism of K_n(C) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q induced by multiplication by the class of the skyscraper sheaf \mathbf k(p) in K_0(C) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q is zero.
lemma_123_point_action_zero.proof:
Both lemmas are confirmed. Now I'll write the complete proof.

**Proof structure:**
1. Apply the localization sequence (lemma_54) to the pair $S = \{p\} \subset C$.
2. Show $j^*([\mathbf{k}(p)] \cdot x) = 0$ using the fact that restriction is a module map and $j^*[\mathbf{k}(p)] = 0$.
3. Exactness forces $[\mathbf{k}(p)] \cdot x$ into the image of $K_n(S) \otimes \mathbf{Q} 	o K_n(C) \otimes \mathbf{Q}$.
4. Since $S \cong \mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbf{k}(p)$ is a finite field, lemma_14 gives $K_n(S) \otimes \mathbf{Q} = 0$.
5. Conclude the action is zero.

{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_123_point_action_zero",
  "cited_lemmas": [
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_54"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_14"}
  ],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "Let $i: S = \{p\} \hookrightarrow C$ denote the closed embedding of the point $p$ into $C$, and let $j: V = C \setminus S \hookrightarrow C$ denote the complementary open embedding. We prove that for every $x \in K_n(C) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q}$, the product $[\mathbf{k}(p)] \cdot x$ is zero in $K_n(C) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q}$.

**Step 1: The localization sequence is exact.** Since $C$ is a smooth projective curve over the field $k$, it is a regular noetherian scheme. The closed subscheme $S = \{p\}$ has structure sheaf $\mathcal{O}_S \cong \mathbf{k}(p)$ (the residue field of $p$), so $S \cong \mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbf{k}(p)$ is a regular scheme of dimension $0$; in particular $S$ is a regular closed subscheme of $C$. The hypothesis $n > 1$ is satisfied. Therefore we may apply the localization exact sequence (lemma_54) to the triple $(S, C, V)$, obtaining an exact sequence of $\mathbb{Q}$-vector spaces
$$K_n(S) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q} \xrightarrow{\;i_*\;} K_n(C) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q} \xrightarrow{\;j^*\;} K_n(V) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q} \xrightarrow{\;\partial\;} K_{n-1}(S) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q}.$$nIn particular, exactness at the middle term gives
$$\ker\bigl(j^*: K_n(C) \otimes \mathbb{Q} \to K_n(V) \otimes \mathbb{Q}\bigr) = \mathrm{im}\bigl(i_*: K_n(S) \otimes \mathbb{Q} \to K_n(C) \otimes \mathbb{Q}\bigr).$$

**Step 2: The restriction map $j^*$ is a $K_0$-module homomorphism.** The restriction map $j^*: K_m(C) \to K_m(V)$ for each $m \geq 0$ is induced by the pullback (restriction) functor $j^*: \mathrm{Vect}(C) \to \mathrm{Vect}(V)$ on the exact category of vector bundles. This functor is exact and commutes with the tensor product: for vector bundles $E, F$ on $C$, there is a canonical isomorphism $j^*(E \otimes_C F) \cong j^*E \otimes_V j^*F$. Since the $K$-theory product $K_0(C) \times K_m(C) \to K_m(C)$ is induced by the tensor product, it follows that $j^*$ is a homomorphism of $K_0$-modules: for every $a \in K_0(C)$ and $y \in K_m(C)$,
$$j^*(a \cdot y) = (j^* a) \cdot (j^* y) \quad \text{in } K_m(V).$$nThis identity is preserved after tensoring with $\mathbb{Q}$.

**Step 3: $j^*[\mathbf{k}(p)] = 0$ in $K_0(V) \otimes \mathbb{Q}$.** The skyscraper sheaf $\mathbf{k}(p)$ is supported at the single point $p$. Since $p \notin V = C \setminus \{p\}$, the restriction $j^*\mathbf{k}(p)$ is the zero sheaf on $V$. Hence
$$j^*[\mathbf{k}(p)] = [j^*\mathbf{k}(p)] = [0] = 0 \quad \text{in } K_0(V) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q}.$$

**Step 4: $j^*([\mathbf{k}(p)] \cdot x) = 0$ for every $x$.** Let $x \in K_n(C) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q}$ be arbitrary. Applying the module homomorphism property from Step 2 with $a = [\mathbf{k}(p)]$ and $y = x$, and using Step 3, we obtain
$$j^*\bigl([\mathbf{k}(p)] \cdot x\bigr) = \bigl(j^*[\mathbf{k}(p)]\bigr) \cdot (j^* x) = 0 \cdot (j^* x) = 0 \quad \text{in } K_n(V) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q}.$$

**Step 5: $[\mathbf{k}(p)] \cdot x$ lies in the image of $i_*$.** From Step 4, $[\mathbf{k}(p)] \cdot x \in \ker(j^*)$. By the exactness relation established in Step 1, $\ker(j^*) = \mathrm{im}(i_*)$, so
$$[\mathbf{k}(p)] \cdot x \in \mathrm{im}\bigl(i_*: K_n(S) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q} \to K_n(C) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q}\bigr).$$

**Step 6: $K_n(S) \otimes \mathbb{Q} = 0$.** Since $S \cong \mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbf{k}(p)$, we have $K_n(S) = K_n(\mathbf{k}(p))$. The residue field $\mathbf{k}(p)$ is a finite extension of the finite field $k$ (as $p$ is a closed point of a variety over $k$), hence $\mathbf{k}(p)$ is itself a finite field. Applying lemma_14 to the finite field $\mathbf{k}(p)$ with $n > 1$ (indeed lemma_14 holds for all $n > 0$), we get
$$K_n(S) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q} = K_n(\mathbf{k}(p)) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q} = 0.$$

**Step 7: Conclusion.** Since $K_n(S) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q} = 0$, the homomorphism $i_*: K_n(S) \otimes \mathbb{Q} \to K_n(C) \otimes \mathbb{Q}$ is the zero map, and its image is $\{0\}$. By Step 5, $[\mathbf{k}(p)] \cdot x$ belongs to this image, hence
$$[\mathbf{k}(p)] \cdot x = 0 \quad \text{in } K_n(C) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q}.$$
Since $x \in K_n(C) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q}$ was arbitrary, the endomorphism $\phi: K_n(C) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q} \to K_n(C) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q}$ defined by $\phi(x) = [\mathbf{k}(p)] \cdot x$ is the zero map. This completes the proof. $\blacksquare$"
}

lemma_125.statement: Let k be a finite field, let U be a smooth affine geometrically integral curve over k, let C be a smooth projective geometrically integral curve over k with U \subset C an open embedding, and let n > 1. Then the restriction homomorphism K_n(C)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} is an isomorphism of \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces.
lemma_125.proof:
Let k be a finite field, let U be a smooth affine geometrically integral curve over k, let C be a smooth projective geometrically integral curve over k with U \subset C an open embedding, and let n > 1. We prove that the restriction map res: K_n(C)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \to K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q is an isomorphism of \mathbf Q-vector spaces.

Step 1 (structure of the complement). Put D = C \setminus U, with its reduced structure; since U is an open subscheme of C, D is the closed subscheme whose underlying closed set is C \setminus U. Because C is an integral curve (smooth projective geometrically integral of dimension 1) and U is a nonempty open subset, D is a proper closed subset of C, hence \dim D = 0. As C is noetherian, D is a finite set of points, and every 0-dimensional point of a curve over k is a closed point with finite residue field. Thus D = \bigsqcup_{i=1}^m \mathrm{Spec}\, k(P_i) for a finite set of closed points P_1,\ldots,P_m of C, and each k(P_i) is a finite extension of the finite field k, hence itself a finite field.

Step 2 (D is a regular closed subscheme of C). C is smooth over k, hence a regular noetherian scheme. The scheme D is a finite disjoint union of spectra of fields; every local ring of D is a field, so D is a regular scheme (0-dimensional and regular at every point). Therefore the hypotheses of lemma_54 (user_id eoinm, lemma_id lemma_54) are satisfied with U_0 := C (regular noetherian), Z := D (regular closed subscheme), and V := C \setminus D = U, for our n > 1.

Step 3 (localization exact sequence). By lemma_54 applied to (C, D, U), the sequence
K_n(D)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \to K_n(C)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \to K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \to K_{n-1}(D)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q
is exact, where the first map is induced by the closed immersion D \hookrightarrow C and the second map is the restriction map res induced by the open immersion U \hookrightarrow C.

Step 4 (vanishing of K_n(D)\otimes\mathbf Q). Algebraic K-theory commutes with finite disjoint unions: for a finite coproduct D = \bigsqcup_{i=1}^m D_i of schemes, the classifying space of the K-theory spectrum is a finite wedge, and its homotopy groups are direct sums, so K_n(D) \cong \bigoplus_{i=1}^m K_n(k(P_i)). For each i, k(P_i) is a finite field, and since n > 1 implies n \ge 2 > 0, lemma_14 (user_id eoinm, lemma_id lemma_14) gives K_n(k(P_i))\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q = 0. Tensoring the finite direct sum with \mathbf Q (which commutes with finite direct sums) yields
K_n(D)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \cong \bigoplus_{i=1}^m \bigl(K_n(k(P_i))\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q\bigr) = \bigoplus_{i=1}^m 0 = 0.

Step 5 (vanishing of K_{n-1}(D)\otimes\mathbf Q). Identically, K_{n-1}(D) \cong \bigoplus_{i=1}^m K_{n-1}(k(P_i)). Since n > 1, we have n-1 \ge 1 > 0, so lemma_14 applies to each summand: K_{n-1}(k(P_i))\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q = 0. Hence
K_{n-1}(D)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \cong \bigoplus_{i=1}^m 0 = 0.

Step 6 (conclusion). Substituting the vanishing of Steps 4 and 5 into the exact sequence of Step 3 gives the exact sequence
0 \to K_n(C)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \xrightarrow{\,res\,} K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \to 0.
Exactness at K_n(C)\otimes\mathbf Q says \ker(res) = \mathrm{im}(0 \to K_n(C)\otimes\mathbf Q) = 0, so res is injective; exactness at K_n(U)\otimes\mathbf Q says \mathrm{im}(res) = \ker(K_n(U)\otimes\mathbf Q \to 0) = K_n(U)\otimes\mathbf Q, so res is surjective. Being a bijective \mathbf Q-linear map between \mathbf Q-vector spaces, res is an isomorphism of \mathbf Q-vector spaces. This completes the proof.

(No use was made of any Lüroth-type identification of k(U) with k(t), of any finite-cover transfer identity f^*\circ N = R\cdot\mathrm{id}, or of any field-extension norm identity; the argument rests only on the localization exact sequence lemma_54 and the finite-field vanishing lemma_14.)

lemma_125_2.statement: Let k be a finite field, let W be a smooth scheme of finite type over k of dimension 0, and let n > 1. Then K_n(W) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.
lemma_125_2.proof: Let W be a smooth scheme of finite type over the finite field k with dim W = 0. If W is empty, then K_n(W) = 0 for n > 1, so K_n(W) ⊗_Z Q = 0; hence assume W is nonempty. Since W is of finite type over the field k, W is noetherian and quasi-compact. A noetherian scheme of Krull dimension 0 is affine and Artinian: it has only finitely many irreducible components, each of which is a closed point, and a 0-dimensional noetherian local ring is Artinian. Thus W = Spec A for an Artinian k-algebra A of finite type. Because A is a finite type k-algebra that is Artinian, A is finite-dimensional as a k-vector space, hence a finite k-algebra. Smoothness of W over k implies that W is regular; a 0-dimensional regular local ring is a field, so every local ring of W is a field. Therefore the finite Artinian ring A is a finite product of fields, A = K_1 × ... × K_m, and W = ∐_{i=1}^m Spec K_i, where each K_i is a finite field extension of k. Since k is finite, each K_i is a finite field. Quillen K-theory is additive on finite coproducts of schemes: the category of vector bundles, equivalently the category of perfect complexes, on a finite disjoint union is the finite product of the categories on the factors, and K-theory of a finite product of categories is the finite product of the K-theories. Hence K_n(W) ≅ ⊕_{i=1}^m K_n(K_i), and tensoring with Q gives K_n(W) ⊗_Z Q ≅ ⊕_{i=1}^m (K_n(K_i) ⊗_Z Q). By lemma_14, for every finite field F and every integer r > 0, one has K_r(F) ⊗_Z Q = 0. Applying this with F = K_i and r = n, noting that n > 1 implies n > 0, gives K_n(K_i) ⊗_Z Q = 0 for each i. A finite direct sum of zero Q-vector spaces is zero, so K_n(W) ⊗_Z Q = 0. This proves the lemma.

lemma_125_curve_rational_point.statement: Let k be a finite field and let C be a smooth projective geometrically integral curve over k. Then there exists a finite separable extension k'/k and a k'-rational point of C_{k'}.
lemma_125_curve_rational_point.proof:
The lemma is confirmed. Now I have everything needed to write the proof.

**Key ingredients:**
- **lemma_119**: gives a finite surjective $k$-morphism $C 	o \mathbb{P}^1_k$.
- **Basic facts**: $\mathbb{P}^1_k$ has $k$-rational points; finiteness is stable under base change; a nonempty finite $k$-scheme has a closed point with finite residue field over $k$; finite fields are perfect (so all finite extensions are separable); the universal property of fiber products identifies $k'$-rational points of $C_{k'}$ with $k$-morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}(k') 	o C$.

{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_125_curve_rational_point",
  "cited_lemmas": [
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_119"}
  ],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "Let k be a finite field and let C be a smooth projective geometrically integral curve over k. We must produce a finite separable extension k'/k and a k'-rational point of C_{k'} = C \times_k \operatorname{Spec}(k').

Step 1 (existence of a finite surjective map to P^1). By lemma_119 (applied to the field k and the smooth projective geometrically integral curve C), there exists a finite surjective k-morphism f : C \to \mathbb{P}^1_k.

Step 2 (choose a k-rational point of P^1). The projective line \mathbb{P}^1_k = \operatorname{Proj}(k[X_0,X_1]) contains the k-rational point P = [1:0], i.e. the morphism i : \operatorname{Spec}(k) \to \mathbb{P}^1_k corresponding to the maximal ideal (X_1) of k[X_1] (the homogeneous prime (X_1) in k[X_0,X_1]).

Step 3 (the fiber is a nonempty finite k-scheme). Form the fiber product
  Y = C \times_{\mathbb{P}^1_k} \operatorname{Spec}(k) = C \times_{\mathbb{P}^1_k} i.
The projection Y \to \operatorname{Spec}(k) is finite because f is finite and finiteness of morphisms is stable under base change (a finite morphism remains finite after any base change). Hence Y is a finite k-scheme, i.e. Y \cong \operatorname{Spec}(A) for some finite-dimensional k-algebra A.

We claim Y is nonempty. Surjectivity of f means the induced map on underlying topological spaces |C| \to |\mathbb{P}^1_k| is onto. The point P = [1:0] is a point of |\mathbb{P}^1_k|, so there exists a point c \in |C| with f(c) = P. The underlying topological space of the fiber product Y = C \times_{\mathbb{P}^1_k} \operatorname{Spec}(k) is precisely the set \{c' \in |C| : f(c') = P\} (the topological fiber of f over P, since \operatorname{Spec}(k) is the scheme associated to the point P). In particular c lies in |Y|, so Y \neq \varnothing.

Step 4 (choose a closed point and define k'). Since Y = \operatorname{Spec}(A) is a nonempty finite k-scheme, A is a nonzero Artinian k-algebra. An Artinian ring has at least one maximal ideal (e.g. by Zorn's lemma, or since A \neq 0 has a maximal ideal by the standard existence theorem for maximal ideals in nonzero rings). Choose a maximal ideal \mathfrak{m} \subset A and let y \in \operatorname{Spec}(A) be the corresponding closed point. Define
  k' := \kappa(y) = A/\mathfrak{m}.
Since A is a finite-dimensional k-vector space, every quotient A/\mathfrak{m} is also a finite-dimensional k-vector space, so k'/k is a finite field extension.

Step 5 (separability). The field k is finite, hence perfect: the Frobenius endomorphism \varphi : k \to k, x \mapsto x^{|k|}, is surjective (every element of k is a (|k|)-th power because the multiplicative group k^\times is cyclic of order |k|-1, so for any a \in k^\times there exists b \in k^\times with b^{|k|-1} = 1 and the map x \mapsto x^{|k|} = x \cdot x^{|k|-1} = x is the identity on k^\times; more directly, for a finite field of characteristic p, the map x \mapsto x^p is an automorphism since it is injective on the finite set k and hence surjective). A standard theorem of field theory states that every finite extension of a perfect field is separable. Therefore k'/k is a finite separable extension.

Step 6 (the closed point gives a k'-rational point of C_{k'}). The closed point y \in Y = \operatorname{Spec}(A) corresponds to the canonical k-morphism
  \varphi : \operatorname{Spec}(\kappa(y)) = \operatorname{Spec}(k') \to Y = \operatorname{Spec}(A).
Let \pi : Y \to C denote the first projection of the fiber product Y = C \times_{\mathbb{P}^1_k} \operatorname{Spec}(k). The composition
  g := \pi \circ \varphi : \operatorname{Spec}(k') \to C
is a k-morphism (a composition of k-morphisms).

We now show that g is a k'-rational point of C_{k'} = C \times_k \operatorname{Spec}(k'). By definition, a k'-rational point of C_{k'} is a \operatorname{Spec}(k')-morphism h : \operatorname{Spec}(k') \to C \times_k \operatorname{Spec}(k'), i.e. a k'-morphism over \operatorname{Spec}(k'). By the universal property of the fiber product C \times_k \operatorname{Spec}(k'), such an h is equivalent to a pair of k-morphisms (g_1 : \operatorname{Spec}(k') \to C, g_2 : \operatorname{Spec}(k') \to \operatorname{Spec}(k')) satisfying:
  (i) the two compositions \operatorname{Spec}(k') \xrightarrow{g_1} C \xrightarrow{} \operatorname{Spec}(k) and \operatorname{Spec}(k') \xrightarrow{g_2} \operatorname{Spec}(k') \xrightarrow{} \operatorname{Spec}(k) are equal, and
  (ii) g_2 = \operatorname{id}_{\operatorname{Spec}(k')} (the "over \operatorname{Spec}(k')" condition).

Set g_1 = g and g_2 = \operatorname{id}_{\operatorname{Spec}(k')}. Condition (ii) is satisfied by construction. For condition (i): the composition \operatorname{Spec}(k') \xrightarrow{g} C \xrightarrow{\text{structure}} \operatorname{Spec}(k) is the structure morphism of the k-algebra k' (since g is a k-morphism), and the composition \operatorname{Spec}(k') \xrightarrow{\operatorname{id}} \operatorname{Spec}(k') \xrightarrow{\text{structure}} \operatorname{Spec}(k) is also the structure morphism of the k-algebra k'. Hence the two compositions are equal, and condition (i) is satisfied.

By the universal property, there exists a unique \operatorname{Spec}(k')-morphism h : \operatorname{Spec}(k') \to C \times_k \operatorname{Spec}(k') = C_{k'} corresponding to the pair (g, \operatorname{id}). This h is a k'-rational point of C_{k'}.

Conclusion. We have constructed a finite separable extension k'/k (Steps 4 and 5) and a k'-rational point h : \operatorname{Spec}(k') \to C_{k'} (Step 6). This completes the proof."
}

lemma_129.statement: Let f: Y \to X be a finite locally free morphism of rank r \ge 1 between regular noetherian schemes, and let n > 0. If the class of f_*\mathcal{O}_Y in K_0(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} equals r times the class of \mathcal{O}_X in K_0(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}, then the composite f_* \circ f^*: K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} \to K_n(X)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q} is multiplication by r.
lemma_129.proof: We prove the corrected trace composite f_* ∘ f^* on K_n(X)⊗_Z Q, not the norm composite. Let v = [f_*O_Y] and u = [O_X] in K_0(X). The hypothesis is v⊗1 = r u⊗1 in K_0(X)⊗_Z Q. Put w = v - r u. Then w⊗1 = 0. Since K_0(X)⊗_Z Q is the localization of the abelian group K_0(X) at the set of nonzero integers, the relation w⊗1 = 0 means that there exists a nonzero integer t with t w = 0 in K_0(X); choose m > 0 with m w = 0. Hence m v = m r u in K_0(X). Form Y' = ∐_{i=1}^m Y and let f': Y' → X be the morphism induced by f on each component. A finite disjoint union of regular noetherian schemes is regular noetherian, because regularity is a property of local rings and noetherianity is preserved under finite disjoint unions. The morphism f' is finite locally free of rank m r: locally on X it is the disjoint union of m copies of f, and f'_*O_{Y'} = ⊕_{i=1}^m f_*O_Y is a vector bundle of rank m r. Its class in K_0(X) is m v = m r u. Apply lemma_58 to f' and the given n > 0. It gives that (f')_* ∘ (f')^* is multiplication by m r on K_n(X)⊗_Z Q. We now identify this endomorphism with m times the original one. For a finite disjoint union, K-theory is additive: the category of vector bundles on Y' is the product of the categories of vector bundles on the m copies of Y, so K_n(Y') is isomorphic to the direct sum over i=1,...,m of K_n(Y), and tensoring with Q preserves this finite direct sum. Under this identification, (f')^* sends x to (f^*x, ..., f^*x), and the transfer (f')_* sends (y_1, ..., y_m) to the sum over i=1,...,m of f_* y_i; this follows because pullback is componentwise and pushforward of a vector bundle on a disjoint union is the direct sum of the component pushforwards, with K-theory additive. Therefore, for every x in K_n(X)⊗_Z Q, ((f')_* ∘ (f')^*)(x) = the sum over i=1,...,m of f_* f^* x = m (f_* ∘ f^*)(x). Thus m (f_* ∘ f^*) = m r id_{K_n(X)⊗_Z Q} as endomorphisms of the Q-vector space K_n(X)⊗_Z Q. Since m is nonzero in Q, multiply by 1/m to obtain f_* ∘ f^* = r id_{K_n(X)⊗_Z Q}. This is the required conclusion.

lemma_133.statement: Let F be a field, let s be an indeterminate over F, and let n > 1. Then the homomorphism K_n(F) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q \to K_n(F[s]) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q induced by the inclusion F \hookrightarrow F[s] is an isomorphism of \mathbf Q-vector spaces.
lemma_133.proof: Let R=F. First note that F is a regular noetherian ring: a field is noetherian, and its only prime ideal is (0), which is generated by the empty set of elements, so it is regular. Let s be an indeterminate over F. We use Quillen's homotopy invariance theorem for algebraic K-theory of regular noetherian rings, which states that if A is a regular noetherian ring and t is an indeterminate over A, then for every integer m \ge 1 the ring inclusion A \hookrightarrow A[t] induces an isomorphism K_m(A) \cong K_m(A[t]) of abelian groups. Applying this theorem with A=F and t=s gives, since n>1 and hence n\ge 1, an isomorphism \varphi: K_n(F) \to K_n(F[s]) induced by the inclusion F \hookrightarrow F[s]. Now tensor this isomorphism with \mathbf{Q} over \mathbf{Z}. Tensoring is a functor from abelian groups to abelian groups, so if \varphi has inverse \varphi^{-1}, then \varphi \otimes 1_{\mathbf{Q}} has inverse \varphi^{-1} \otimes 1_{\mathbf{Q}}. Therefore \varphi \otimes 1_{\mathbf{Q}}: K_n(F) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} \to K_n(F[s]) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} is an isomorphism of \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces. By construction, this map is precisely the homomorphism induced by the inclusion F \hookrightarrow F[s] after tensoring with \mathbf{Q}. Hence the stated homomorphism is an isomorphism of \mathbf{Q}-vector spaces.

lemma_134.statement: Let k be a finite field, let t be an indeterminate over k, let F be a finite separable extension of k(t), and let A be the integral closure of k[t] in F. Then Spec A is a smooth affine curve over k.
lemma_134.proof:
Let R=k[t] and K=k(t). Put S=A. Since k is a field, R is a PID; in particular R is Noetherian, integrally closed in K, and dim R=1.

First we show S is finite over R. For x in F, let m_x(T)=T^m+a_{m-1}T^{m-1}+...+a_0 in K[T] be its monic minimal polynomial over K. Write a_i=u_i/v_i with u_i,v_i in R and v_i != 0. Let c=v_0 v_1 ... v_{m-1}. If y=c x, then x=y/c, so 0=(y/c)^m+a_{m-1}(y/c)^{m-1}+...+a_0. Multiplying by c^m gives y^m+a_{m-1} c y^{m-1}+...+a_0 c^m=0, and each coefficient a_i c^{m-i} is in R. Thus y is integral over R, hence y in S. Therefore for every x in F there exists 0 != c in R with c x in S.

Choose a K-basis x_1,...,x_d of F. By the preceding paragraph choose 0 != c_i in R with c_i x_i in S. Set B=sum_{i=1}^d R c_i x_i. Then B is a finite R-submodule of S, and B spans F over K because each x_i=(1/c_i)(c_i x_i) lies in K B.

Define B^* to be the set of y in F such that Tr_{F/K}(y b) in R for all b in B. We claim B^* is finite over R. The module B is torsion-free and finitely generated over the PID R, hence free of finite rank. The trace pairing (u,v) -> Tr_{F/K}(u v) is nondegenerate because F/K is finite separable. Since B spans F, the R-linear map B^* -> Hom_R(B,R), y -> (b -> Tr(y b)), is injective. Its target is a finite free R-module, so B^* is finite over R.

We now show S subset B^*. Let s in S and b in B. By construction b in S, and S is the integral closure of R in F, hence a subring of F (sums and products of integral elements are integral); therefore s b in S and s b is integral over R. Let sigma_1,...,sigma_d be the K-embeddings of F into a fixed algebraic closure of K. Each sigma_i(s b) satisfies the same monic polynomial over R as s b, so each sigma_i(s b) is integral over R; hence Tr(s b)=sum_i sigma_i(s b) is integral over R. Since R is integrally closed in K, Tr(s b) in R. Thus s in B^*. Consequently S is a submodule of the finite R-module B^*, so S is finite over R.

Thus A=S is a finite k[t]-module. In particular A is Noetherian and of finite type over k, and Spec A is affine and finite over the affine line over k.

Next we identify A as a Dedekind domain. It is a domain because A subset F. Its fraction field is F: if x in F, the first paragraph gives 0 != c in R with c x in A, so x=(c x)/c in Frac(A). It is integrally closed in F: if y in F is integral over A, then y is integral over R by transitivity of integrality, and therefore y in A by definition of A. It is Noetherian, and because it is integral (indeed finite) over R, dim A=dim R=1; this follows from lying over and incomparability for integral extensions. Hence A is a Noetherian integrally closed domain of dimension one, i.e. a Dedekind domain.

By the standard local description of Dedekind domains (equivalently, a noetherian integrally closed local domain of dimension one is a DVR), for every nonzero prime p of A the localization A_p is a DVR, and A_(0)=F is a field. A DVR is a regular local ring, and a field is regular; therefore every local ring A_p is regular, so A is a regular ring.

Finally, k is a finite field, hence perfect. A is a regular k-algebra of finite type. For a perfect field, a finite type k-algebra is smooth over k if and only if it is regular; one way to see this is that regularity over a perfect field is stable under all field extensions, so A is geometrically regular, and flatness over k is automatic. Hence Spec A is smooth over k.

Since Spec A is an integral affine k-scheme of finite type of dimension one and is smooth over k, it is a smooth affine curve over k.

lemma_135.statement: Let k be a finite field, let C be a smooth projective geometrically integral curve over k, and let n > 1. Then the direct sum over all closed points p of C of K_{n-1}(k(p)) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} is zero.
lemma_135.proof:
Let k be a finite field, let C be a smooth projective geometrically integral curve over k, and let n > 1. We must show that the direct sum \bigoplus_{p \in C^{(1)}} K_{n-1}(k(p)) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q} equals zero, where C^{(1)} denotes the set of closed points of C.

Step 1 (each residue field k(p) is a finite field). Since C is a smooth projective variety over k of dimension 1, in particular C is a scheme of finite type over k. Let p be any closed point of C. Choose an affine open neighbourhood U = Spec(A) of p, where A is a finitely generated k-algebra (this exists because C is of finite type over k). The point p corresponds to a maximal ideal \mathfrak{m} of A, and the residue field is k(p) \cong A/\mathfrak{m}. Since A is a finitely generated k-algebra, A/\mathfrak{m} is a finitely generated field extension of k. By Zariski's lemma (a finitely generated field extension of a field is a finite algebraic extension), k(p) is a finite extension of k. Since k is a finite field, every finite extension of k is again a finite field. Therefore k(p) is a finite field for every closed point p of C.

Step 2 (each summand vanishes). Since n > 1, the integer n - 1 satisfies n - 1 > 0. Fix a closed point p of C. By Step 1, k(p) is a finite field. Applying the proved lemma lemma_14 (user eoinm) to the finite field k(p) and the positive integer n - 1, we obtain K_{n-1}(k(p)) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q} = 0. Since p was arbitrary, K_{n-1}(k(p)) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q} = 0 for every closed point p \in C^{(1)}.

Step 3 (the direct sum of zero vector spaces is zero). We have shown that for every p \in C^{(1)}, the vector space K_{n-1}(k(p)) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q} is the zero vector space. The direct sum \bigoplus_{p \in C^{(1)}} 0 is itself the zero vector space: an element of a direct sum is, by definition, a tuple with only finitely many nonzero coordinates; since every coordinate space is {0}, every such tuple is the zero tuple. Hence \bigoplus_{p \in C^{(1)}} K_{n-1}(k(p)) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Q} = \bigoplus_{p \in C^{(1)}} 0 = 0.

This completes the proof.

lemma_137.statement: Let k be a field, let k'/k be a finite extension of degree r, let X be a scheme of finite type over k, let X_{k'}=X\times_k \operatorname{Spec} k', and let f:X_{k'}\to X be the base change morphism. Then f_*\mathcal{O}_{X_{k'}} is isomorphic to \mathcal{O}_X^{\oplus r} as an \mathcal{O}_X-module.
lemma_137.proof: Let S = Spec k and S' = Spec k'. Since k'/k is a finite field extension of degree r, the morphism S' -> S is finite, hence affine. The morphism f: X_{k'} = X ×_S S' -> X is the base change of S' -> S along X -> S, and base change of an affine morphism is affine, so f is affine. Now take any affine open U = Spec R of X. Because X is a k-scheme, R is a k-algebra, and f^{-1}(U) = U ×_S S' = Spec(R ⊗_k k'). Therefore (f_* O_{X_{k'}})(U) = Γ(f^{-1}(U), O_{X_{k'}}) = Γ(Spec(R ⊗_k k'), O) = R ⊗_k k'. Consider the quasi-coherent O_X-module O_X ⊗_k k'. By definition, on the affine open U = Spec R its sections are R ⊗_k k'. Since f is affine, f_* O_{X_{k'}} is quasi-coherent, and the natural O_X-linear map O_X ⊗_k k' -> f_* O_{X_{k'}} is an isomorphism on every affine open; hence it is an isomorphism of sheaves of O_X-modules. It remains to identify O_X ⊗_k k' with O_X^{⊕ r}. As a k-vector space, k' has dimension r, so choose a k-basis e_1,...,e_r of k'. Define Φ: O_X^{⊕ r} -> O_X ⊗_k k' by Φ((a_1,...,a_r)) = Σ_{i=1}^r a_i ⊗ e_i. This is O_X-linear. Define Ψ: O_X ⊗_k k' -> O_X^{⊕ r} by Ψ(a ⊗ x) = (a x_1,...,a x_r) whenever x = Σ_{i=1}^r x_i e_i. The coefficients x_i are uniquely determined, so Ψ is well-defined, and it is O_X-linear. For (a_1,...,a_r) in O_X^{⊕ r}, we have Ψ(Φ((a_1,...,a_r))) = Ψ(Σ a_i ⊗ e_i) = (a_1,...,a_r). Conversely, if x = Σ x_i e_i, then Φ(Ψ(a ⊗ x)) = Φ((a x_1,...,a x_r)) = Σ a x_i ⊗ e_i = a ⊗ Σ x_i e_i = a ⊗ x. Thus Ψ is the inverse of Φ, and O_X ⊗_k k' ≅ O_X^{⊕ r} as O_X-modules. Composing the isomorphisms f_* O_{X_{k'}} ≅ O_X ⊗_k k' and O_X ⊗_k k' ≅ O_X^{⊕ r} gives the desired isomorphism f_* O_{X_{k'}} ≅ O_X^{⊕ r} as O_X-modules.

lemma_142.statement: Let $k$ be a finite field, let $d\ge 1$ and $n>1$, let $t_1,\ldots,t_d$ be indeterminates over $k$, and let $p$ range over the height-one prime ideals of $k[t_1,\ldots,t_d]$, where $k(p)$ denotes the fraction field of $k[t_1,\ldots,t_d]/p$. Then the natural Gersten homomorphism $K_n(k(t_1,\ldots,t_d))\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q\to \bigoplus_{p} K_{n-1}(k(p))\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$ is injective.
lemma_142.proof:
Let A = k[t_1,...,t_d] and F = k(t_1,...,t_d). Let p range over the height-one prime ideals of A, and let k(p) = Frac(A/p). Denote by ∂: K_n(F) → ⊕_p K_{n-1}(k(p)) the Gersten boundary map. We prove that ∂⊗1_Q: K_n(F)⊗_Z Q → ⊕_p K_{n-1}(k(p))⊗_Z Q is injective.

1. Exactness of the Gersten sequence. A is a regular noetherian domain: it is a polynomial ring over a field, hence noetherian by the Hilbert basis theorem and a domain because k is a field; it is regular because every local ring of a polynomial ring over a field is a regular local ring. We use the standard Gersten form of Quillen's localization theorem: if A is a regular noetherian domain with fraction field F, then for n>1 the sequence K_n(A) → K_n(F) → ⊕_{ht p=1} K_{n-1}(Frac(A/p)) is exact at K_n(F). Applying this to our A gives ker(∂) = im(K_n(A) → K_n(F)).

The ring Z is a PID, so Q is flat over Z. Tensoring the exact three-term sequence with Q therefore preserves exactness at K_n(F)⊗_Z Q. Tensor product also commutes with direct sums, so (⊕_p K_{n-1}(k(p)))⊗_Z Q ≅ ⊕_p (K_{n-1}(k(p))⊗_Z Q). Consequently, ker(∂⊗1_Q) = im((K_n(A) → K_n(F))⊗1_Q). The right-hand side is a quotient of K_n(A)⊗_Z Q, namely the image of the map K_n(A)⊗_Z Q → K_n(F)⊗_Z Q. Hence it is enough to show K_n(A)⊗_Z Q = 0.

2. Vanishing of K_n(A)⊗_Z Q. We use Quillen's homotopy invariance theorem: for any commutative ring R and any integer m>1, the inclusion R → R[s] induces an isomorphism K_m(R) → K_m(R[s]); after tensoring with Q, K_m(R)⊗_Z Q ≅ K_m(R[s])⊗_Z Q. In particular it applies to the noetherian commutative rings that occur below. When R = A_i, this adds the variable t_{i+1} to the polynomial ring itself; it does not replace A_i by its fraction field.

Set A_i = k[t_1,...,t_i] for 0≤i≤d, with A_0 = k. First consider A_1 = k[t_1]. By the proved lemma lemma_133 with F = k and s = t_1, the map K_n(k)⊗_Z Q → K_n(k[t_1])⊗_Z Q is an isomorphism. By the proved lemma lemma_14, since k is finite and n>0, K_n(k)⊗_Z Q = 0. Therefore K_n(A_1)⊗_Z Q = 0.

Now assume i≥1 and K_n(A_i)⊗_Z Q = 0. Apply homotopy invariance with R = A_i and s = t_{i+1}. Since A_i[t_{i+1}] = A_{i+1} and n>1, we obtain an isomorphism K_n(A_{i+1})⊗_Z Q ≅ K_n(A_i)⊗_Z Q = 0. By induction on i from 1 to d-1, K_n(A_d)⊗_Z Q = 0. If d=1, the induction is empty and the conclusion already follows from lemma_133 and lemma_14.

3. Conclusion. Since K_n(A)⊗_Z Q = 0, the image im((K_n(A) → K_n(F))⊗1_Q) is zero. By the equality in step 1, ker(∂⊗1_Q)=0. Thus ∂⊗1_Q is injective, which is the desired statement.

lemma_146.statement: Let $k$ be a finite field, let $d \geq 0$, let $t_1, \ldots, t_d$ be indeterminates over $k$, and let $n > 1$. Then $K_n(k[t_1, \ldots, t_d]) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0$.
lemma_146.proof:
Let k be a finite field, let d ≥ 0, let t_1,...,t_d be indeterminates over k, and let n > 1. We split according to d.

Case d = 0. Then the polynomial ring k[t_1,...,t_d] is the ring k itself (the polynomial ring in zero variables). Since n > 1 implies n > 0, the proved lemma lemma_14 applies and gives K_n(k) ⊗_Z Q = 0. Hence K_n(k[t_1,...,t_d]) ⊗_Z Q = 0.

Case d ≥ 1. Put r = d. Then r is a positive integer, and t_1,...,t_r are indeterminates over the finite field k. The proved lemma lemma_38 states that for a finite field k, a positive integer r, indeterminates t_1,...,t_r over k, and n > 1, one has K_n(k[t_1,...,t_r]) ⊗_Z Q = 0. Applying this with r = d yields K_n(k[t_1,...,t_d]) ⊗_Z Q = 0.

Both possible cases for d are covered, so the desired vanishing holds.

lemma_147.statement: Let $U$ be a regular noetherian scheme, let $Z$ be a regular closed subscheme of $U$, let $V=U\setminus Z$, and let $n>1$. If $K_n(Z)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0$ and $K_n(V)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0$, then $K_n(U)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q=0$.
lemma_147.proof:
Let U be a regular noetherian scheme, let Z be a regular closed subscheme of U, let V = U \setminus Z, and let n > 1. We are given that K_n(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q = 0 and K_n(V) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q = 0. By the proved lemma_54, the sequence

K_n(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q \to K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q \to K_n(V) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q \to K_{n-1}(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q

is exact. Under the two vanishing hypotheses, this exact sequence becomes

0 \to K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q \to 0 \to K_{n-1}(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q.

Exactness at the middle term K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q says that the kernel of the map K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q \to 0 equals the image of the map 0 \to K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q. The kernel of the map to 0 is all of K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q, while the image of the map from 0 is 0. Hence K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q = 0. This proves the desired conclusion.

lemma_149_boundary_t_nonzero.statement: Let $k$ be a finite field, let $d \ge 0$, let $t_1,\ldots,t_d$ be indeterminates over $k$, and let $t$ be another indeterminate. Put $R=k[t_1,\ldots,t_d]$. Then the image of the class of $t$ in $K_1(R[t,t^{-1}])\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$ under the boundary map $K_1(R[t,t^{-1}])\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q \to K_0(R)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$ in the localization sequence for $R\subset R[t]$ is nonzero.
lemma_149_boundary_t_nonzero.proof:
Looking at the target lemma and the feedback, I need to prove that the boundary map sends the class of $t$ to a nonzero element. The key correction from the feedback is to use the correct form of the localization sequence and the correct naturality square. Let me check the relevant lemmas I found.

Now I have what I need:
- **lemma_11**: $K_0(k) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ for a field $k$
- **lemma_30a_k1**: $K_1(\mathbf{A}^1_k) \otimes \mathbb{Q} \cong K_1(k) \otimes \mathbb{Q}$
- **lemma_15**: $K_1(k) \otimes \mathbb{Q} = 0$ for a finite field $k$

These let me handle the base case cleanly. The strategy is: (1) base case $d=0$ via the localization sequence for $k[t]$, showing $\delta_k \otimes \mathrm{id}$ is an isomorphism $\mathbb{Q} 	o \mathbb{Q}$; (2) general case via the naturality square with the evaluation map $\mathrm{ev}: R[t] 	o k[t]$.

{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_149_boundary_t_nonzero",
  "cited_lemmas": [
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_11"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_30a_k1"},
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_15"}
  ],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "We prove that (delta_R \otimes id)([t] \otimes 1) \neq 0 in K_0(R) \otimes_Z Q, where delta_R: K_1(R[t,t^{-1}]) -> K_0(R) is the connecting (boundary) homomorphism in the Quillen localization sequence for the inclusion R \subset R[t] (equivalently, for A = R[t] with the non-zero-divisor f = t, giving A/f \cong R and A_f = R[t,t^{-1}]).

STEP 1: The localization sequence and its exactness.

For a regular ring A and a non-zero-divisor f \in A, the Quillen localization theorem gives the long exact sequence
  ... -> K_n(A/f) -> K_n(A) -> K_n(A_f) ->^{delta_A} K_{n-1}(A/f) -> K_{n-1}(A) -> ...
where A_f = A[1/f] and delta_A is the connecting homomorphism. In the present case A = R[t] = k[t_1,...,t_d,t] and f = t. Since R[t] is a polynomial ring over a field, it is a domain, so t is a non-zero-divisor. We have A/f = R[t]/(t) \cong R and A_f = R[t,t^{-1}]. The relevant fragment (for n = 1) is
  K_1(R) -> K_1(R[t]) -> K_1(R[t,t^{-1}]) ->^{delta_R} K_0(R) -> K_0(R[t]).
By exactness at K_1(R[t,t^{-1}]):
  (1)  ker(delta_R) = im( K_1(R[t]) -> K_1(R[t,t^{-1}]) ).

STEP 2: The base case d = 0 (R = k).

We show that delta_k([t] \otimes 1) \neq 0 in K_0(k) \otimes_Z Q.

By (1) with R = k:
  ker(delta_k) = im( K_1(k[t]) -> K_1(k[t,t^{-1}]) ).
Tensoring with Q (an exact functor on abelian groups) preserves kernels and images of the induced maps, so
  ker(delta_k \otimes id) = im( (K_1(k[t]) \otimes Q) -> (K_1(k[t,t^{-1}]) \otimes Q) ).
By lemma_30a_k1 (with A^1_k = Spec(k[t])), K_1(k[t]) \otimes_Z Q \cong K_1(k) \otimes_Z Q. By lemma_15 (k is a finite field), K_1(k) \otimes_Z Q = 0. Hence K_1(k[t]) \otimes_Z Q = 0, and therefore
  ker(delta_k \otimes id) = 0.
So delta_k \otimes id: K_1(k[t,t^{-1}]) \otimes Q -> K_0(k) \otimes Q is injective.

We now compute the dimensions of source and target.
- Source: k[t,t^{-1}] is a PID (Euclidean with the degree function on Laurent polynomials), so K_1(k[t,t^{-1}]) \cong (k[t,t^{-1}])^\times. The units of k[t,t^{-1}] are exactly { a t^n : a \in k^\times, n \in Z }, so (k[t,t^{-1}])^\times \cong k^\times \times Z, with t corresponding to (1,1). Since k is finite, k^\times is a finite group, so k^\times \otimes_Z Q = 0. Thus
  K_1(k[t,t^{-1}]) \otimes_Z Q \cong (k^\times \times Z) \otimes_Z Q \cong (k^\times \otimes Q) \oplus (Z \otimes Q) \cong 0 \oplus Q \cong Q.
- Target: By lemma_11, K_0(k) \cong Z (every finitely generated projective k-module is free, and the Grothendieck group of finitely generated free k-modules is Z, generated by [k]). Hence K_0(k) \otimes_Z Q \cong Z \otimes_Z Q \cong Q.

Therefore delta_k \otimes id is an injective linear map Q -> Q, i.e., an isomorphism.

Under the identification K_1(k[t,t^{-1}]) \otimes Q \cong Q, the element [t] \otimes 1 corresponds to (1,1) \otimes 1 = (1\otimes 1, 1\otimes 1) = (0, 1) = 1 \in Q, so [t] \otimes 1 \neq 0. Since delta_k \otimes id is an isomorphism,
  (2)  delta_k([t] \otimes 1) \neq 0  in K_0(k) \otimes_Z Q.

STEP 3: The general case d > 0, via naturality of the localization sequence.

Let ev: R -> k be the k-algebra homomorphism defined by ev(t_i) = 0 for i = 1,...,d. It extends to a k-algebra homomorphism ev: R[t,t^{-1}] -> k[t,t^{-1}] by ev(t) = t (and ev(t_i) = 0).

The Quillen localization sequence is functorial in the following sense: if phi: A -> B is a homomorphism of regular rings and f \in A is a non-zero-divisor with phi(f) a non-zero-divisor in B, then phi induces a morphism of the associated localization triangles (A/f -> A -> A_f ->), and hence for each n >= 1 the square
  K_n(A_f) --delta_A--> K_{n-1}(A/f)
    | phi_*                | phi_*
    v                      v
  K_n(B_f) --delta_B--> K_{n-1}(B/f)
commutes, i.e., phi_* \circ delta_A = delta_B \circ phi_*.

Apply this with A = R[t], B = k[t], phi = ev, and f = t. The hypotheses are verified:
- R[t] = k[t_1,...,t_d,t] and k[t] are regular rings (polynomial rings over a field).
- t is a non-zero-divisor in R[t] because R[t] is a domain.
- ev(t) = t is a non-zero-divisor in k[t] because k[t] is a domain.

For n = 1, the commutative square is
  K_1(R[t,t^{-1}]) --delta_R--> K_0(R)
    | ev_*                       | ev_*
    v                            v
  K_1(k[t,t^{-1}]) --delta_k--> K_0(k).

Tensoring the entire commutative diagram with Q (the functor - \otimes_Z Q is additive and preserves commutative squares of group homomorphisms) gives
  (3)  (ev_* \otimes id) \circ (delta_R \otimes id) = (delta_k \otimes id) \circ (ev_* \otimes id).

Now, ev_*([t]) = [t] in K_1(k[t,t^{-1}]): the homomorphism ev: R[t,t^{-1}] -> k[t,t^{-1}] sends the unit t \in R[t,t^{-1}]^\times to the unit t \in k[t,t^{-1}]^\times, and K_1 of a ring is generated by the classes of its units (for a PID A, K_1(A) \cong A^\times).

Applying (3) to the element [t] \otimes 1 \in K_1(R[t,t^{-1}]) \otimes_Z Q:
  (ev_* \otimes id)( (delta_R \otimes id)([t] \otimes 1) )
    = (delta_k \otimes id)( ev_*([t] \otimes 1) )
    = (delta_k \otimes id)( [t] \otimes 1 )
    \neq 0,
where the last inequality is (2).

Since ev_* \otimes id: K_0(R) \otimes_Z Q -> K_0(k) \otimes_Z Q is a group homomorphism, it sends 0 to 0. By contrapositive, if (delta_R \otimes id)([t] \otimes 1) were 0, then (ev_* \otimes id)(0) = 0, contradicting the displayed inequality. Hence
  (delta_R \otimes id)([t] \otimes 1) \neq 0  in K_0(R) \otimes_Z Q.

This is the desired conclusion. QED."
}

lemma_148_vector_bundle_extension.statement: Let $U$ be a regular noetherian scheme, let $V$ be a nonempty open subset of $U$, and let $E$ be a vector bundle on $V$. Then there exists a coherent sheaf $F$ on $U$ such that $F|_V \cong E$.

lemma_152.statement: Let U be a regular noetherian scheme, let Z be a regular closed subscheme of U, let V=U\setminus Z, and let n>1. If K_n(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q = 0 and K_{n-1}(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q = 0, then the restriction map K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q \to K_n(V) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q is an isomorphism.
lemma_152.proof:
Let U be a regular noetherian scheme, let Z be a regular closed subscheme of U, let V = U \setminus Z, and let n > 1. Assume K_n(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q = 0 and K_{n-1}(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q = 0.

By lemma_54, the sequence
K_n(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q \to K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q \to K_n(V) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q \to K_{n-1}(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q
induced by the inclusion Z \hookrightarrow U and the restriction U \to V is exact. Denote the middle map by res: K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q \to K_n(V) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q.

First, we show res is injective. Exactness at K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q says that the kernel of res is the image of the map K_n(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q \to K_n(U) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q. Since K_n(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q = 0, this image is {0}. Hence ker(res) = {0}, so res is injective.

Next, we show res is surjective. Exactness at K_n(V) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q says that the image of res is the kernel of the map K_n(V) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q \to K_{n-1}(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q. Since K_{n-1}(Z) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q = 0, this map is the zero map, and the kernel of the zero map is all of K_n(V) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q. Therefore im(res) = K_n(V) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q, so res is surjective.

Thus res is both injective and surjective. Since it is a homomorphism of \mathbf Q-vector spaces, it is an isomorphism. This proves the claim.

lemma_151.statement: Let f:Y \to X be a finite locally free morphism of rank r \ge 1 between regular noetherian schemes, let n > 0, and suppose f_*\mathcal O_Y is isomorphic to \mathcal O_X^{\oplus r}. If K_n(Y) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q = 0, then K_n(X) \otimes_{\mathbf Z} \mathbf Q = 0.
lemma_151.proof:
Let f: Y → X be a finite locally free morphism of rank r ≥ 1 between regular noetherian schemes, let n > 0, and suppose f_*O_Y is isomorphic to O_X^{⊕ r} as O_X-modules. We prove K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q = 0.

Step 1 (the class hypothesis for lemma_129). Since f is finite locally free of rank r, f_*O_Y is a locally free O_X-module of rank r, hence defines a class [f_*O_Y] in K_0(X). The given isomorphism f_*O_Y ≅ O_X^{⊕ r} of O_X-modules implies, by the defining relations of the Grothendieck group K_0(X) (namely [E ⊕ F] = [E] + [F] for locally free sheaves E, F), that
  [f_*O_Y] = [O_X^{⊕ r}] = [O_X] + [O_X] + ⋯ + [O_X] (r summands) = r·[O_X]
in K_0(X). Tensoring with Q (which is exact, as Q is flat over Z), the image of [f_*O_Y] in K_0(X) ⊗_Z Q equals r times the image of [O_X] in K_0(X) ⊗_Z Q. Thus the hypothesis of lemma_129 is satisfied.

Step 2 (apply lemma_129). By lemma_129 (cited above: user_id eoinm, lemma_id lemma_129), applied to the finite locally free morphism f: Y → X of rank r ≥ 1 between regular noetherian schemes with n > 0 and the class equality from Step 1, the composite
  f_* ∘ f^*: K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q → K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q
where f^*: K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q → K_n(Y) ⊗_Z Q is the pullback (base-change) map and f_*: K_n(Y) ⊗_Z Q → K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q is the transfer (pushforward) map, is multiplication by r. That is, for every v ∈ K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q,
  (f_* ∘ f^*)(v) = r·v.

Step 3 (the composite is zero). By hypothesis, K_n(Y) ⊗_Z Q = 0. The transfer map f_*: K_n(Y) ⊗_Z Q → K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q is a Q-linear map whose domain is the zero Q-vector space; there is exactly one Q-linear map from the zero vector space to any vector space, namely the zero map. Hence f_* = 0 as a map K_n(Y) ⊗_Z Q → K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q. Consequently, for every v ∈ K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q,
  (f_* ∘ f^*)(v) = f_*(f^*(v)) = 0,
since f^*(v) ∈ K_n(Y) ⊗_Z Q = 0. Thus the composite f_* ∘ f^* is the zero endomorphism of K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q.

Step 4 (conclusion). Combining Steps 2 and 3: for every v ∈ K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q, we have r·v = 0. Now K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q is a Q-vector space, and r is a positive integer, hence a nonzero element of Q. Multiplication by r on a Q-vector space is an automorphism, with inverse given by multiplication by 1/r ∈ Q. Therefore r·v = 0 implies v = (1/r)·(r·v) = (1/r)·0 = 0. Since v was arbitrary, every element of K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q is zero, i.e.,
  K_n(X) ⊗_Z Q = 0.

This completes the proof.

lemma_153_purely_inseparable_differentia.statement: Let F be a field and let M/F be a finite purely inseparable extension. Then M=F if and only if the module of Kähler differentials Ω_{M/F} is zero.
lemma_153_purely_inseparable_differentia.proof:
THEOREM. Let F be a field and let M/F be a finite purely inseparable extension. Then M = F if and only if the module of Kähler differentials Ω_{M/F} is zero.

PROOF.

(⇒) Assume M = F. Then Ω_{M/F} = Ω_{F/F}. The module Ω_{F/F} is, by definition, the module generated as an F-module by the symbols {d(a) : a ∈ F} subject to the relations d(a+b) = d(a)+d(b), d(ab) = a·d(b) + b·d(a), and d(c) = 0 for all c ∈ F (the last being part of the definition of an F-derivation). Since d(c) = 0 for every c ∈ F, every generator is zero, hence Ω_{F/F} = 0.

(⇐) We prove the contrapositive: if M ≠ F, then Ω_{M/F} ≠ 0.

STEP 1 (The characteristic is p > 0). Suppose for contradiction that char(F) = 0. Since M/F is finite, it is algebraic. In characteristic zero, every algebraic extension is separable: for any α ∈ M, the minimal polynomial m_α(T) ∈ F[T] has no repeated roots (equivalently, gcd(m_α, m_α') = 1 in F[T], since char 0 implies m_α' ≠ 0 for m_α nonconstant, and a common root of m_α and m_α' would give a repeated root, contradicting separability of the algebraic closure in char 0). On the other hand, since M/F is purely inseparable, every α ∈ M has m_α(T) with exactly one distinct root in an algebraic closure F̄, namely α itself. A polynomial over a field that is both separable (all roots distinct) and has exactly one distinct root must have degree 1. Thus m_α(T) = T − a for some a ∈ F, giving α = a ∈ F. Since this holds for every α ∈ M, we get M = F, contradicting M ≠ F. Therefore char(F) = p > 0 for some prime p.

STEP 2 (A claim about minimal polynomials of purely inseparable elements).

CLAIM. Let K be a field of characteristic p > 0, let α be purely inseparable over K with α ∉ K, and let m(T) ∈ K[T] be the minimal polynomial of α over K. Then m(T) = T^{p^e} − c for some integer e ≥ 1 and some c ∈ K, and deg m = p^e.

PROOF OF CLAIM. Let n = deg m. Since α ∉ K, we have n ≥ 2. Since α is purely inseparable over K, in K̄[T] (where K̄ is an algebraic closure of K), the polynomial m(T) has α as its only root, with multiplicity n. Hence m(T) = (T − α)^n in K̄[T].

We first prove that n = p^e for some e ≥ 1. Suppose for contradiction that n is not a power of p. Write n = p^s · q where s ≥ 0, p ∤ q, and q ≥ 2 (this is the unique factorization of n into a p-power times a p-foreign part, and n not being a p-power forces q ≥ 2).

Then m(T) = (T−α)^{p^s q} = ((T−α)^q)^{p^s}. Let h(T) = (T−α)^q = Σ_{i=0}^{q} a_i T^i where a_i = C(q,i)·(−α)^{q−i} ∈ K̄ (with C(q,i) = binomial coefficient). In characteristic p, the Freshman's dream gives h(T)^{p^s} = Σ_{i=0}^{q} a_i^{p^s} T^{i·p^s} (since (Σ b_i)^{p^s} = Σ b_i^{p^s} in characteristic p).

Since m(T) = h(T)^{p^s} ∈ K[T], each coefficient a_i^{p^s} ∈ K. In particular, a_{q−1} = C(q,q−1)·(−α) = −qα, so a_{q−1}^{p^s} = (−qα)^{p^s} = (−1)^{p^s} · q^{p^s} · α^{p^s} ∈ K. Since p ∤ q, the integer q is nonzero in K (its image under Z → K is not zero), hence q^{p^s} ≠ 0 in K. Also (−1)^{p^s} = ±1 ∈ K^×. Therefore α^{p^s} = a_{q−1}^{p^s} / ((−1)^{p^s} · q^{p^s}) ∈ K.

Now consider g(T) = T^{p^s} − α^{p^s} ∈ K[T] (the coefficients are in K since α^{p^s} ∈ K). We have g(α) = α^{p^s} − α^{p^s} = 0. Since m(T) is the minimal polynomial of α over K, m(T) divides g(T) in K[T] (by the division algorithm in K[T]: any polynomial in K[T] vanishing at α is a multiple of the minimal polynomial). But deg m = p^s·q and deg g = p^s. Since q ≥ 2, deg m > deg g. If g = m·r for some r ∈ K[T], r ≠ 0, then deg g = deg m + deg r ≥ deg m > deg g, a contradiction. (If r = 0, then g = 0, but g is a nonzero polynomial of degree p^s.) This is impossible, contradicting the assumption that n is not a power of p.

Hence n = p^e for some e ≥ 1 (the bound e ≥ 1 follows from n ≥ 2 and p^0 = 1 < 2).

Finally, m(T) = (T−α)^{p^e}. By the Freshman's dream in characteristic p, (T−α)^{p^e} = T^{p^e} − α^{p^e}. To verify: for e = 1, (T−α)^p = T^p + (−α)^p + Σ_{i=1}^{p−1} C(p,i)T^i(−α)^{p−i}, and C(p,i) ≡ 0 (mod p) for 0 < i < p, so (T−α)^p = T^p − α^p (noting (−1)^p = ±1 and absorbing the sign: (−α)^p = (−1)^p α^p, so T^p + (−1)^p α^p; for p odd this is T^p − α^p, for p = 2 it is T^2 + α^2 = T^2 − α^2 since −1 = 1 in F_2). For e ≥ 2, apply the e = 1 case to (T−α)^{p^e} = ((T−α)^{p^{e−1}})^p = (T^{p^{e−1}} − α^{p^{e−1}})^p = T^{p^e} − α^{p^e}. Thus m(T) = T^{p^e} − α^{p^e}. Since m(T) ∈ K[T], the constant term −α^{p^e} ∈ K, so c := α^{p^e} ∈ K, and m(T) = T^{p^e} − c. This proves the claim. ∎ (end of claim)

STEP 3 (Induction on [M:F]). We prove by induction on n = [M:F] ≥ 2 that Ω_{M/F} ≠ 0.

Induction hypothesis: For every finite purely inseparable extension L/K of fields with [L:K] < n and L ≠ K, we have Ω_{L/K} ≠ 0.

Inductive step: Let M/F be a finite purely inseparable extension with [M:F] = n ≥ 2. Since M ≠ F, choose α ∈ M \ F. Then α is purely inseparable over F (as M/F is purely inseparable). Let m(T) ∈ F[T] be the minimal polynomial of α over F. By the Claim (Step 2), m(T) = T^{p^e} − c for some e ≥ 1 and c ∈ F, and deg m = p^e. Set K = F(α). Then K/F is a finite purely inseparable extension with [K:F] = p^e, and F ⊆ K ⊆ M.

CASE A: K = M (equivalently, n = p^e).
Then M = F(α) = F[α] (since α is integral over F, being a root of the monic polynomial m(T)). Thus M ≅ F[T]/(m(T)) via the evaluation map T ↦ α (the kernel is exactly (m(T)) since m is the minimal polynomial, and the image is F[α] = M).

We compute Ω_{M/F} using the standard exact sequence for a quotient. Since M = F[T]/(m(T)), there is a canonical exact sequence:
    (m(T))/(m(T))^2 → Ω_{F[T]/F} ⊗_{F[T]} M → Ω_{M/F} → 0.
Here Ω_{F[T]/F} is the free F[T]-module of rank 1 generated by dT, so Ω_{F[T]/F} ⊗_{F[T]} M is the free M-module of rank 1 generated by dα (the image of dT). The map (m(T))/(m(T))^2 → M·dα sends the class of m(T) to m'(T)·dα evaluated at T = α, i.e., to m'(α)·dα. Since (m(T))/(m(T))^2 is a cyclic M-module generated by the class of m(T), the image of the first map is the M-submodule m'(α)·dα of M·dα.

Therefore Ω_{M/F} ≅ M·dα / (m'(α)·dα).

Now m(T) = T^{p^e} − c, so m'(T) = p^e · T^{p^e−1}. Since char(F) = p, we have p^e = 0 in F, hence m'(T) = 0 in F[T], and m'(α) = 0 in M. The relation module is thus 0·dα = 0, and Ω_{M/F} ≅ M·dα, a free M-module of rank 1.

Since M is a field (hence M ≠ 0 as a ring, so 1_M ≠ 0), the element dα = 1_M·dα is nonzero in the free M-module M·dα. Therefore Ω_{M/F} ≠ 0. ✓

CASE B: K ⊊ M (equivalently, [M:K] = n/p^e ≥ 2).
Then M/K is a finite purely inseparable extension (purely inseparability is transitive: for any β ∈ M, β is purely inseparable over F, hence over K since F ⊆ K) with [M:K] = n/p^e. Since p^e ≥ p ≥ 2, we have [M:K] = n/p^e ≤ n/2 < n. Also M ≠ K by assumption. By the induction hypothesis applied to L = M, K = K (the base field of the extension M/K), we get Ω_{M/K} ≠ 0.

We now use the tower sequence for Kähler differentials. For the tower F ⊆ K ⊆ M, there is a canonical map ψ: Ω_{M/F} → Ω_{M/K} defined as follows: the universal K-derivation d_{M/K}: M → Ω_{M/K} is in particular an F-derivation (since for f ∈ F ⊆ K, d_{M/K}(f) = 0 by K-linearity of d_{M/K}, and the Leibniz rule is inherited). By the universal property of Ω_{M/F}, there exists a unique M-linear map ψ: Ω_{M/F} → Ω_{M/K} such that ψ(d_{M/F}(a)) = d_{M/K}(a) for all a ∈ M, where d_{M/F}: M → Ω_{M/F} is the universal F-derivation.

We verify that ψ is surjective. The module Ω_{M/K} is, by definition, generated as an M-module by the set {d_{M/K}(a) : a ∈ M} (this is part of the universal property: Ω_{M/K} is the quotient of the free M-module on the symbol set M by the relations encoding additivity, the Leibniz rule, and K-linearity, so the images of the generators span). For each a ∈ M, d_{M/K}(a) = ψ(d_{M/F}(a)) ∈ im(ψ). Hence im(ψ) contains all generators of Ω_{M/K} as an M-module, so im(ψ) = Ω_{M/K}, i.e., ψ is surjective.

Since ψ: Ω_{M/F} → Ω_{M/K} is surjective and Ω_{M/K} ≠ 0, it follows that Ω_{M/F} ≠ 0. ✓

This completes the induction. Therefore, for every finite purely inseparable extension M/F with M ≠ F, we have Ω_{M/F} ≠ 0.

CONCLUSION. We have shown: (i) if M = F then Ω_{M/F} = 0; (ii) if M ≠ F then Ω_{M/F} ≠ 0. These two statements together give: M = F if and only if Ω_{M/F} = 0. ∎

lemma_156.statement: Let k be a finite field, let t be an indeterminate over k, and let n > 1. Then K_n(k(t)) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \mathbf{Q} = 0.
lemma_156.proof:
Let R = k[t]. Since k is a field, R is a principal ideal domain. Its nonzero prime ideals are exactly the ideals (f) generated by monic irreducible polynomials f in R, and these are precisely the height-one prime ideals of R; the zero ideal has height 0 and is therefore not among them. For such a prime p = (f), the quotient R/p is a field, and k(p), the fraction field of R/p, is equal to R/p.

Fix a height-one prime p = (f), where f is monic irreducible of degree m ≥ 1. By the polynomial division algorithm applied to the monic polynomial f, every g ∈ R can be written uniquely as g = qf + r with r = 0 or deg r < m. Hence every class in R/(f) is represented by a polynomial of degree < m, so the classes of 1, t, t^2, ..., t^{m-1} span R/(f) as a k-vector space. If a linear combination ∑_{i=0}^{m-1} a_i t^i maps to 0 in R/(f), then f divides ∑_{i=0}^{m-1} a_i t^i. Since f is monic of degree m and ∑_{i=0}^{m-1} a_i t^i has degree < m, this forces ∑_{i=0}^{m-1} a_i t^i = 0, so all a_i = 0. Thus the classes of 1, t, ..., t^{m-1} are linearly independent and form a k-basis of R/(f). Therefore R/(f) is a finite extension of k of degree m, and in particular k(p) = R/(f) is a finite field.

Now apply lemma_142 with d = 1. It gives that the Gersten homomorphism
K_n(k(t)) ⊗_Z Q → ⊕_{p} K_{n-1}(k(p)) ⊗_Z Q
is injective, where p ranges over the height-one prime ideals of k[t]. For each such p, we have just shown that k(p) is a finite field. Since n > 1, we have n - 1 > 0, so by lemma_14 applied to the finite field k(p) and the positive integer n - 1, we get K_{n-1}(k(p)) ⊗_Z Q = 0. Hence every summand in the direct sum is the zero Q-vector space, and therefore the whole direct sum is zero.

An injective linear map whose codomain is the zero vector space has zero domain: if x lies in the domain, its image is 0, and injectivity implies x = 0. Consequently K_n(k(t)) ⊗_Z Q = 0.

lemma_156_galois_tensor_intertwining.statement: Let F be a field, let M/F be a finite Galois extension with Galois group G, and let m \ge 1. Define \theta: M^m \otimes_F M \to \bigoplus_{\sigma \in G} M^m by \theta(v \otimes y) = (\sigma(v) y)_{\sigma \in G}, where \sigma acts entrywise on v \in M^m, where M^m \otimes_F M is an M-module via the second factor, and where \bigoplus_{\sigma \in G} M^m is an M-module componentwise. Then \theta is an isomorphism of M-modules and, for every A \in \mathrm{GL}_m(M), \theta \circ (A \otimes 1) = (\bigoplus_{\sigma \in G} \sigma(A)) \circ \theta.
lemma_156_galois_tensor_intertwining.proof:
Let r = [M:F] = |G|.

(1) Well-definedness and linearity. The map \beta: M^m \times M \to \bigoplus_{\sigma \in G} M^m, \beta(v,y) = (\sigma(v) y)_{\sigma \in G}, is F-bilinear: for a \in F, \sigma(v a) y = \sigma(v) \sigma(a) y = \sigma(v) (a y) because \sigma fixes F and M is commutative; additivity in each variable follows from the additivity of \sigma and of multiplication in M. Hence \beta descends to a group homomorphism \theta: M^m \otimes_F M \to \bigoplus_{\sigma} M^m. Moreover, \theta is M-linear for the stated module structures: \theta((v \otimes y) w) = \theta(v \otimes y w) = (\sigma(v) y w)_\sigma = \theta(v \otimes y) w.

(2) Reduction to m=1. Under the natural M-module isomorphisms M^m \otimes_F M \cong (M \otimes_F M)^m, v \otimes y \mapsto (v_1 \otimes y, \ldots, v_m \otimes y), and \bigoplus_{\sigma} M^m \cong (\bigoplus_{\sigma} M)^m, (z_\sigma)_\sigma \mapsto ((z_\sigma)_1)_\sigma, \ldots, ((z_\sigma)_m)_\sigma, the map \theta is the m-fold direct sum of \theta_1: M \otimes_F M \to \bigoplus_{\sigma} M, \theta_1(x \otimes y) = (\sigma(x) y)_\sigma. (To verify: for v = (v_1,\ldots,v_m) and y \in M, the j-th component of \theta(v \otimes y) under the second isomorphism is (\sigma(v_j) y)_\sigma = \theta_1(v_j \otimes y).) Thus \theta is an isomorphism if and only if \theta_1 is.

(3) The case m=1. Since M/F is finite Galois, it is finite separable, so by the primitive element theorem M = F(\alpha) for some \alpha \in M. Let e_i = \alpha^i for 0 \le i \le r-1; then \{e_i\} is an F-basis of M.

First, \{e_i \otimes 1\} is an M-basis of M \otimes_F M (action on the second factor). Generation: if x = \sum_i a_i e_i with a_i \in F, then x \otimes y = \sum_i (e_i \otimes 1)(a_i y). Independence: if \sum_i (e_i \otimes 1) c_i = 0 with c_i \in M, write c_i = \sum_j b_{ij} e_j with b_{ij} \in F; then \sum_{i,j} b_{ij} e_i \otimes e_j = 0, and \{e_i \otimes e_j\} is an F-basis of M \otimes_F M, so c_i = 0.

Now consider \theta_1(e_i \otimes 1) = (\sigma(\alpha)^i)_\sigma. Suppose \sum_i c_i \theta_1(e_i \otimes 1) = 0 with c_i \in M. Then for each \sigma \in G, \sum_i c_i \sigma(\alpha)^i = 0. Let V be the r \times r matrix with V_{\sigma,i} = \sigma(\alpha)^i (rows indexed by \sigma, columns by i). Ordering G as \{\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r\}, the determinant of V is the Vandermonde product \det(V) = \prod_{1 \le i < j \le r} (\sigma_j(\alpha) - \sigma_i(\alpha)). Since M = F(\alpha), distinct \sigma, \tau \in G satisfy \sigma(\alpha) \ne \tau(\alpha) (otherwise \sigma and \tau agree on \alpha, hence on F(\alpha) = M). Thus every factor is nonzero in the field M, so \det(V) \ne 0. Hence V is invertible over M, and the equations force c_i = 0. Therefore the vectors \theta_1(e_i \otimes 1) are M-linearly independent.

As \theta_1 is M-linear and maps the M-basis \{e_i \otimes 1\} to an M-linearly independent set of r elements in the free M-module \bigoplus_{\sigma} M of rank r, \theta_1 is injective. Both M \otimes_F M and \bigoplus_{\sigma} M are free M-modules of rank r, so \theta_1 is an isomorphism.

(4) By (2), \theta is an isomorphism of M-modules.

(5) Intertwining. Let A \in \mathrm{GL}_m(M). We show \theta \circ (A \otimes 1) = (\bigoplus_{\sigma} \sigma(A)) \circ \theta. It suffices to check on simple tensors v \otimes y, since the simple tensors generate M^m \otimes_F M as an abelian group and both sides are group homomorphisms. Compute:
\theta((A \otimes 1)(v \otimes y)) = \theta(A v \otimes y) = (\sigma(A v) y)_\sigma.
Since \sigma is a ring automorphism, \sigma(A v) = \sigma(A) \sigma(v) entrywise, so (\sigma(A v) y)_\sigma = (\sigma(A) \sigma(v) y)_\sigma.
On the other hand,
((\bigoplus_{\sigma} \sigma(A)) \theta(v \otimes y))_\sigma = \sigma(A) (\sigma(v) y) = \sigma(A) \sigma(v) y.
Thus the two expressions coincide for each \sigma, so the equality holds on simple tensors, hence everywhere.

This completes the proof.

lemma_157.statement: Let f:Y \to X be a finite locally free morphism of rank r \ge 1 between regular noetherian schemes, let n > 0, and suppose f_*\mathcal O_Y is isomorphic to \mathcal O_X^{\oplus r}. Then the endomorphism (1/r) f^* \circ f_* of K_n(Y)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q, with f^* the pullback and f_* the transfer, is idempotent.
lemma_157.proof:
Let f:Y -> X be a finite locally free morphism of rank r >= 1 between regular noetherian schemes, let n > 0, and suppose f_* O_Y is isomorphic to O_X^{\oplus r}. We prove that the Q-linear endomorphism P := (1/r) f^* \circ f_* of K_n(Y) \otimes_Z Q is idempotent, i.e. P^2 = P.

(1) The maps are Q-linear. The pullback f^*: K_n(X) -> K_n(Y) and the transfer f_*: K_n(Y) -> K_n(X) (the transfer for a finite locally free morphism, exactly as it appears in lemma_58) are group homomorphisms. Tensoring with Q, they extend uniquely to Q-linear maps f^*: K_n(X)\otimes Q -> K_n(Y)\otimes Q and f_*: K_n(Y)\otimes Q -> K_n(X)\otimes Q. Define A := f^* \circ f_*: K_n(Y)\otimes Q -> K_n(Y)\otimes Q; then P = (1/r) A.

(2) The class of f_* O_Y in K_0(X). Since f is finite locally free of rank r, f_* O_Y is a vector bundle on X. The hypothesis gives an isomorphism f_* O_Y \cong O_X^{\oplus r}, so their classes in the Grothendieck group K_0(X) coincide: [f_* O_Y] = [O_X^{\oplus r}]. By additivity of the class under direct sums, [O_X^{\oplus r}] = r [O_X]. Hence [f_* O_Y] = r [O_X] in K_0(X).

(3) Apply lemma_58. Taking X' = Y in lemma_58, the condition that the class of f_* O_Y in K_0(X) equals r [O_X] holds by (2). Therefore the composite f_* \circ f^*: K_n(X)\otimes Q -> K_n(X)\otimes Q is multiplication by r; i.e. f_* \circ f^* = r \cdot id_{K_n(X)\otimes Q}.

(4) Compute A^2. By associativity of composition, A^2 = (f^* \circ f_*) \circ (f^* \circ f_*) = f^* \circ (f_* \circ f^*) \circ f_*. Substituting (3), A^2 = f^* \circ (r \cdot id) \circ f_*. Since f^* is a group homomorphism, f^*(r \cdot x) = r \cdot f^*(x) for every x in K_n(X)\otimes Q, so f^* \circ (r \cdot id) = r \cdot f^*; hence A^2 = r \cdot (f^* \circ f_*) = r A.

(5) Conclude. P^2 = ((1/r) A)^2 = (1/r^2) A^2 = (1/r^2)(r A) = (1/r) A = P. Thus P = (1/r) f^* \circ f_* is idempotent.

Edge case r = 1: then f_* O_Y \cong O_X, and a finite locally free morphism of rank 1 whose pushforward of the structure sheaf is O_X is an isomorphism; consequently f^* and f_* are mutually inverse Q-linear maps, so A = f^* \circ f_* = id and P = id is idempotent. This is consistent with the argument above (Step 3 gives f_* f^* = id, Step 4 gives A^2 = A). The proof is complete.

lemma_154_proj_colimit.statement: Let I be a directed set, let (R_i)_{i \in I} be a diagram of rings indexed by I, and let R = \operatorname{colim}_{i \in I} R_i. For a ring A, let \operatorname{proj}(A) denote the category of finitely generated projective A-modules. Then the canonical functor \operatorname{colim}_{i \in I} \operatorname{proj}(R_i) \to \operatorname{proj}(R) is an equivalence of categories.
lemma_154_proj_colimit.proof: Proof. We fix the convention that A-modules are left A-modules; the right-module convention is identical with the roles of left and right interchanged. All rings are associative unital rings and all homomorphisms preserve 1. For i≤j write φ_{ij}:R_i→R_j, and put R=colim_i R_i. For a ring A, A^m denotes the column free left A-module of rank m. A matrix E∈M_m(A) acts on A^m by right multiplication, x↦xE; this action is left A-linear, and E is idempotent as an endomorphism iff E^2=E. An idempotent e∈M_m(A) determines the direct summand A^m e={xE:x∈A^m}. Every finitely generated projective left A-module P is isomorphic to A^m e for some m and idempotent e: choose a surjection A^m→P; projectivity gives a section P→A^m, so P is a direct summand. If π:A^m→P and ι:P→A^m are the projection and inclusion with πι=id_P, then e=ιπ is an idempotent in End_A(A^m), hence is right multiplication by a unique idempotent matrix e∈M_m(A), and im(e)=P. We record two matrix facts. Fact 1. If P=A^m e and Q=A^n f with e∈M_m(A), f∈M_n(A) idempotents, then Hom_A(P,Q) is naturally bijective to eM_{m,n}(A)f:={C∈M_{m,n}(A):C=eCf}. Here M_{m,n} means m rows and n columns, so xC is defined for x∈A^m and gives a vector in A^n. Proof of Fact 1. Given φ:P→Q, extend it to A^m by composing with the projection A^m→P; after including Q in A^n, this extension is right multiplication by a unique B∈M_{m,n}(A). The condition that the image of A^m e lies in A^n f says (x e B) f=x e B for all x∈A^m, i.e. e B f=e B. Put C=e B f=e B; then C=e C f, and φ(x e)=x C. Conversely, if C=e C f, the formula φ_C(x e)=x C is well defined (if x e=y e then (x-y)e C=0), A-linear, and its image lies in A^n f because x C=x e C f=(x C) f. If φ_C=φ_D, then x e(C-D)=0 for all x∈A^m, hence e(C-D)=0; since C-D=e(C-D)f, C-D=0. This proves the bijection, and it is compatible with ring homomorphisms because the formulas are entrywise. Fact 2. For a ring homomorphism α:A→B, B⊗_A(A^m e)≅B^m e_B, where e_B is the image of e in M_m(B). Indeed, A^m e is a direct summand of A^m, so B⊗_A A^m e is a direct summand of B⊗_A A^m. The isomorphism B⊗_A A^m≅B^m via b⊗x↦b x identifies this direct summand with B^m e_B. Consequently, by Fact 1, Hom_B(B⊗_A P,B⊗_A Q)≅e_B M_{m,n}(B) f_B whenever P=A^m e and Q=A^n f. Now let C=colim_i proj(R_i) with its usual definition: objects are pairs (i,P_i), and Hom_C((i,P_i),(j,Q_j))=colim_{k≥i,j} Hom_{R_k}(R_k⊗_{R_i}P_i,R_k⊗_{R_j}Q_j). The canonical functor F:C→proj(R) sends (i,P_i) to R⊗_{R_i}P_i and a class (k,φ) to R⊗_{R_k}φ. This is well defined: if two representatives of a morphism become equal after passing to a common later stage, their base changes to R are equal. We first prove essential surjectivity. Let P be a finitely generated projective left R-module. By the paragraph above, P≅R^m e for an idempotent e∈M_m(R). Each entry of e lies in R=colim R_i, so for the finitely many entries there is a stage i_0 with a lift e_{i_0}∈M_m(R_{i_0}). The equation e_{i_0}^2=e_{i_0} has finitely many entries; each entry is zero in R, hence is zero at some stage. By directedness there is k≥i_0 such that e_k^2=e_k in M_m(R_k), where e_k is the image of e_{i_0}. Then P_k=R_k^m e_k is finitely generated projective over R_k, and by Fact 2, R⊗_{R_k}P_k≅R^m e≅P. Thus P is isomorphic to F(k,P_k). Next prove full faithfulness. Fix (i,P_i) and (j,Q_j). Choose isomorphisms P_i≅R_i^m e_i and Q_j≅R_j^n f_j with e_i,f_j idempotents. For k≥i,j, let e_{i,k},f_{j,k} be their images in R_k. By Fact 2 and Fact 1, Hom_{R_k}(R_k⊗_{R_i}P_i,R_k⊗_{R_j}Q_j) is identified with e_{i,k}M_{m,n}(R_k)f_{j,k}, and the transition maps in the colimit are the evident ones induced by the ring homomorphisms. Since a matrix has finitely many entries, colim_k M_{m,n}(R_k)≅M_{m,n}(R). Under this identification, Hom_C((i,P_i),(j,Q_j)) is the filtered colimit of the sets e_{i,k}M_{m,n}(R_k)f_{j,k}. We claim that this filtered colimit is exactly e_{i,R}M_{m,n}(R)f_{j,R}. Inclusion of the colimit in the target is immediate: if C_k=e_{i,k}C_k f_{j,k}, its image C in R satisfies C=e_{i,R}C f_{j,R}. For the reverse inclusion, let C∈M_{m,n}(R) satisfy C=e_{i,R}C f_{j,R}. All mn entries of C come from some common stage k_0≥i,j, so choose a lift C_{k_0}∈M_{m,n}(R_{k_0}). For each entry of the matrix C_{k_0}-e_{i,k_0}C_{k_0}f_{j,k_0}, the image in R is zero; hence each entry is zero at some stage. Since there are finitely many entries and I is directed, there is k≥k_0 such that e_{i,k}C_k f_{j,k}=C_k, where C_k is the image of C_{k_0}. Thus C is represented in the filtered colimit by an element of e_{i,k}M_{m,n}(R_k)f_{j,k}. This proves the claim. Finally, under the identifications R⊗_{R_i}P_i≅R^m e_{i,R} and R⊗_{R_j}Q_j≅R^n f_{j,R}, Fact 1 gives Hom_R(F(i,P_i),F(j,Q_j))≅e_{i,R}M_{m,n}(R)f_{j,R}. By the claim this is canonically the same as Hom_C((i,P_i),(j,Q_j)), and the identification is precisely the one induced by F (a matrix C_k at stage k maps to its image C in R). Hence F is fully faithful. Since F is essentially surjective and fully faithful, it is an equivalence of categories. QED.
